with the external auditor, Head of Group Internal Audit, CEO and Group Executive 
Committee, assisting the Board in work to evaluate and ensuring the reliability 
and effectiveness of financial reporting, which includes sustainability reporting. 
The Audit Committee ensures, among other things, that the bank’s CEO estab -
lishes and maintains effective procedures for risk management and internal con-trols of the Group’s financial and sustainability reporting. This is among the mea -
sures the Board takes to monitor the internal control in connection with financial 
and sustainability reporting is working properly.
The tasks of the Governance Committee include assisting the Board of Direc-
tors in monitoring, evaluating and ensuring that Swedbank’s governance model 
and processes are effective and appropriate, and ensuring that they are adopted 
in a way that enables effective governance and control.
The Risk and Capital Committee supports the Board in its work to ensure that 
procedures are in place to identify, assess, manage and report risks in business activities, and to assess and monitor risks faced by the Group based on the risk 
appetite adopted by the Board. The responsibilities of the Risk and Capital 
 Committee include sustainability-related risks, including risks identified through 
Swedbank’s materiality assessment. 
Regarding the delegation of areas of responsibility for impacts, risks and 
opportunities within the Board's committees, the Remuneration and Sustain -
ability Committee has the overall responsibility for sustainability matters, and 
for employees, while the Risk and Capital Committee is responsible for matters 
concerning risks in relation to consumers and end users, such as information 
security, cybersecurity and financial crime. All committees are responsible for 
business conduct.
Additional information about the Board’s committees is presented in the Cor -
porate Governance Report under the section entitled The Board’s committees.
Competence in sustainability matters
The Board’s competence is assessed partly by the Nomination Committee in 
 connection with the nomination of Board members, and partly through the annual 
internal Board evaluation. A member of the Remuneration and Sustainability 
Committee has been appointed to maintain a special focus on sustainability mat-
ters. New Board members undergo introductory training in which they are given 
in-depth information about the Group’s organisation and operations, the control 
functions as well as Swedbank’s corporate governance framework and model. 
Issues relating to the Group's organisation, as well as Swedbank's corporate gov-
ernance framework and model are primarily discussed in the Governance Com -
mittee. New members of the Board also undergo Nasdaq’s Board training pro-
gramme, which covers topics including stock exchange regulations. 
The Board receives training in sustainability-related issues, and various units 
within the Group support the Board and management with expertise, as the 
requirements for sustainability competence on the Board increase. Sustainability 
training is one of Group Sustainability’s primary tasks, as is regularly informing 
the Board about sustainability work in the Group. Group Sustainability provides 
regular information in respect of Swedbank’s sustainable business transactions, primarily to the Remuneration and Sustainability Committee. Group Finance pro -
vides the Board’s Audit Committee with continuous information related to sus-tainability reporting. The Board also ensures that specific training initiatives are 
carried out as necessary. The Board underwent in-depth training in the areas of 
anti-corruption and bribery in 2022. In 2024, the Board also underwent the ethics 
training programme that is mandatory for employees, which includes a section 
on anti-corruption and bribery. During the year, the Board’s training programmes focused on current sustainability regulations, including the CSRD. General com -
petence within the Group with regard to sustainability is reviewed as new regula -
tions that affect the Group come into force. Business Areas and Group Functions 
are responsible for ensuring that the correct knowledge and competence are in 
place, with training as one of the tools applied.
CEO and Group Executive Committee
Swedbank’s Group Executive Committee consists of 15 members, all of whom have operational roles in the bank. The gender distribution of the Group Executive 
Committee is 47 per cent women and 53 per cent men. In order to increase the 
Group’s focus on diversity and inclusion, the Group Executive Committee has 
a Chief Diversity Officer function, which rotates within the Group Executive 
 Committee for two years. The Group’s Chief Information Officer and Head of 
Group Channels and Technologies was appointed Group Chief Diversity Officer 
during the year.
The CEO is responsible for executing, implementing and following up opera-
tions based on strategies decided by the Board, i.e. to ensure that Swedbank fol-
lows its strategic direction. To monitor this, the CEO has sustainability-related key 
indicators that are reported semi-annually to the Board. Corresponding KPIs for 
Business Areas, Product Areas and Group Functions are reported quarterly to the CEO. The CEO is responsible for the Group’s position statements on business issues linked to the defence industry and climate change, as well as instructions 
to support the implementation of the Group’s policies. Swedbank’s position state -
ments specify how sustainability is integrated in business decisions, and are 
more operational than Swedbank’s policies. 
The CEO has established a number of committees to gather expertise for the 
preparation of various matters. With a few exceptions, the committees do not have 
any collective decision-making authority; instead, decisions are taken by the chair 
of each committee or escalated to the CEO. The following committees established 
by the CEO, are illustrated in the map of Sustainability Governance:
The Group Asset Allocation Committee's responsibilities include managing 
the Group's financial risks. Sustainability factors must be considered across all risk types as well as in all risk management. Swedbank's Group Chief Financial 
Officer is the chair and decision-maker of the committee. Depending on the 
nature of the matter, the Group Asset Allocation Committee may provide recom -
mendations before decisions are escalated to the appropriate body, such as the Head of Group Risk, the CEO, or the Board.
Group Risk and Compliance Committee.  The purpose of the committee is to 
acquire and communicate a holistic view of the Group’s non-financial risks, and also to ensure consistent and appropriate governance within the risk area and 
contribute to a sound risk culture. Sustainability factors must be considered in 
all risk types and also in all risk management. The Head of Group Risk chairs the 
committee. Depending on the matter in hand, the Head of Group Risk or the Head 
of Group Compliance is the decision-maker in the committee. Depending on the nature of the matter, the Group Risk and Compliance Committee may recom -
mend escalating decisions to an appropriate body, such as the CEO or the Board. 
Sustainability Committee.  The Sustainability Committee provides support for 
the effective management and governance of the sustainability perspective within the Group. The Head of Group Brand, Communication & Sustainability, who 
is a member of the Group Executive Committee, chairs the committee. Other 
members include the Head of Group Sustainability and representatives from Group Compliance and Group Risk. The committee’s chairman makes decisions 
in the committee, but can also issue recommendations and, depending on the 
nature of the matter, escalate matters to the CEO for a decision. All Business 
Areas, Product Areas and Group Functions have the opportunity to escalate 
issues to the committee. 
ESG Reporting Forum.  The ESG Reporting Forum has been established to 
ensure reviews of, and to be a governing body for, operational ESG reporting issues at Group level. This includes approving the adoption of interpretations, 
definitions and assessments relating to ESG reporting. The Head of Group 
Finance is the chair and decision-maker of the committee. 
Sustainable Bond Committee.  The Sustainable Bond Committee has been 
established as a decision-making body to approve whether a proposed loan 
should constitute a green or social asset and thus be included in Swedbank’s 
Sustainable Asset Registry. The Head of Group Sustainability chairs the 
 committee and holds the right of veto. However, decisions are made by  
a majority of the members of the Sustainable Bond Committee.
Swedbank uses reporting channels that are already in place for information 
to the Board and the CEO relating to impacts, risks and opportunities, and there -
fore does not have a specific position within GEC to fulfil this responsibility.
Reporting on special controls and how procedures are applied to manage 
impacts, risks and opportunities, as well as how they are integrated with other internal functions, is described in the reporting of each thematic chapter under the paragraph entitled “Metrics and targets”. 
Information on how the Board and the CEO supervise the establishment of 
 targets, and monitor progress towards the targets linked to significant impacts, 
risks and opportunities, is found in each thematic chapter under the paragraph entitled “Metrics and targets”.
For E1 Climate change, equivalent reporting is found in the section  entitled 
GOV-1 Role of the Board of Directors and management. Regarding the monitoring 
of progress, there is additional reporting for S1 Own workforce,  T argets 1–5.

title: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by the undertaking’s Board of Directors and CEO
heading: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by the undertaking’s Board of Directors and CEO, GOV-2
start_phrase: The Board and the CEO, including relevant committees, are regularly informed about material impacts, risks and opportunities by relevant units.
summary:
- Governance structure and committee mandates:
  - Audit Committee: Oversees reliability and effectiveness of financial and sustainability reporting; ensures CEO maintains effective risk management and internal controls for these areas.
  - Governance Committee: Monitors and evaluates the effectiveness and appropriateness of Swedbank’s governance model and processes.
  - Risk and Capital Committee: Ensures procedures exist to identify, assess, manage and report risks, including sustainability-related risks identified via materiality assessment; responsible for risks affecting consumers/end users (information security, cybersecurity, financial crime).
  - Remuneration and Sustainability Committee: Overall responsibility for sustainability matters and employees.
  - All Board committees share responsibility for business conduct. Further details are in the Corporate Governance Report.

- Board sustainability competence and training:
  - Competence assessed by the Nomination Committee and through annual Board evaluations; a committee member has a special sustainability focus.
  - New directors receive induction on the Group, control functions, and governance framework; Nasdaq Board training provided.
  - Ongoing sustainability training coordinated by Group Sustainability; regular updates to the Board and committees (e.g., Audit Committee via Group Finance).
  - Recent focus areas: anti-corruption and bribery (in-depth training in 2022; ethics training incl. anti-corruption in 2024), current sustainability regulations (including CSRD). Business Areas and Group Functions ensure needed competencies as regulations evolve.

- CEO and Group Executive Committee (GEC):
  - GEC has 15 operational members; gender distribution 47% women, 53% men. Rotating Chief Diversity Officer function; during the year the CIO/Head of Group Channels and Technologies served in the role.
  - CEO executes Board strategy, with sustainability KPIs reported semi-annually to the Board; Business Areas/Product Areas/Group Functions report quarterly KPIs to the CEO.
  - CEO sets position statements on defense industry and climate change and issues instructions to implement policies.

- CEO-established committees integrating sustainability:
  - Group Asset Allocation Committee (chaired by CFO): Manages financial risks with sustainability considered across all risk types; can recommend escalation to Head of Group Risk, CEO, or Board.
  - Group Risk and Compliance Committee (chaired by Head of Group Risk): Holistic view of non-financial risks; embeds sustainability across risk types; decisions by Head of Group Risk or Head of Group Compliance; escalation to CEO/Board as needed.
  - Sustainability Committee (chaired by Head of Group Brand, Communication & Sustainability): Supports effective management/governance of sustainability; decisions by chair with escalation to CEO; open escalation channel from all Business Areas, Product Areas and Group Functions.
  - ESG Reporting Forum (chaired by Head of Group Finance): Governs operational ESG reporting issues, interpretations, definitions, and assessments.
  - Sustainable Bond Committee (chaired by Head of Group Sustainability with veto right): Decides on eligibility of loans as green/social assets for the Sustainable Asset Registry by majority vote.

- Reporting and oversight of impacts, risks, and opportunities (GOV-2):
  - Board and CEO receive regular information on material impacts, risks and opportunities, stakeholder views, due diligence implementation, and effectiveness of policies, measures, metrics and targets.
  - In 2024, quarterly reporting to the CEO, GEC and Board covered implementation of new sustainability reporting regulations.
  - Risk management processes for impacts/risks/opportunities described in IRO-1; Climate-related governance also reported under GOV-1; S1 Own workforce targets reported under S1-5.
  - Regular reporting on conflicts of interest and corruption; Corporate Governance Report lists topics discussed by the Board, CEO and GEC.
  - Material topics discussed in 2024 included climate change mitigation/adaptation, energy, working conditions, equal opportunities, employment rights, consumer information impacts, corporate culture, whistleblower protection, supplier relationship management and payment practices, corruption/bribery, and financial crime.

- Incentives and targets (GOV-3 and E1 GOV-3):
  - Board, CEO and GEC are excluded from Swedbank’s variable remuneration program; Board sets overarching sustainability targets aligned with strategy.
  - GEC is evaluated on sustainability metrics (e.g., employee engagement, net-zero by 2050, portfolio alignment with 1.5°C, increased sustainable financing) but without variable pay linkage.
  - Climate-related considerations are not factored into remuneration for Swedbank or for Swedbank Robur Fonder’s Board/management.

- Due diligence statement (GOV-4):
  - Due diligence is integrated throughout the Sustainability Report, covering:
    - Integration into governance, strategy and business model.
    - Stakeholder engagement across due diligence steps.
    - Identification and assessment of adverse impacts.
    - Actions to address adverse impacts.
    - Monitoring effectiveness and communicating outcomes.
  - Cross-references to ESRS disclosure requirements (ESRS 2, E1, S1, S4, G1) and relevant report sections/pages are provided.

- Additional notes:
  - Existing reporting channels to the Board/CEO are used for impacts/risks/opportunities; no dedicated GEC position for this.
  - Committee decision-making is generally by the chair with escalation paths; most committees are advisory except where specified.
  - Thematic chapters contain “Metrics and targets” sections detailing controls, procedures, targets and monitoring for each material topic.

title: Risk management and internal controls - Introduction
heading: Risk management and internal controls, GOV-5
start_phrase: The Board of Directors has overarching responsibility for ensuring that Swed-bank’s sustainability reporting is conducted in accordance with current legisla -tion.
summary: Overview of Swedbank’s governance and controls for sustainability reporting (GOV-5): the Board holds ultimate responsibility for compliance with legislation, while Group Finance (CFO Office) coordinates consolidation and the CSRD-aligned double materiality assessment with Group Functions and external experts. In 2024, Swedbank began developing risk assessments and internal controls for sustainability reporting, integrating them into ICFR, with initial focus on mapping processes, high-risk areas, and controls under ESRS E1 and S1, expanding to additional material ESRS in 2025. Key reporting risks identified are poor data quality, extensive manual handling, and incorrect consolidation; targeted control activities include system support, data validation for uncertain-quality data, duality controls in manual handling, manager-led validations and reconciliations, and ongoing reasonableness checks with random sampling. EU Taxonomy controls were enhanced, applying EBA definitions (e.g., property-collateralized loans) and establishing reconciliations with EBA reports and Pillar 3 (e.g., building energy classes). Continuous evaluation seeks to improve procedures and data availability via supplier requirements and engagement. Implementation progress and internal controls will be reported regularly to the CEO and, from Q4 2024, to the Board.
text:
Risk management and internal controls, GOV-5 
The Board of Directors has overarching responsibility for ensuring that Swed-
bank’s sustainability reporting is conducted in accordance with current legisla -
tion. Internally, Group Finance, part of the Group Function CFO Office, coordinates the work to consolidate the information for the sustainability report and to ensure 
that the double materiality assessment is conducted in accordance with the 
requirements that follow from CSRD. The assessments in the analysis and parts 
of the reporting are conducted in close collaboration with Group Functions that 
have relevant subject matter expertise.
Swedbank has an established support and control process to identify, address 
and implement new and/or amended legislation. Both the CSRD and the EU Tax-onomy have been managed in accordance with this process. In 2024, Swedbank 
started internal work to develop risk assessments and internal controls for the 
main risks related to sustainability reporting. This work also includes the integra-
tion of these new controls into existing internal control processes in accordance 
with ICFR. The main focus has been on mapping the reporting processes, identi -
fying areas posing the greatest risk within these processes and establishing ini -
tial internal controls. These efforts are aimed at improving and quality-assuring reporting. The project covered the ESRS standards E1 and S1, with the aim of 
gradually expanding these controls to include more material ESRS standards. 
This work will continue in 2025.
In its sustainability reporting, Swedbank has identified the following main risks 
of reporting errors: a lack of sufficiently high-quality data, high levels of manual handling and incorrect consolidation of data. To manage these risks, Swedbank 
is conducting an overall analysis focusing on the areas where there is the highest 
risk of reporting errors. This is to enable control activities to be implemented 
 specifically for these areas.
To establish a solid basis for the continued implementation of regulatory 
requirements for sustainability reporting, transparency and comparability, the 
method for the double materiality assessment and its outcome have undergone several rounds of consultation. Internal subject matter experts representing the 
Group have contributed base data and insights to the materiality assessment. 
In addition, Swedbank has consulted external experts to ensure that the double 
materiality assessment is conducted in accordance with current regulatory 
requirements.
Swedbank has started work to establish system support to facilitate future 
reporting. In 2024, controls were designed to validate data for which there is uncertainty in data quality. Furthermore, duality controls were implemented when 
manually handling data or reporting. To avoid the risk of incorrect information 
being reported, control validations and reconciliations are carried out by 
 managers responsible within relevant units for selected areas.
Internal controls for EU Taxonomy reporting were further developed during the 
year. In the EU Taxonomy reporting, Swedbank applies definitions including those from the EBA’s reporting requirements, for example with regard to loans with col-
lateral in property. Reconciliation points have been developed between EU Taxon-
omy reporting and reporting to the EBA’s reporting requirements for the purpose 
of checking consistency. There are also reconciliation points between EU Taxon -
omy reporting and Pillar 3, for example in the form of energy classes for buildings used as collateral for loans. Reasonableness assessments are conducted on an ongoing basis, and random samples are taken from base data where this is 
deemed relevant.
The internal control process is continuously evaluated to improve procedures 
and reduce the risk of incorrect reporting. Work is also under way to increase 
data availability by setting requirements for suppliers and conducting dialogues 
with external data suppliers. The implementation of legal requirements in the 
area of sustainability reporting, including internal controls, will be reported 
 regularly to the CEO via management and to the Board of Directors from the last 
quarter of 2024.

summary:
- Governance and accountability for sustainability reporting: The Board holds ultimate responsibility; Group Finance (CFO Office) coordinates consolidation and ensures the double materiality assessment complies with CSRD, working with subject-matter experts across Group Functions.
- Establishing sustainability reporting controls: In 2024 Swedbank began mapping processes, identifying high-risk areas, and designing initial internal controls under ICFR for ESRS E1 (climate) and S1 (own workforce), with expansion to additional ESRS standards planned in 2025.
- Key reporting risk areas and mitigations: Principal risks include data quality gaps, manual handling, and consolidation errors. Mitigations include targeted control activities, data validation for uncertain data, duality controls for manual steps, and manager-led control validations and reconciliations.
- EU Taxonomy internal control enhancements: Further developed controls include application of EBA-aligned definitions (e.g., property collateral), reconciliations between Taxonomy, EBA reporting, and Pillar 3 (e.g., building energy classes), ongoing reasonableness checks, and sampling.
- Systems and data improvements: Initiated system support for future reporting, enhanced data availability via supplier requirements and engagement with external data providers, and continuous evaluation of internal controls. Implementation progress reported regularly to the CEO and Board from Q4 2024.
- Double materiality methodology: Underwent multiple consultation rounds; internal experts provided inputs and external experts reviewed for regulatory compliance, transparency, and comparability.
- Governance framework overview: Comprehensive suite of policies, instructions, and directives defines processes and responsibilities for managing material impacts, risks, and opportunities. Regulatory framework owners (GEC members or designated security leaders) ensure implementation and follow-up.
- Governance document lifecycle: Annual review and updates incorporate external stakeholder feedback (e.g., AGM inputs) and internal viewpoints to ensure alignment with regulations and the governance model; public documents are published on Swedbank’s website; internal updates are communicated via Group Legal channels.
- Example governance topics: Code of Conduct; Credit Policy integrating ESG risk into credit processes; Environmental and Human Rights Policies; Enterprise Risk Management with ESG as a separate risk type; Diversity, Equity & Inclusion; Financial crime (AML/CTF, sanctions, anti-bribery, anti-fraud); whistleblowing; climate and controversial weapons position statements; work environment; procurement.
- External commitments and collaborations: Swedbank aligns with UN Global Compact, UNEP FI, UN Principles for Responsible Banking, the Net-Zero Banking Alliance, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and UN Women’s Empowerment Principles.

Reporting expanded over time—from eligibility (since 2021) to alignment for climate objectives (2023) and, in 2024, eligibility for the remaining four environmental objectives.

adopted by the Board of Directors, instructions by the CEO and directives by the 
person responsible in Swedbank's Group Executive Committee. Each respective 
regulatory framework owner is responsible for the implementation of and fol-
low-up on their respective regulatory framework. Regulatory owners must always 
be a member of the Group Executive Committee, the Head of Protective Security 
or the Chief Security Officer, unless the Board of Directors or the CEO specifically decides otherwise. 
All governance documents are reviewed annually and updated as required. 
As part of the annual update, the views of external stakeholders are taken into 
consideration, for example through questions asked at the Annual General Meet -
ing (AGM), discussions with organisations or external reports. Internal view-points are taken into account through established processes for the annual review. The review is also intended to ensure the quality of the governance docu -
ments, as well as ensuring that they meet external and internal regulatory require-ments and are aligned with Swedbank’s governance model and organisation. 
Where relevant, it also includes affected stakeholders through an indirect or 
direct dialogue. The terms "upstream" and "downstream" are not usually used in

title: Development of Taxonomy reporting
heading: Development of Taxonomy reporting
start_phrase: Swedbank is subject to the EU Taxonomy Regulation, a classification system that defines the criteria used to determine when economic activities, that are eligible for the EU Taxonomy, can be considered environmentally sustainable.
summary:
- Context and scope: Swedbank reports under the EU Taxonomy Regulation, outlining criteria for environmental sustainability (substantial contribution to one of six objectives, do no significant harm, minimum social safeguards, and technical screening criteria).
- Reporting evolution: Since 2021 Swedbank has reported Taxonomy-eligible assets; in 2023 alignment reporting for climate objectives was added for credit institutions; in 2024 eligibility reporting expands to the remaining four environmental objectives. A new consolidated, segment‑weighted KPI (banking, asset management, insurance) is introduced, with new detailed tables for insurance and asset managers. Non‑financial activities are not aligned but included in the consolidated KPI. Fees/commissions and the trading book will be added to the consolidated KPI in 2025.
- Segment and consolidation treatment: Asset manager table covers Swedbank Robur AB and subsidiaries and provides detail beyond the credit institutions’ AuM line. Life insurance includes Robur‑managed holdings. In credit institution tables, insurance subs are reported as equities in non‑NFRD/CSRD companies (equity method). Detailed EU Taxonomy tables are referenced (pages 144–226).
- Key results as of 31 Dec 2024:
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: 3.37% (turnover) and 3.59% (capex); aligned assets SEK 64 290m (turnover) and SEK 68 504m (capex). Increases driven by better data quality (more mortgage loans shown as aligned) and improved KPIs from NFRD/CSRD companies; inclusion of all six objectives has a positive, though smaller, effect.
  - GAR flow: 3.08% (turnover) and 3.15% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8 412m (turnover) and SEK 8 646m (capex).
  - Asset management green ratio (stock): 1.38% (turnover; SEK 32 571m) and 2.23% (capex; SEK 52 450m). Denominator changed to total AuM, lowering KPIs versus prior year; 2023 restated. Alignment increased with inclusion of financial institutions and all six objectives.
  - Asset management green ratio (flow, first year reported): 1.20% (turnover; SEK 8 299m) and 1.75% (capex; SEK 12 126m).
  - Consolidated KPIs: 3.05% (turnover) and 3.38% (capex).
  - Gas and nuclear KPIs: mostly 0.00%, at most 0.70% for both turnover and capex.
- Data considerations: Reported Taxonomy alignment data remains limited but is expected to improve, affecting both stock and flow KPIs over time.
- Methodology and interpretation: Reporting follows the CRR consolidated situation (differs from IFRS consolidation for insurance, JVs, subsidiaries), with otherwise consistent principles. Swedbank is implementing ongoing EU guidance, engaging via the Swedish Bankers’ Association, and strengthening internal controls. In credit institution tables 3–4, the KPI denominator is Total GAR assets (Total gross carrying amount), while total assets are used for the coverage proportion. Definitions are referenced (page 381), and segment breakdowns for aligned assets are noted (page 78).
text:
Development of Taxonomy reporting
Swedbank is subject to the EU Taxonomy Regulation, a classification system that 
defines the criteria used to determine when economic activities, that are eligible 
for the EU Taxonomy, can be considered environmentally sustainable. The EU 
Taxonomy is a key element of the EU Action Plan for Financing Sustainable 
Growth and provides a framework to help companies identify environmentally 
sustainable investments. For assets to be considered Taxonomy-aligned, the 
underlying economic activity must: 
• contribute substantially to at least one of the EU’s six environmental 
 objectives; 
• do no significant harm to any other environmental objectives; 
• fulfil the social minimum safeguards and
• fulfil the technical screening criteria for a specific environmental objective.
Since 2021, Swedbank has reported its share of EU Taxonomy-eligible assets. In 2023, reporting for credit institutions was expanded to include information 
about the share of assets, financial guarantees and assets under management that are aligned with the EU Taxonomy’s climate objectives. This year, reporting 
will be expanded to include the remaining four environmental objectives in terms 
of  eligibility. 
As a supplement to the main KPIs, Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability 
Report presents for the first time a consolidated KPI, weighted according to Swedbank’s business segments: banking, asset management and insurance, and 
the business segments’ share of the Group’s net income. In connection with this 
change, Swedbank is also introducing tables for insurance and asset manage-
ment. Information from the tables for credit institutions and insurance tables is 
used in the calculation of the consolidated KPI. Income from fees and commis -
sions, as well as trading book will be included in the calculation of the consoli -
dated KPI in the 2025 Annual and Sustainability Report. Swedbank’s non-financial activities are not Taxonomy-aligned but are included in the calculation of the con -
solidated KPI.
The information in the table for the KPI for asset managers is presented for 
Swedbank’s subsidiary, Swedbank Robur AB, including Swedbank Robur AB’s subsidiaries. The table for asset managers is based on the same information as 
in the line for assets under management in Table 1 for credit institutions but is presented in more detail.
The EU Taxonomy-specific tables for life and non-life insurance present details 
regarding the Taxonomy alignment of the insurance operations. In life insurance 
operations, holdings managed by Swedbank Robur AB are also included. In the 
tables for credit institutions, the insurance subsidiaries are reported as equities 
in non-NFRD/CSRD companies according to the equity method.
For tables according to the EU Taxonomy Regulation, see pages 144–226.

title: KPIs
heading: KPIs
start_phrase: The main KPI for banks, the Green Asset Ratio in stock (GAR), aims to increase transparency and accelerate the sustainable transition.

  - Asset management “green ratio” stock: 1.38% (turnover) and 2.23% (capex); alignment of SEK 32,571m (turnover) and SEK 52,450m (capex). Denominator changed to total AUM, lowering KPIs vs. prior method; 2023 figures restated.
  - Asset management flow (first-time): 1.20% (turnover) and 1.75% (capex); alignment of SEK 8,299m (turnover) and SEK 12,126m (capex).

text:
KPIs
The main KPI for banks, the Green Asset Ratio in stock (GAR), aims to increase 
transparency and accelerate the sustainable transition. Swedbank’s GAR is pri-
marily affected by the energy performance of Swedbank’s mortgage portfolio 
and the proportion of environmentally sustainable economic activities of compa -
nies covered by the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD/CSRD) in Swed-bank’s corporate lending.
GAR was 3.37 per cent (1.36) in respect of turnover and 3.59 per cent (1.41) 
in respect of capex as of 31 December 2024. In 2024, Taxonomy alignment increased in the stock to SEK 64 290 million (25 470) for assets in respect of turn-
over and SEK 68 504 million (26 505) in respect of capex. A table with taxonomy 
aligned assets per operating segment both in respect of turnover and capex is 
found on page 78. The largest increase of Taxonomy aligned assets is explained 
by improved data quality and that Swedbank thereby has been able to demon-
strate Taxonomy alignment in more loans to households collateralised by resi -
dential immovable property. Another contributing factor is improved KPIs from 
NFRD/CSRD companies. For example, for 2024, all six environmental objectives 
were included, as opposed to 2023, when only the climate objectives were included. Despite that the majority of Taxonomy alignment is found whitin the 
 climate objectives the inclusion of the four environmental objectives has some 
 positive effect.
GAR flow is 3.08 per cent (2.00) in respect of turnover and 3.15 per cent (1.96) 
in respect of capex as of 31 December 2024. During 2024 Taxonomy alignment has increased in flow to SEK 8 412 million (5 994) for assets in respect of turn-
over and to SEK 8 646 (5 886) in respect of capex.
Green ratio for assets under management in the stock is 1.38 per cent (0.96) 
in respect of turnover and 2.23 (1.53) in respect of capex as of 31 December 
2024. In 2024 the green ratio for assets under management has increased to 
SEK 32 571 million (19 515) for assets in respect of turnover and to SEK 52 450 million (31 107) in respect of capex. The denominator in the calculation of these 
figures has been changed to include total assets under management, resulting 
in lower KPIs compared with the preceding year. These KPIs are impacted by the 
underlying holdings in funds and discretionary portfolio management, as well as 
their investment strategies. For 2023, the green ratio for assets under manage -
ment was calculated in relation to investments in NFRD/CSRD companies, but for 2024, the KPI was calculated in relation to total investments. The key figures for 2023 have therefore been adjusted. 
In 2024, Taxonomy alignment in asset management increased. A contributing 
factor is that financial institutions’ Taxonomy alignment was included in this 
year’s reporting. Furthermore, all six environmental objectives were included in 
2024, unlike in 2023 when only the climate objectives were included. Although 
the majority of Taxonomy alignment is within the climate objectives, the inclusion 
of the four new objectives has a certain positive effect.
The reporting for 2024 includes for the first time the flow for asset manage -
ment, which shows the Taxonomy alignment of investments made during the year. The green ratio for assets under management for flow is 1.20 per cent in 
respect of turnover and 1.75 per cent in respect of capex. In 2024 the Taxonomy 
alignment in flow was SEK 8 299 million for assets in respect of turnover and 
SEK 12 126  million in respect of capex.
Data availability on reported Taxonomy alignment is still limited but is 
expected to increase in the future, thereby affecting the key figures for stock 
and flow.
The consolidated KPIs are 3.05 per cent in respect of turnover and 3.38 per 
cent in respect of capex as of 31 December 2024. The KPIs for gas and nuclear, 
reflecting Swedbank’s assets, financial guarantees, and assets under manage-
ment related to economic activities in gas and nuclear, are mostly 0.00 per cent 
and at most 0.70 per cent for both turnover and capex.

title: Interpretation and implementation
heading: Interpretation and implementation
start_phrase: EU Taxonomy reporting is based on the consolidated situation as defined in Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 of the European Parliament and the Council on prudential requirements for credit institutions.
summary:
- Purpose and framework: Explains Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy reporting, the criteria for alignment (substantial contribution, do no significant harm, minimum safeguards, technical screening), and the Taxonomy’s role in financing sustainable growth.

- Reporting development and scope:
  - Since 2021: reporting of Taxonomy-eligible assets.
  - 2023: expanded to Taxonomy-aligned disclosure for credit institutions (climate objectives) and assets under management (AUM).
  - 2024: eligibility expanded to all six environmental objectives; first-time introduction of a consolidated KPI weighted by business segments (banking, asset management, insurance) by share of Group net income; first-time detailed tables for insurance and asset management.
  - 2025: fees, commissions and trading book to be included in consolidated KPI.
  - Non-financial activities are not Taxonomy-aligned but are included in the consolidated KPI denominator.
  - Separate standardised tables provided for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities in nuclear and fossil gas; additional consolidated KPIs by segment.

- Key KPIs and results (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – stock: 3.37% (turnover), 3.59% (capex); aligned assets SEK 64,290m (turnover) and SEK 68,504m (capex).
  - GAR – flow: 3.08% (turnover), 3.15% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8,412m (turnover) and SEK 8,646m (capex).
  - AUM green ratio – stock: 1.38% (turnover), 2.23% (capex); aligned assets SEK 32,571m (turnover) and SEK 52,450m (capex). Denominator changed to total AUM, lowering KPIs vs prior year; 2023 figures restated.
  - AUM green ratio – flow (first-time): 1.20% (turnover), 1.75% (capex); aligned flow SEK 8,299m (turnover) and SEK 12,126m (capex).
  - Consolidated KPIs: 3.05% (turnover), 3.38% (capex).
  - Gas and nuclear KPIs mostly 0.00%, at most 0.70% for turnover/capex.
  - Increases mainly driven by better data quality (especially mortgages), inclusion of all six environmental objectives, and improved KPIs from NFRD/CSRD companies; inclusion of financial institutions’ alignment in AUM also contributed.

- Methodology, interpretation and governance:
  - Reporting based on the “consolidated situation” under CRR (EU 575/2013), which differs from IFRS consolidation for certain entities; otherwise consistent principles.
  - Denominators: in credit institution tables 3–4, Total GAR assets (total gross carrying amount) for KPI calculations; “proportion of total assets covered” uses total assets.
  - Ongoing implementation work, interpretation clarifications, internal controls, and participation in industry working groups (Swedish Bankers’ Association).
  - Quarterly monitoring of alignment/KPIs by Business Areas; updates to customer processes and products to evidence loan-level alignment.
  - Climate strategy linkage: increasing Taxonomy-aligned assets supports 2030 financed emissions targets (e.g., commercial properties, mortgages); some funds commit to minimum Taxonomy alignment; Taxonomy used as a key tool in asset management and for climate targets.

- Loans collateralised by residential immovable property:
  - Largest source of Taxonomy-eligible assets; energy efficiency in housing is central to emissions reduction.
  - Alignment criteria differ by build date:
    - Pre-31 Dec 2020: within top 15% primary energy or energy class A.
    - Post-31 Dec 2020: at least 10% below NZEB threshold.
  - DNSH for climate adaptation assessed via climate risk assessments (aligned with Pillar 3 methodology); external data provider used; both energy compliance and low climate risk required.
  - Swedish thresholds based on Fastighetsägarna; analogous approach in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania.

- Dependence on NFRD/CSRD company data:
  - Financial institutions rely on counterparties’ Taxonomy reporting; external provider used to source corporates’ data.
  - Corporate lending: 24% of assets, but only 2% are NFRD/CSRD reporters, limiting alignment.
  - AUM: 35% invested in NFRD/CSRD companies; global/ex-EU and small/mid-cap strategies reduce alignment.

- Data availability and quality challenges:
  - No central database; external data gaps/quality issues for corporate KPIs and property energy data; lack of “use of proceeds” data for loans.
  - 55% of mortgages lack valid energy performance certificates; non-harmonised energy classes (Sweden stricter for class A) hinder alignment.
  - Incomplete identification of new assets in flow denominators leads to overstated flow GAR.
  - Data expected to improve over time, affecting stock and flow KPIs.
text:
Interpretation and implementation
EU Taxonomy reporting is based on the consolidated situation as defined in 
 Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 of the European Parliament and the Council on 
 prudential requirements for credit institutions. The consolidated situation differs 
from the consolidated financial statements, which are prepared in accordance with IFRS Accounting Standards for the consolidation of insurance companies, 
joint  v entures and subsidiaries. Otherwise, the same principles are applied. 
Definitions related to EU Taxonomy reporting are provided on page 381.The reporting requirements under the EU Taxonomy are under development, 
and the EU is continuously publishing guidance on these requirements as well as definitions. Swedbank is working actively to implement these clarifications and 
participates in discussions within the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s working 
group on the EU Taxonomy. Interpretation issues and industry practice are dis -
cussed on an ongoing basis, and work to analyse and implement the require-ments is expected to continue. During the year, Swedbank continued to carry out a number of activities to further develop the processes for reporting in accor -
dance with the EU  T axonomy guidance, including internal controls.
In table 3 and 4 for credit institutions the denominator in the calculations is 
the Total GAR assets in the column Total gross carrying amount. In the column 
for proportion of total assets covered, the denominator is total assets.

alignment of an individual loan. Increasing the proportion of environmentally sus -
tainable assets in the portfolio is an important element of Swedbank’s climate

The EU Taxonomy is one of several tools for identifying activities carried out by 
Swedbank’s customers that can contribute to the Group’s work to achieve its cli -
mate targets. Increasing Taxonomy-aligned assets and assets under manage-ment is important for Swedbank to be able to ensure that the targets are 
achieved.
As a financial company, Swedbank presents its EU Taxonomy reporting in the 
standardised tables for credit institutions, asset management, insurance and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas. In addition to these tables, 
tables are presented with consolidated KPIs for each of the Group’s business

Tables for activities relating to nuclear energy and fossil gas provide detailed

title: Loans collateralised by residential immovable property
heading: Loans collateralised by residential immovable property
start_phrase: The acquisition and ownership of property by households is an activity covered by the EU Taxonomy.
summary:
- Swedbank monitors EU Taxonomy KPIs quarterly across Business Areas and aims to improve them by supporting customers’ sustainable operations, energy‑efficient housing, and sustainable investments.
- The bank is updating customer processes and developing products to evidence Taxonomy alignment at the individual loan level, with a focus on increasing environmentally sustainable assets and meeting 2030 financed‑emissions targets in sectors like commercial real estate and mortgages.
- In asset management, several funds commit to minimum proportions of Taxonomy‑aligned investments; the Taxonomy is a key tool for sustainability monitoring and for achieving climate targets.
- Reporting follows EU‑standardized tables for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas, plus consolidated, segment‑weighted KPIs for banking, asset management, and insurance.
- Detailed disclosures are provided for six nuclear and fossil gas activities, including GAR, Green ratio for assets under management, Green ratio for financial guarantees, and Green ratio for life insurance AUM.
- Loans collateralised by residential property constitute most of Swedbank’s Taxonomy‑eligible assets; the bank finances energy‑efficiency improvements and relies on high‑quality energy data.
- Alignment criteria for residential collateral vary by building age:
  - Built before 31 Dec 2020: primary energy within top 15% of national stock or energy class A.
  - Built after 31 Dec 2020: primary energy at least 10% below nearly‑zero energy building thresholds.
- Swedbank applies Swedish thresholds from Fastighetsägarna and corresponding data in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania; it conducts climate risk assessments (per Pillar 3 methodology) to meet Do No Significant Harm for Climate Change Adaptation. Loans are aligned only if energy criteria and low climate risk are both met; external data is used, with ongoing improvements.
- Swedbank’s Taxonomy reporting depends on counterparties’ NFRD/CSRD disclosures; current coverage is limited:
  - Corporate lending is 24% of assets; only 2% are NFRD/CSRD reporters.
  - 35% of AUM is in NFRD/CSRD companies; global, non‑EU, and small/mid‑cap strategies reduce alignment.
- Data constraints hinder alignment and KPI accuracy:
  - No central external database and variable data quality for customer KPIs and property energy performance.
  - Missing “use of proceeds” data for some corporate loans.
  - 55% of residential mortgage collateral lacks valid energy performance certificates, limiting proof of alignment.
  - Non‑harmonized energy class systems (stricter class A in Sweden) depress alignment.
  - Incomplete flow denominator data leads to inaccuracies and an overstated flow GAR.
- Overall, increasing Taxonomy‑aligned assets and AUM is central to meeting Swedbank’s climate targets, with ongoing efforts to enhance data, processes, and product offerings to support alignment and reporting.
text:
Loans collateralised by residential immovable property
The acquisition and ownership of property by households is an activity covered by the EU Taxonomy. The majority of Swedbank’s Taxonomy-eligible assets con-
sist of loans collateralised by residential immovable property. Housing accounts 
for a significant part of the EU’s energy  consumption and greenhouse gas emis -
sions, which can be reduced through increased energy efficiency. Swedbank 
 contributes to the financing of energy efficiency improvements in residential 
properties and is dependent on high-  quality energy data.
The EU Taxonomy sets different requirements for a loan collateralised by 
 residential immovable property to be classified as Taxonomy-aligned, depending 
on when the building was built. For buildings built before 31 December 2020, the 
primary energy requirement of the property must be within the top 15 per cent of 
the national housing stock or have energy class A. 
Swedbank has based its energy requirements on threshold values developed 
on behalf of Fastighetsägarna for the Swedish loans collateralised by residential 
immovable property. Corresponding information was used for loans collater-
alised by residential immovable property in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. 
For buildings built after 31 December 2020, the requirement is instead that the 
primary energy requirement must be at least 10 per cent below the threshold for 
nearly  -z ero energy buildings.
To meet the requirements to do no significant harm to the Climate Change 
Adaptation objective, Swedbank conducted climate risk assessments for resi -
dential properties used as collateral for loans, in accordance with the same meth -
odology used in the Pillar 3 report. Loans collateralised by residential immovable property are reported as Taxonomy-aligned when both of the following criteria are 
met: the property meets the energy requirements, and the climate risk assess -
ment indicates low risk. Data for the climate risk assessment is purchased from an external supplier. Work is under way to improve these assessments.

title: NFRD/CSRD companies
heading: NFRD/CSRD companies
start_phrase: Financial companies rely heavily on customers and counterparties reporting in accordance with the EU Taxonomy, so that they can fulfil their own reporting obligations.
summary:
- Swedbank monitors EU Taxonomy alignment and related KPIs quarterly, aiming to improve them by supporting customers’ sustainable operations, energy‑efficient housing, and sustainable investments. The bank is updating customer processes and developing products to evidence loan‑level Taxonomy alignment, while targeting a higher share of environmentally sustainable assets and setting 2030 financed‑emissions targets in sectors like commercial property and mortgages.
- In asset management, several funds commit to a minimum share of Taxonomy‑aligned investments; the Taxonomy is a core tool for sustainability monitoring and for meeting the Group’s climate targets.
- The bank reports EU Taxonomy metrics in standardized tables for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas, and provides consolidated KPIs for banking, asset management, and insurance weighted by each segment’s share of net income. Detailed tables cover six identified nuclear and fossil gas activities, including GAR and Green ratios for AUM, guarantees, and life insurance.
- Loans collateralised by residential property comprise the majority of Taxonomy‑eligible assets. Alignment criteria differ by construction date: pre‑2021 buildings must be in the top 15% for primary energy or have energy class A; post‑2020 buildings must be at least 10% below the nearly‑zero energy building threshold. Swedbank applies Swedish thresholds from Fastighetsägarna and comparable data for Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
- To meet Do No Significant Harm for Climate Change Adaptation, Swedbank conducts climate risk assessments (per its Pillar 3 methodology) on collateral; loans are Taxonomy‑aligned only if energy criteria are met and climate risk is low. External data providers are used, with ongoing improvements planned.
- Reliance on NFRD/CSRD company disclosures affects Swedbank’s alignment and eligibility figures; data from corporate sustainability statements is sourced externally. As reporting expands, data quality and availability should improve and influence alignment levels.
- Portfolio context: corporate lending is 24% of assets, but only 2% are to NFRD/CSRD reporters. In AUM, 35% is invested in NFRD/CSRD companies. Global non‑EU exposures and small/mid‑cap strategies lower overall Taxonomy alignment.
- Data gaps and quality issues hinder KPI accuracy: no central external database, limited “use of proceeds” data for corporate loans, and insufficient property energy data. For 55% of residential mortgage collateral, no valid energy performance certificate is available, constraining proof of alignment. Non‑harmonized energy classes (with stricter Swedish thresholds) further limit alignment. Incomplete flow‑denominator data reduces KPI accuracy and results in a higher reported flow GAR.
text:
NFRD/CSRD companies
Financial companies rely heavily on customers and counterparties reporting in accordance with the EU Taxonomy, so that they can fulfil their own reporting 
 obligations. Swedbank’s reporting thus reflects the companies’ reporting, both 
in terms of eligibility and alignment. The information from corporate customers’ sustainability statements has been obtained from an external supplier. As the 
legal requirements are gradually implemented and more companies report, both 
data availability and data quality are expected to improve over time, which will 
in turn affect Swedbank’s Taxonomy alignment.
Corporate lending accounts for 24 per cent of Swedbank’s assets, of which 
only 2 per cent are NFRD/CSRD companies that report in accordance with the 
EU Taxonomy. Assets under management in NFRD/CSRD companies account for 35 per cent of total assets under management. Assets under management 
in global portfolios outside the EU and funds with an investment focus on small 
and mid-cap enterprises, which do not report under the EU Taxonomy, contribute 
to lower Taxonomy alignment.

title: Data availability and quality
heading: Data availability and quality
start_phrase: The absence of a central external database and the continued inadequate quality of external data pose difficulties in collecting quality-assured data regarding KPIs from corporate customers and energy performance for properties used as collat-eral.
summary:
- Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy alignment and KPIs are monitored quarterly across business areas, with a stated ambition to improve KPIs by supporting sustainable customer activities, energy‑efficient housing, and sustainable investments.
- The bank is updating customer processes and developing products to evidence Taxonomy alignment at individual loan level, aiming to increase the share of environmentally sustainable assets; 2030 financed‑emissions targets are set for several sectors, including commercial real estate and mortgages.
- In asset management, selected funds commit to minimum proportions of Taxonomy‑aligned investments; the Taxonomy is a key monitoring tool and a lever to meet Group climate targets.
- EU Taxonomy reporting follows standardized templates for credit institutions, asset management, insurance, and activities related to nuclear energy and fossil gas, plus consolidated, income‑weighted KPIs by business segment (banking, asset management, insurance).
- Dedicated tables disclose details for six nuclear/fossil gas activities, covering GAR (Green Asset Ratio), Green ratio for assets under management (including life insurance), and Green ratio for financial guarantees.
- Loans collateralised by residential property constitute the majority of Taxonomy‑eligible assets; alignment criteria depend on building age (pre‑2021: top 15% energy performance or energy class A; post‑2020: ≥10% below nearly‑zero energy building threshold).
- DNSH for climate adaptation is assessed via climate risk analyses of residential collateral; loans are counted as aligned only when both energy criteria and low climate risk are met; data is sourced from an external provider, with ongoing improvements.
- Reporting relies on NFRD/CSRD company disclosures; currently only a small share of corporate lending (2% of corporate assets) is to reporting entities, while 35% of AUM is in reporting companies; non‑EU/global and small/mid‑cap exposures reduce overall alignment, expected to improve as CSRD expands.
- Data availability and quality are key constraints: no central database, missing or inconsistent external data (e.g., “use of proceeds”), non‑harmonised EPC systems, and 55% of residential mortgages lacking valid EPCs; incomplete flow denominators inflate the flow GAR and reduce KPI accuracy.
- E1 Climate change section outlines mitigation, adaptation, and energy across the value chain (lending, asset management, own operations), with climate deemed material throughout; it references the double materiality process (IRO‑1).
- Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan, aligned with its business strategy, targets net‑zero by 2050 and 1.5°C‑aligned sector pathways by 2030; it emphasizes steering lending and investments via engagement, advice, and product development.
- Fossil‑related restrictions: no new financing for companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal or peat (limited exceptions for defined transition cases); no dedicated financing for coal/peat power, new oil/gas power plants, oil tankers, or refineries; investment exclusions for companies with >5% revenue from fossil extraction or fossil‑based power (with narrow transition exceptions; indirect third‑party funds/discretionary mandates excluded).
- Lending focus in the transition plan is the real estate sector (~80% of loan exposure), with actions to support customers’ transition, build partnerships, and scale financing of sustainable activities; the plan is CEO‑approved, Board‑reviewed, and will be updated to reflect CSRD/CSDDD.
text:
Data availability and quality
The absence of a central external database and the continued inadequate quality 
of external data pose difficulties in collecting quality-assured data regarding KPIs 
from corporate customers and energy performance for properties used as collat-
eral. Inadequate availability and quality of data affects Taxonomy alignment and 
thereby the KPIs GAR and Green ratio for assets under management. Swedbank 
does not currently have data for all data points requested, for example “use of 
proceeds” in connection with corporate loans.
For 55 per cent of Swedbank’s loans collateralised by residential immovable 
property, a valid energy performance certificate is missing, which limits the ability to demonstrate Taxonomy alignment. The system of energy classes is not 
 harmonised, which is why, for example, in Sweden there are higher requirements 
than in many other EU countries for a   pr operty to be assigned energy class A, 
and thus meet the requirements of the EU Taxonomy.
The information about the assets in the denominator for the flow calculation 
is incomplete, as Swedbank has not been able to identify all new assets on all 
rows, which means that the KPIs are not accurate and resulting in a higher GAR 
for the flow.

title: Introduction
heading: Introduction
start_phrase: E1 Climate change covers Swedbank’s reporting relating to climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation and energy.
summary:
- Scope and structure: The E1 Climate change section reports on climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy across Swedbank’s full value chain. It is divided into three areas—Lending, Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), and Own operations—reflecting the double materiality assessment. Climate is material upstream, in own operations, and downstream, with differing methods, targets, and metrics per area.  
- Materiality and IRO linkage: Impacts, risks, and opportunities (positive and negative) are identified across the value chain, with cross-references to the Group’s process for identifying and assessing material IROs (IRO-1).  
- Strategy and transition plan: Sustainability is integrated into business strategy, with a Group-wide commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 and alignment with the 1.5°C pathway. Swedbank has published a Climate Transition Plan, emphasizing the lending portfolio where most climate impact occurs, and prioritizing customer transition support. The plan is approved by the CEO, reviewed by the Board, and will be updated in line with CSRD and CSDDD.  
- Targets:  
  - Lending: Six sector-specific 2030 climate targets aligned with 1.5°C reduction trajectories, focusing especially on the real estate sector (about 80% of loan exposure).  
  - Asset management: Climate targets for fund management aligned with the 1.5°C pathway.  
  - Own operations: Covers direct operational impacts such as energy use, travel, and procurement (details implied to be elsewhere).  
- Portfolio steering and client engagement: Swedbank aims to steer financing and investments toward sustainable activities through engagement, advice, tailored financial solutions, monitoring, and partnerships to enable customers’ transition.  
- Fossil fuel position and exclusions:  
  - Lending/financing: No new financing or capital market financing to companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat; no dedicated financing for coal/peat power generation or for companies with over 5% revenue from these; no dedicated financing for new oil or gas power plants, new oil tankers, or new oil refineries. Limited exceptions may be granted for transition companies (with criteria) or in extraordinary circumstances, with an expectation of Paris-aligned transition plans.  
  - Investments: Exclusion of companies with more than 5% of revenues from extraction or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat, with possible exceptions for transition companies. Indirect investments (third-party funds, discretionary mandates) are not covered.  
- Implementation actions to 2030:  
  - Support and engage customers to stimulate transition with adapted solutions and advice.  
  - Develop partnerships and collaborations to aid customer transition.  
  - Increase financing of sustainable and transition-enabling activities.

title: Transition plan - Introduction
heading: Transition plan, E1-1
start_phrase: Sustainability is at the heart of Swedbank’s business strategy, which means that sustainability aspects are integrated into the Group’s work and business deci-sions.
summary: Overview of Swedbank’s Climate Transition Plan (E1-1), detailing how sustainability is integrated into strategy and operations, with a Group-wide commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 and alignment of lending and investment portfolios to the 1.5°C target. The plan emphasizes Swedbank’s role as a systemically important bank driving customer transition (seven million private and 550,000 corporate customers) and sets six sector-specific 2030 climate targets for the loan portfolio, alongside fund management targets. Execution focuses on steering financing and investments via dialogue, advice, and monitoring, with the largest impact occurring through customers. Policy restrictions include no new financing or capital market financing for companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat (limited exceptions for transition companies or extraordinary circumstances with Paris-aligned plans), no dedicated financing for coal/peat power or companies with >5% revenues from these activities, and no dedicated financing for new oil/gas power plants, oil tankers, or refineries. Investment exclusions apply to companies with >5% revenues from extraction or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat (with certain transition exceptions); indirect investments via third parties or discretionary mandates are excluded from these restrictions. text:
Transition plan, E1-1
Sustainability is at the heart of Swedbank’s business strategy, which means that 
sustainability aspects are integrated into the Group’s work and business deci-
sions. One important element of Swedbank’s core business operations is the 
ongoing transition to a more sustainable society. The Group’s Climate Transition 
Plan is based on the business strategy.
In Swedbank’s societally important role as a systemically-important bank, the 
Group can drive change. The biggest contribution to achieving net-zero emis -
sions can be achieved by supporting Swedbank’s seven million private custom -
ers and more than 550 000 corporate customers to become more sustainable. 
Swedbank’s business model is to offer customers secure and efficient solu-
tions to manage their savings while meeting their financing needs. Based on its vision of a financially sound and sustainable society, the bank empowers the 
many people and businesses to create a better future. An important part of align -
ing the business model with the 1.5-degree target is to steer lending and invest -
ment portfolios towards this target. Swedbank has set six sector-specific climate targets for 2030 for its loan portfolio and has also adopted climate targets for 
fund management to be in line with the 1.5-degree target. To achieve the targets, 
Swedbank is working to steer financing and investments towards sustainable 
activities, also by such means as dialogue, advice and monitoring. There is addi -
tional information about each of the climate targets in section Targets, E1-4.
Swedbank’s commitment to net-zero emissions applies to the entire Group, 
and includes emissions relating to its own operations, lending and asset manage -
ment. During the year, Swedbank published the first version of its transition plan, the Swedbank Climate Transition Plan. The biggest climate impact occurs via 
customers, which means that customers making the transition are a key compo -
nent of the Group’s work to reduce emissions. The transition plan therefore places particular emphasis on the financing provided by the Group.
Swedbank’s climate-related targets are based on an overarching objective of 
achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 and aligning lending and investment port -
folios with the 1.5-degree target. The various 2030 climate targets for the loan 
portfolio are aligned with 1.5-degree sector-specific reduction trajectories. 
In its Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature, Swedbank has made 
statements regarding fossil fuels. According to this, Swedbank shall not provide 
new financing or offer capital market financing to companies that extract oil, gas, 
thermal coal or thermal peat. Exceptions can be approved for transition compa -
nies in the field of thermal peat if specific criteria are met. Exceptions can also be 
approved in extraordinary circumstances for companies within the restrictions, but companies are expected to draw up a transition plan in line with the Paris Agreement. Swedbank also has restrictions stating that it will not provide dedi -
cated financing to power generation from coal or peat, or companies whose 
 revenues from these activities exceed five per cent. Nor does Swedbank provide 
dedicated financing to new oil or gas power plants, new oil tankers or new oil refineries.
For Swedbank’s investments, i.e. when Swedbank makes investment deci-
sions for financial products, companies with more than five per cent of their reve-
nues from the extraction of or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal or 
thermal peat are excluded. Exceptions may be approved for transition companies 
in the areas of oil, gas or thermal peat if specific criteria are met. Indirect invest -
ments, such as funds managed by third parties or investment decisions based 
on a discretionary mandate, are not covered.

title: Lending
heading: Lending
start_phrase: Swedbank’s published transition plan aims to describe how Swedbank is working towards the net-zero target in Swedbank’s lending portfolio as well as the ambition to increase sustainable financing volumes.
summary:
- Scope and structure: The E1 Climate change section covers climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and energy across Swedbank’s entire value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream). Reporting is organized into three areas: Lending, Asset management (Swedbank Robur Fonder), and Own operations (e.g., energy use, travel, IT/office purchases). Climate change is assessed as material in all value chain divisions, with methods, targets, and metrics tailored per area. References are made to the materiality process in IRO-1.

- Strategy and transition plan (E1-1): Sustainability is embedded in Swedbank’s business strategy and underpins the Group’s Climate Transition Plan, which is aligned with limiting warming to 1.5°C and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050. The plan emphasizes steering lending and investment portfolios, sets six sector-specific 2030 climate targets for the loan portfolio, and includes climate targets for fund management. The plan prioritizes enabling customer transition, given the largest impacts occur via customers. It was approved by the CEO, reviewed by the Board, and will be updated in line with developments and requirements under CSDDD and CSRD.

- Fossil fuel position and exclusions: Swedbank will not provide new financing or capital market financing to companies extracting oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat, with limited exceptions for defined transition companies or extraordinary cases requiring Paris-aligned transition plans. The bank will not provide dedicated financing to coal/peat power generation or to companies with more than 5% revenue from these activities, nor to new oil/gas power plants, new oil tankers, or new oil refineries. For investments, companies with more than 5% revenue from extraction or power generation from oil, gas, thermal coal, or thermal peat are excluded, with possible exceptions for transition companies; indirect investments (third-party funds/discretionary mandates) are not covered.

- Lending portfolio focus: The transition plan details how Swedbank will progress toward net zero in its lending portfolio and increase sustainable financing. Primary focus is on the real estate sector, which represents about 80% of loan exposure. Integrated 2030 credit portfolio targets align with a 1.5°C pathway. Key actions include: engaging and advising customers to stimulate transition; developing partnerships to support customer transition; and increasing financing of sustainable and transition-enabling activities.

- Cross-references and next steps: Additional details on targets appear in E1-4 and on materiality in IRO-1. The section maps climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities across the value chain and underscores that climate work is Group-wide while being executed with area-specific tools and metrics.
text:
Lending
Swedbank’s published transition plan aims to describe how Swedbank is working towards the net-zero target in Swedbank’s lending portfolio as well as the ambi-
tion to increase sustainable financing volumes. The transition plan has been 
approved by the CEO and reviewed by the Board of Directors.
The Climate Transition Plan will be updated and adapted as climate work 
develops and in accordance with upcoming legislation, including requirements 
from both the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) and the 
Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), to strive to ensure that the right conditions are in place to achieve the Group’s climate targets. 
The primary focus is to enable and drive the green energy transition in the real 
estate sector, a sector that accounts for approximately 80 per cent of Swedbank’s 
loan exposure. Integrated into the plan are the Group’s climate targets for the 
credit portfolio for 2030, which are aligned with limiting global warming to 1.5°C. 
Important actions included in the work to achieve the climate targets are:
• Support and engage with our customers to stimulate a sustainable transition, for example by offering adapted financial solutions and advice. 
• Continue to develop partnerships and collaborations that support our 
 customers in their transition.

title: Drivers in the transition
heading: Drivers in the transition
start_phrase: Swedbank has multiple opportunities to contribute to the phasing out of fossil fuels and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions.
summary:
- Swedbank’s role in the climate transition centers on sustainable financing, advice, and awareness across its broad customer base, with priority on the real estate sector and other high-emission areas (power generation, oil and gas, shipping, steel).
- Business drivers include partnerships in green technology, rising market demand for green financial products, investor expectations, and tightening regulation; however, Swedbank is not yet conducting quantitative analysis of emission-reduction drivers.
- The bank aims to reduce exposure to customers unwilling to transition, guided by its Position Statement on Climate Change and Nature; it identifies potential locked-in emissions in fossil-intensive sectors and has set 2030 climate targets for these sectors, emphasizing engagement, advice, and monitoring.
- Tools were developed to assess corporate customers’ transition plans, informing internal decisions and client advice; achieving group climate targets depends on customers’ emissions trajectories and risk management, as well as Swedbank’s sector exposures.
- The Climate Transition Plan is not embedded in financial planning; no separate operating or capital expenditures are identified for the plan, and 2024 serves as the baseline year with no measurable results yet (further actions referenced in Actions, E1-3; sector targets in Targets, E1-4).
- Asset management: Swedbank Robur Fonder’s climate strategy and Responsible Investment Policy (board-approved, annually revised) guide net-zero alignment; as an NZAM signatory, it targets net-zero by 2040 (ahead of Paris 2050) via investing in transition solutions, active ownership to drive net-zero, exclusions that conflict with the strategy, and fulfilling external commitments and reporting.
- Own operations: target to reduce direct GHG emissions by 60% by 2030 versus 2019 (covering scope 1, scope 2, and selected scope 3); alignment with 1.5°C has not been evaluated.
- Strategy and business model: Swedbank sees both risk and opportunity, with its largest climate impact occurring through customers and investments; it aims to lead in financing sustainable solutions, especially energy efficiency in buildings, but cannot yet assess the effects/resources of listed measures.
- Climate-related risks are primarily indirect and dominated by transition risk; sectors with significant exposure include energy, property management, transport, forestry and agriculture, and manufacturing. Examples of credit risk drivers include stricter building energy regulations (potential property devaluation and cash flow impacts), disruptive low-carbon technologies and electrification (competitiveness risks for laggards), and shifting consumer/investor preferences toward sustainable products (demand and valuation impacts).
text:
Drivers in the transition
Swedbank has multiple opportunities to contribute to the phasing out of fossil 
fuels and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Through its broad cus-
tomer base, Swedbank has the opportunity to contribute to the transition through 
sustainable financing together with advice and raising awareness. 
Swedbank has a focus on enabling the energy transition in the real estate 
sector, given the Group’s exposure to this sector in all four home markets. There 
is also a focus on other emission-intensive sectors in the lending portfolio, 
including power generation, oil and gas, shipping and steel, as they represent a significant part of Swedbank’s financed emissions. Business opportunities and 
partnerships in green technology and the financing of sustainable solutions are 
important drivers. Changing market trends and increased demand for green 
financial products and services from both private and corporate customers also 
play a significant role. Changing demands from investors and compliance with 
legislation are also key, as regulatory requirements increase. Swedbank is not 
currently conducting a quantitative analysis of and follow-up on the various 
 factors that bring about cuts in emissions. 
It is also important to reduce exposure to customers with little or no willing -
ness to change. Swedbank’s expectations for the provision of financial services 
and restrictions on fossil fuels are specified in Swedbank’s Position Statement 
on Climate Change and Nature. Swedbank’s potentially locked-in greenhouse gas 
emissions are primarily identified in assets linked to customers in sectors with 
major investments in fossil fuels and carbon-intensive processes, where it is diffi -
cult and expensive to quickly reduce emissions, such as oil and gas, power gener-ation, steel and shipping. Swedbank has decided on climate targets for 2030 for these sectors, and therefore has a special focus on them. Swedbank engages in 
dialogue with, advice to and monitoring of customers of these sectors. Swed-
bank’s ability to achieve its climate targets in these sectors will depend on the 
ability of customers to make the transition, and on Swedbank’s exposure to cus-
tomers within these sectors. There is additional information about the climate 
impact of these sectors in Targets, E1-4. 
In order to better understand the transition of corporate customers, Swedbank 
developed tools during the year to facilitate the analysis of transition plans. Insights from this work have provided valuable input for internal decision-making 
processes and when advising customers. Swedbank’s ability to achieve the 
Group’s climate targets depends on customers’ continued emissions, ability to 
adapt and ability to manage climate-related risks in a satisfactory manner. 
The Climate Transition Plan is not an integral element of the financial planning 
process. Swedbank has not identified significant operating or capital expenditure specifically for the transition plan; these expenses are an integral part of Swed-
bank’s running costs.
No measurable results of the transition plan can be presented for 2024, as 
2024 is the baseline year. There is additional information about Swedbank’s 
 climate measures taken during the year in Actions, E1-3.

title: Asset management
heading: Asset management
start_phrase: The Swedbank Climate Transition Plan describes the Group’s overall approach to achieving net-zero emissions in fund management, which is described in more detail in Swedbank Robur Fonder’s climate strategy.
summary:
- Swedbank’s transition role centers on sustainable financing, advice, and awareness, leveraging its broad customer base to phase out fossil fuels and cut greenhouse gas emissions.

- The bank’s ability to meet sector targets depends on clients’ transition progress and Swedbank’s exposure levels; 2024 is a baseline year, so no measurable results are reported yet.
