heading: 5.2.8.5.4 Lending portfolio – commercial real estate
start_phrase: The table below presents financed emissions for the lending portfolio for commercial real estate based on the gross carrying amount broken down by country.
summary:
- Focus: Financed emissions across the bank’s lending portfolio, presented by asset class with country/sector breakdowns, using PCAF methodology and data quality scoring.
- Asset classes covered:
  - Commercial real estate (CRE): split by Sweden, Baltics, Other.
  - Motor vehicles: split by Sweden, Baltics, Other.
  - Business loans: split by sectors and selected high‑emitting subsectors.
- Key metrics reported for each segment:
  - Gross carrying amount (SEKm).
  - Financed emissions (scopes 1 & 2; scope 3 additionally for business loans).
  - Activity metrics and physical emission intensity:
    - CRE: financed area (thousand m2) and kgCO2e/m2.
    - Motor vehicles: financed km (thousand km) and kgCO2e/km.
  - PCAF data quality scores (1 = high quality, 5 = low).
  - Share of portfolio value based on asset-/company-specific data.
- Portfolio totals and notable results:
  - Commercial real estate: 272,924 SEKm; 354,358 tCO2e (S1&2); 19,328 thousand m2; intensity 18.3 kgCO2e/m2; PCAF 3.5; 71% asset-specific data.
    - Sweden shows lower intensity (6.8) and stronger data coverage (79%) than Baltics, where intensity is much higher (83.8) and coverage lower (52%); “Other” has minimal asset-specific data (0%) and lowest quality (5.0).
  - Motor vehicles: 36,691 SEKm; 266,048 tCO2e (S1&2); 1,565,748 thousand km; intensity 0.17 kgCO2e/km; PCAF 3.2; 68% asset-specific data.
    - Baltics exhibit higher intensity (0.21) than Sweden (0.14).
  - Business loans: 312,703 SEKm; 2,303,507 tCO2e (S1&2); 4,340,475 tCO2e (S3); PCAF 4.3 for both S1&2 and S3; 10% company-/asset-specific data.
    - Major sector contributors include manufacturing, public sector and utilities (notably power generation with higher-quality data, PCAF 2.5–2.7), retail and wholesale, transportation, and shipping/offshore.
    - Subsector highlights: oil & gas, steel, cement, chemicals, food production, wood & paper, transportation manufacturing. Coal exposure reported as zero.
    - Forestry shows negative financed emissions in S1&2, indicating net removals.
- Methodology notes (from footnotes):
  - Physical intensities: CRE in kgCO2e/m2; vehicles in kgCO2e/km.
  - PCAF data quality scoring: 1 (high) to 5 (low). Scores 1–3 (or 1–2 for business loans) indicate asset-/company-specific data.
  - Reported “asset-/company-specific data (%)” reflects the share of gross carrying amount with specific data inputs.

- Commercial real estate:
  - Coverage: Commercial mortgages and loans for rental residential properties; broken down by Sweden, Baltics, and Other.
  - Totals: SEKm 272,924 gross carrying amount; 354,358 tCO2e (scopes 1 & 2); 19,328 thousand m2 financed area; physical emission intensity 18.3 kgCO2e/m2; average PCAF data quality 3.5; 71% asset-specific data.
  - Geographic highlights: Sweden intensity 6.8 kgCO2e/m2 (data quality 3.4, 79% asset-specific); Baltics intensity 83.8 kgCO2e/m2 (data quality 3.5, 52% asset-specific); Other intensity 7.8 kgCO2e/m2 (data quality 5.0, 0% asset-specific).
- Motor vehicles:
  - Coverage: By Sweden, Baltics, and Other.
  - Totals: SEKm 36,691 gross carrying amount; 266,048 tCO2e (scopes 1 & 2); 1,565,748 thousand km financed; physical emission intensity 0.17 kgCO2e/km; average PCAF data quality 3.2; 68% asset-specific data.

- Business loans:
  - Coverage: Sectoral breakdown with scopes 1 & 2 and scope 3 financed emissions, PCAF data quality by scope, and share of company-/asset-specific data.
  - Totals: SEKm 312,703 gross carrying amount; 2,303,507 tCO2e (scopes 1 & 2); 4,340,475 tCO2e (scope 3); average PCAF data quality 4.3 for both scopes; 10% company-/asset-specific data.

title: Lending portfolio – business loans
heading: 5.2.8.5.6 Lending portfolio – business loans
start_phrase: The table below presents financed emissions for the lending portfolio for business loans based on gross carrying amount.
summary:
- Focus: 2024 financed emissions from Swedbank’s lending portfolio, covering three asset classes—commercial real estate, motor vehicles, and business loans—within the Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 (Board of Directors’ report, Sustainability section).
- What’s reported for each portfolio: gross carrying amount (SEKm), financed emissions (Scopes 1 & 2; plus Scope 3 for business loans), activity metrics (financed area for real estate; financed kilometres for vehicles), physical emission intensities (kgCO2e per m2 or per km), PCAF data quality scores (1 = high, 5 = low), and the share of asset-/company-specific data used.

Commercial real estate (by geography: Sweden, Baltics, Other)
- Totals: gross carrying amount 272,924 SEKm; financed emissions (Scopes 1 & 2) 354,358 tCO2e; financed area 19,328 thousand m2; physical emission intensity 18.3 kgCO2e/m2; weighted PCAF data quality 3.5; asset-specific data coverage 71%.
- Highlights: Sweden dominates exposure and shows much lower physical intensity (6.8) than the Baltics (83.8), with “Other” small and limited data quality (5.0; 0% asset-specific).

Motor vehicles (by geography: Sweden, Baltics, Other)
- Totals: gross carrying amount 36,691 SEKm; financed emissions (Scopes 1 & 2) 266,048 tCO2e; financed kilometres 1,565,748 thousand km; physical emission intensity 0.17 kgCO2e/km; weighted PCAF data quality 3.2; asset-specific data coverage 68%.
- Highlights: Sweden shows lower physical intensity (0.14) than the Baltics (0.21).

Business loans (by sector and selected subsectors)
- Totals: gross carrying amount 312,703 SEKm; financed emissions Scopes 1 & 2 of 2,303,507 tCO2e; Scope 3 of 4,340,475 tCO2e; weighted PCAF data quality 4.3 for both scopes; company-/asset-specific data coverage 10%.
- Sector coverage includes: agriculture/forestry/fishing; manufacturing (with subsectors such as aluminium, oil and gas, steel, cement, food production, chemicals, transportation manufacturing, wood and paper); public sector and utilities (with power generation highlighted); construction; retail and wholesale; transportation; shipping and offshore; and “other business loans” (hotels/restaurants, ICT, finance/insurance, property management excluding the CRE method, professional services, and other lending).
- Notable data points: power generation within public sector and utilities shows relatively better data quality (2.5–2.7) and significant emissions; shipping and offshore has high emissions and low data quality; several carbon-intensive manufacturing subsectors are explicitly disclosed with their data-quality and data-coverage levels.

Footnotes and methodology
- Physical emission intensity is defined as financed emissions per financed activity (kgCO2e/m2 for real estate; kgCO2e/km for vehicles).
- PCAF data quality scores are gross carrying amount-weighted; lower scores indicate higher quality; thresholds for when asset-/company-specific data are considered are specified.
- Shares of portfolio value based on asset-/company-specific data are disclosed for transparency on data provenance.

start_phrase: The Energy sub-area is indirectly material via the lending portfolio downstream in Swedbank’s value chain.
summary:
- Focus area: Entity-specific disclosures on Energy in the downstream value chain, where energy impacts are considered indirectly material through Swedbank’s lending portfolio.
- Approach: Swedbank supports customers in improving property energy efficiency and collects Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) data to assess the energy classes of properties in its mortgage and commercial real estate portfolios.
- Scope of disclosure: Year-on-year (2024 vs 2023) breakdowns of gross carrying amounts by EPC class (A–G, H, and Not classified) and by geography (Sweden, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Other) for:
  - Mortgages
  - Commercial real estate
- Key observations:
  - A significant share of exposures remains “Not classified” by EPC in both portfolios.
  - Total portfolio sizes disclosed: Mortgages about SEK 1,127bn (2024) vs SEK 1,115bn (2023); Commercial real estate about SEK 273bn (2024) vs SEK 255bn (2023).
- Purpose: Enhance transparency on the energy performance of financed properties, support transition efforts, and track changes in energy efficiency across the lending book and geographies.

title: Introduction
heading: 6.1.1 Introduction
start_phrase: Chapter S1 Own workforce covers Swedbank’s reporting related to working conditions, equal treatment and equal opportunities for all, as well as other work-related rights.
summary:
- Focus and scope: Section S1 (Social information – Own workforce) covers Swedbank’s impacts, risks and opportunities related to working conditions, equal treatment and opportunities for all, and other work‑related rights within its own operations. The value chain mapping identifies material issues only in the own workforce. Reporting applies to all Swedbank employees; external consultants, self‑employed contractors and agency staff are not covered by Swedbank’s employment terms.

- Strategy and culture: Employees are central to the Group’s success. The workforce strategy prioritizes competitive conditions, development opportunities, and an attractive, inclusive, and responsible workplace anchored in the values “open, simple, caring.” Sustainability is integrated into the business strategy, with diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) as key focus areas. The strategy is continuously adapted to meet evolving expectations. The bank relies on key competencies and, at times, external resources for specialized expertise or peak workloads.

- Policies and commitments: Swedbank does not operate in markets permitting forced or child labor. Its Human Rights Policy commits to preventing misuse of the financial system to violate the rights of children and other vulnerable groups.

- Materiality and coverage: A materiality assessment identified the own workforce topic as material. Material areas include working conditions, equal treatment/equal opportunities, and other work‑related rights across the Group’s own operations.

- Positive impacts and opportunities: 
  - Competitive, good working conditions, career development, and an inclusive, accountable culture.
  - Freedom of association and coverage by collective or locally applicable labor agreements.
  - Flexible work to support work‑life balance.
  - Occupational health services in Sweden and healthcare insurance in the Baltic countries.
  - Investments in training, skills development, and harassment prevention.
  - Ability to attract and retain committed, motivated employees, supporting stronger performance and long‑term growth.

- Risks and negative impacts:
  - Sector change driving high demands on employee adaptability; potential for stress and unsuitable working hours.
  - Failure to ensure equity, gender equality, and equal opportunities can harm wellbeing and motivation, reduce innovation, and increase turnover.
  - Financial risks from weakened engagement, higher recruitment and retention costs, and loss of key talent.

- Overall emphasis: Strong governance and processes are used to manage identified impacts, risks, and opportunities, aiming to sustain a committed, engaged workforce essential to Swedbank’s long‑term success.

title: Strategy and business model, SBM-3
heading: 6.1.2 Strategy and business model, SBM-3
start_phrase: Swedbank’s employees are essential to the Group’s operations, culture and success.
summary:
- Scope and purpose: Section S1 “Own workforce” details Swedbank’s approach and reporting on working conditions, equal treatment and opportunities for all, and other work-related rights across the Group’s own employees; it references the materiality process (IRO-1) and links to the strategy and business model (SBM-3).
- Value chain mapping: Impacts, risks and opportunities are identified within Swedbank’s own operations; none are identified upstream or downstream.
- Strategic context: Employees are central to the Group’s success. The workforce strategy aims to offer competitive working conditions, development opportunities, and an attractive, inclusive, and responsible culture aligned with the values open, simple and caring. It addresses stress, work–life balance and inequality, and is continuously adapted to meet employee expectations. Sustainability and a value-driven approach support talent attraction, with DEI as key focus areas.
- Workforce dependencies: Critical capabilities exist in key competence areas; the bank also relies on external resources (consultants, self-employed, temp staff) for specialized expertise and peak workloads. Swedbank’s employment terms and benefits apply only to its own employees, not contractors.
- Human rights stance: Swedbank does not operate in markets permitting forced or child labour and commits to preventing misuse of the financial system to violate human rights, particularly of children and vulnerable groups.
- Material impacts, risks and opportunities:
  - Positive impacts: Competitive conditions, development paths, inclusive/accountable culture; freedom of association; collective or local labour agreements; flexible working hours; occupational health services in Sweden; healthcare insurance for employees in the Baltic countries.
  - Risks/negative impacts: Stress and unsuitable working hours; failure to ensure equity and equal opportunities harms wellbeing and motivation; insufficient progress on gender equality may increase recruitment costs and hinder attraction/retention; decreased motivation/innovation and higher turnover drive financial risk.
  - Opportunities: Stronger recruitment and retention via competitive conditions; investments in training, skills development and harassment prevention enhance engagement and support long-term positive results.
text:
Swedbank’s employees are essential to the Group’s operations, culture and 
 success. One of the cornerstones of the Group’s strategy is committed 
 employees who contribute and take responsibility. Swedbank employees are all 
part of the business, which is governed by the Group’s strategy and business 
model and may be exposed to identified impacts, risks and opportunities. This 
applies to employees of Swedbank, as well as those who perform assignments 
on behalf of the Group as self-employed or employees via consultancies or staff 
agencies. As an employer, Swedbank has a great responsibility to use gover-
nance documents and processes to manage impacts, risks and opportunities 
and to continue to take these into account in the overall strategy. To ensure con-
tinued success and promote long-term growth, it is crucial for Swedbank to have committed and engaged employees.
Swedbank’s worforce strategy focuses on providing employees competitive 
working conditions, development opportunities and an attractive workplace with 
an inclusive and responsible culture. Swedbank’s values - open, simple and 
caring reflects a culture where high engagement and continuous learning are 
important. These fundamentals are vital for addressing concerns like stress, 
work-life imbalance and inequality. Swedbank has developed its employee strat-egy to meet employees’ requirements and expectations, and to be perceived as 
an attractive employer. This provides opportunities for better results and the 
 successful development of the Group. The strategy is constantly modified to 
meet these interests and requirements. 
Through a strong commitment to sustainability and a value-driven approach, 
Swedbank can attract talent, and sustainability is naturally integrated in Swed -
bank’s business strategy. Diversity, equity and inclusion are key focus areas.
Swedbank depends on a competent and motivated workforce in all areas of 
the business. Certain capability areas of employees who possess key compe -
tences are particularly critical to the Group. Furthermore, Swedbank is to some 
extent dependent on external resources to obtain specific expertise or in peak workload times when temporary manpower is hired. It is vital that all employees 
are offered terms and conditions, work tasks and conditions that contribute to 
a positive working climate.
Swedbank does not operate in markets where forced labour and child labour 
are permitted, and Swedbank’s Human Rights Policy states that Swedbank 
undertakes to prevent the financial system from being used to violate the human 
rights of children and other vulnerable groups.

title: Impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 6.1.3 Impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: In the materiality assessment performed during the year, the own workforce sustain ability topic was identified as material.
summary:
- Scope and focus: The S1 Own workforce chapter covers Swedbank’s management and reporting of working conditions, equal treatment and opportunities, and other work-related rights for the Group’s employees. Material impacts, risks and opportunities are identified primarily within Swedbank’s own operations; no material impacts are identified upstream or downstream.

- Strategy and integration: Employees are central to Swedbank’s strategy and business model. The workforce strategy emphasizes competitive terms, development opportunities, an attractive, inclusive and responsible culture, and values of being open, simple and caring. Sustainability and DEI are integrated to attract and retain talent. The bank relies on key competencies internally and, when needed, external resources; maintaining a positive work climate is critical.

- Material impacts, risks and opportunities: Positive impacts stem from competitive working conditions, development, freedom of association and collective bargaining, flexible work for work–life balance, and health services/insurance (occupational health in Sweden; healthcare insurance in the Baltics). Negative impacts may arise from stress and unsuitable hours. Opportunities include improved recruitment, retention, motivation and results; risks include decreased motivation/innovation, higher turnover and recruitment costs. Non-compliance with equal pay could lead to fines/legal action. Contractors and agency workers are not covered by Swedbank employment terms/benefits. Employee data and information handling pose privacy risks if poorly managed.

- Human rights commitments (Policies, S1-1): Swedbank’s Human Rights Policy aligns with the UDHR, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO Declaration, UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and UNGPs. It commits to non-discrimination; freedom of association and collective bargaining; prohibition of child and forced labour; safe, healthy workplaces; statutory hours and remuneration (often via collective agreements). Human trafficking is not explicitly in the policy but is prohibited in the markets where the bank operates. A whistleblower process is in place.

- Healthy and sustainable work environment: The Work Environment Directive governs systematic management of physical, digital, organizational and social aspects, with regular risk assessment, actions and follow-up to prevent ill health and accidents.

- Diversity, equity and inclusion: The DEI Policy mandates equal opportunities, zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment and bullying across a broad range of protected characteristics. It promotes diversity in boards and senior management. Governance includes a GEC member accountable for DEI and DEI leads per home market, a key activity plan, regular employee surveys on inclusion and harassment, required investigations of alleged inappropriate behavior (including rumors), manager training, workshops, and communications. Monitoring covers equal treatment, gender balance in leadership, sick leave, parental leave, age distribution, and equal pay. Employee networks (e.g., LGBTQ+) and whistleblowing channels support the culture.

- Workforce engagement (S1-2): Engagement occurs via the Code of Conduct (signed annually), regular manager–employee dialogue, intranet and internal communications, Town Halls with the CEO and GEC, the European Works Council, union and health/safety forums, employee board representatives, and recurring People Pulse surveys. Managers must monitor well-being and act on issues per the Work Environment Directive.

- Remediation (S1-3): Swedbank fosters an accountable culture, investigates reported irregularities, and takes appropriate measures, including counseling support when relevant. Employees can report concerns on employment terms, equal treatment and opportunities, and other work-related rights via managers, Group HR, the whistleblower channel, or a digital incident system.

- Boundaries and expectations: Swedbank does not operate where child or forced labour is permitted and aims to prevent misuse of the financial system to violate human rights of children and vulnerable groups. Consulting firms engaged by Swedbank are expected to respect these principles even though Swedbank employment terms apply only to employees. Governance documents are available on the intranet and public website.
text:
In the materiality assessment performed during the year, the own workforce 
sustain  ability topic was identified as material. By accessing analyses, reports 
and internal and external expertise, Swedbank was able to identify working con -
ditions, equal treatment and equal opportunities for everyone, as well as other work-related rights, as material. The reporting covers all employees in the Swed-
bank Group and describes material impacts, risks and opportunities in the 
Group’s own operations, based on the materiality assessment. 
Good, competitive working conditions such as development opportunities and 
an attractive workplace with a culture based on inclusion and accountability can 
have a positive impact on Swedbank's employees. This also includes freedom of 
association, collective agreements or local agreements covered by labour law provisions, flexible working hours for a good work-life balance and, in Sweden, 
occupational health services. In the Baltic countries, Swedbank offers healthcare 
insurance to employees, to meet a need for private or occupation-related care. 
The banking and finance industry is changing where requirements on employee’s 
development and ability to adapt are high. Stress and unsuitable working hours 
are two factors that can have a negative impact on the workforce. Risks and 
opportunities related to working conditions were also identified, where Swed-bank sees opportunities to recruit and retain committed and motivated employ-
ees by offering competitive working conditions, which can contribute to positive 
results. The contrary, which constitutes a financial risk, can be that motivation 
and innovation decrease and that employees leave the company, resulting 
increased costs for example for new recruitment. Swedbank’s terms of employ-
ment and benefits apply solely to employees of Swedbank. This means that par-
ties undertaking assignments for Swedbank, such as self-employed persons or employees of consultancies or temporary staff agencies, are not covered. 
Equal treatment and opportunities for all are a key element of the workforce 
strategy. Swedbank sees diversity, equity and inclusion as key focus areas. If 
Swedbank fails to manage equity and equal opportunities for all, this can have 
a negative impact on the well-being and motivation of the workforce. Further -
more, investments in training, skills development and prevention of harassment represent an opportunity for Swedbank when engaged employees who are happy can contribute to a positive result in the long run.
 On the other hand, if Swedbank fails to maintain its work with increased 
gender equality, this can present a financial risk in the form of increased recruit -
ment costs if there are difficulties in attracting and retaining employees. Further -

title: Human rights
heading: 6.1.4.1 Human rights
start_phrase: Swedbank’s human rights strategy is based on the international human rights framework, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s governance of its own workforce under ESRS S1: Policies (S1-1), Engagement with workforce (S1-2), and Remediation processes (S1-3).
- Compliance and risk context: notes potential legal exposure (e.g., fines) for breaches such as unequal pay; highlights employee data/information management risks to privacy.
- Policies and governance: Group-wide policies available internally and public documents on the website; references to additional governance sections (e.g., MDR-P, S4-1, G1-1).
- Human rights commitments: aligns with the UDHR, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, ECHR, ILO Declaration, UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. Prohibits discrimination, child labour, and forced labour; supports freedom of association and collective bargaining; expects the same standards from consultants. Human trafficking not explicitly in policy but prohibited in operating markets. Whistleblower process available to employees and external stakeholders.
- Healthy and sustainable working environment: an internal Work Environment Directive sets systematic management across physical, digital, organizational, and social dimensions; includes regular examination, risk assessment, action, and follow-up to prevent ill health and accidents.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI): zero tolerance of discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment, and bullying; equal opportunity in career and development; aims for diverse leadership and boards (gender, age, geography, education, background). DEI is led by a GEC member with DEI Leads in each home market; ongoing training, workshops, communications, and mandatory investigations by HR/managers for inappropriate behavior, including rumors. Monitors equal treatment metrics (e.g., gender balance in senior roles, sick/parental leave, age distribution, equal pay), with unit and market breakdowns; supports employee networks (e.g., LGBTQ+); whistleblower and case-handling processes run by trained investigators.
- Workforce engagement (S1-2): Code of Conduct signed annually; employee dialogue via managers and multiple internal channels; biannual CEO/GEC Town Halls with Q&A; European Works Council since 2007 for cross-border representation; continuous dialogue with Swedish trade unions and health and safety reps; two employee representatives on the Board. Regular People Pulse surveys gather views on business and well-being. Managers must hold ongoing 1:1s and act on issues affecting well-being per the Work Environment Directive.
- Remediation processes (S1-3): promotes an accountable culture; investigates reported irregularities and takes appropriate measures; offers counseling/psychological support where relevant. Identified potential negative impact areas include employment terms, equal treatment, equal opportunities, and other work-related rights. Multiple reporting channels: immediate manager, Group HR, Group-wide whistleblower process, and an internal digital incident system.
text:
Human rights 
Swedbank’s human rights strategy is based on the international human rights framework, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the ILO Declaration on 
Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and the United Nations Convention 
on the Rights of the Child. The Swedbank Human Rights Policy states that Swed-
bank respects human rights in its labour practices and accepts no discrimination. 
This includes, but is not limited to, freedom of association, the right to collective 
bargaining and the prohibition of child labour and forced labour. Employees in 
Swedbank’s operations must have the right to a safe and healthy workplace, with statutory working hours and remuneration, which may be stipulated in collective 
agreements. Swedbank expects the same approach from the consulting firms 
that the Group engages. 
The policy also states that Swedbank has a whistleblower process that 
encourages all employees and other external stakeholders to report suspected 
potential or actual violations of Swedbank’s obligations and policies. 
Swedbank bases its definition of human rights and its commitments on the 
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and 
 Fundamental Freedoms. Swedbank also supports the principles of fundamental 
rights set out in the ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at 
Work, as well as the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. In addi -
tion, Swedbank is committed to applying the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights in its Human Rights Policy. 
Child labour and forced labour are explicitly addressed in the policy, but not 
human trafficking. Human trafficking is also prohibited in the markets in which 
Swedbank operates. If the Group’s operations entail a direct violation of human 
rights, Swedbank must take measures to prevent this. There is additional infor -
mation about human rights in Policies, S4-1.

title: Healthy and sustainable working environment
heading: 6.1.4.2 Healthy and sustainable working environment
start_phrase: To prevent ill health and accidents and create a healthy and sustainable working environment, Swedbank has introduced the internal Work Environment Directive.
summary:
- Highlights risks and obligations related to employee rights, including equal pay compliance (with potential fines/legal action) and the need for robust data/information management to protect employee privacy.
- Outlines Group-wide policies and governance for workforce matters, available internally and publicly, with cross-references to governance sections.
- Details Human Rights Policy and strategy grounded in UDHR, ILO Core Principles, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, ECHR, UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
- Commits to non-discrimination, freedom of association, collective bargaining, and prohibition of child and forced labour; expects equivalent standards from consultants; has a whistleblower process; human trafficking not explicitly in policy but prohibited in operating markets; mandates prevention/mitigation if direct violations occur.
- Describes the Work Environment Directive to ensure a healthy, sustainable workplace, addressing physical, digital, organizational, and social factors through systematic risk assessment, action, and follow-up.
- Presents the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Policy: equal opportunities; zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment, and bullying across a broad list of protected characteristics; promotes diverse representation on boards and in senior management.
- Explains DEI governance and activities: executive ownership, DEI Leads per home market, regular employee surveys on inclusion and harassment awareness, preventive training/workshops for managers and staff, mandatory investigations (including of rumors), and established procedures handled by trained investigators; ongoing monitoring of equal treatment metrics (e.g., gender distribution in senior roles, sick/parental leave, age distribution, and equal pay) by unit and market; employee networks (e.g., LGBTQ+).
- Describes workforce engagement (S1-2): annual Code of Conduct sign-off; communication via managers, intranet, meetings, newsletters; biannual Town Halls with CEO/management; European Works Council; continuous dialogue with unions and health/safety reps per collective agreements; employee representatives on the Board; “People Pulse” survey; managers’ duty to hold individual well-being discussions and act per the Work Environment Directive.
- Details remediation processes (S1-3): procedures to investigate reported irregularities, take appropriate measures, and provide counselling/psychological support when relevant; identifies potential negative impact areas (employment terms, equal treatment and opportunities, other work-related rights); multiple reporting channels (line manager, Group HR, whistleblower process, internal digital incident tool).
text:
Healthy and sustainable working environment 
To prevent ill health and accidents and create a healthy and sustainable working environment, Swedbank has introduced the internal Work Environment Directive. 
This describes how working conditions should be designed within Swedbank’s 
operations in order to achieve these objectives. The directive sets out Swed -
bank’s overarching targets, direction and approach to long-term work environ-ment management, to ensure sustainable employees. It takes account of physi -
cal, digital, organisational and social factors that affect the working environment. 
The directive describes how Swedbank works system  atically with the working 
environment by regularly examining, risk assessing, addressing and following up all aspects of the working environment in accordance with a Group-wide work 
environment management agenda.

title: Diversity, equity and inclusion
heading: 6.1.4.3 Diversity, equity and inclusion
start_phrase: Swedbank’s Policy on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion states that all employees must have equal opportunities when working for Swedbank and access to the same career and development opportunities.
summary:
- Emphasizes legal and regulatory compliance on equal pay and employee data/privacy, noting risks such as fines and privacy impacts from poor information management.
- Outlines Group-wide workforce-related policies and governance documents accessible on the intranet and public website, with cross-references to governance sections.
- Details a comprehensive Human Rights Policy aligned with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO core principles, UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and UN Guiding Principles; prohibits discrimination, child and forced labor; supports freedom of association and collective bargaining; expects the same standards from consultants; includes a whistleblower process; notes human trafficking is not explicitly in the policy but is illegal in operating markets; commits to preventive and remedial actions for any direct rights violations.
- Describes a Work Environment Directive aimed at a healthy, sustainable workplace, addressing physical, digital, organizational, and social factors through systematic examination, risk assessment, action, and follow-up.
- Presents a Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Policy guaranteeing equal opportunities, zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment, and bullying across a broad set of protected characteristics; promotes diverse leadership; governed by a GEC member with DEI Leads per home market; uses recurring employee surveys on inclusion and misconduct awareness; mandates training, workshops, and clear procedures; requires HR and managers to investigate all inappropriate behavior, including rumors; monitors indicators such as equal pay, gender balance in leadership, sick leave, parental leave, and age distribution; provides employee information and supports networks for marginalized groups (e.g., LGBTQ+); operates a whistleblower and case-handling process with trained investigators.
- Explains workforce engagement (S1-2) via an annually signed Code of Conduct, manager dialogues, intranet and meeting channels, biannual Town Halls with the CEO and GEC, a European Works Council, ongoing union and safety representative dialogues (notably in Sweden), employee representation on the Board, and the People Pulse survey; managers are responsible for continuous well-being discussions and actions under the Work Environment Directive.
- Outlines remediation processes (S1-3) fostering an accountable speak-up culture, with procedures to investigate irregularities, take appropriate measures, and provide support (e.g., counseling); identifies potential negative impacts around employment terms, equal treatment and opportunities, and other work-related rights; lists reporting channels including line managers, Group HR, a Group-wide whistleblower system, and an internal digital incident tool.
text:
Swedbank’s Policy on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion states that all employees 
must have equal opportunities when working for Swedbank and access to the 
same career and development opportunities. There is zero tolerance of discri -
mination, harassment, sexual harassment and bullying. 
Swedbank and its employees may not discriminate or harass based on gender, 
gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, age, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, membership of a national minority, prop-
erty, birth, disability, religion or belief, political or any other opinion.To encourage 
independent and critical thinking, this policy states that the board of directors, 
boards of subsidiary companies and senior management, taking due account of 
local regulations, must represent diversity in terms of, for example, gender, age, geographical origin, and educational and professional background. 
Swedbank has a key activity plan for diversity, equity and inclusion. The area 
is headed by a member of the Group Executive Committee with responsibility for 
equity and diversity, with additional DEI Leads in each home market. Employee 
surveys carried out several times a year ask whether Swedbank is perceived as 
an inclusive workplace, whether employees experience discrimination or harass -ment, and whether they know how to act in cases where discrimination or harass -
ment is observed. Work to prevent discrimination and harassment is a priority at Swedbank. 
In addition to the Policy on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, Swedbank has pro-
cesses and guidelines for the work to counteract negative impacts in the area of 
equal treatment and opportunities for everyone. The policy is implemented in accordance with ordinary procedures and is clearly communicated in Swed-
bank’s various channels and in ongoing operations. Through training, workshops 
and regular communication on these issues, managers are reminded of their 
responsibility to cultivate a respectful culture in their teams and of how to act if 
inappropriate behaviour does occur. It is a requirement for both Group Human 
Resources (Group HR) and managers to initiate an investigation in cases of inap -
propriate behaviour, including rumours thereof. Swedbank continuously monitors 
developments in such areas as equal treatment, gender distribution in manage-
ment and senior roles, sick leave, parental leave, age distribution and equal pay 
for equal work. This is broken down at unit level and for each home market. Infor-
mation is available to all employees about the company’s policy and the proce -
dures used in the event of discrimination or harassment. Swedbank also has net -
works and associations aimed at raising and working on issues for marginalised 
groups, such as LGBTQ+. During the year, managers received communication and participated in workshops for preventive and educational purposes. Training 
for other employees also took place. A whistleblower process and a process for 
addressing reported cases of discrimination and harassment have been estab -
lished and are conducted by trained investigators in Swedbank. There is addi -
tional information about the whistleblower process in G1-1.

title: Engaging with own workforce, S1-2
heading: 6.1.5 Engaging with own workforce, S1-2
start_phrase: Swedbank has established processes for engaging with the employees and employee representatives about actual and potential impacts on its own work - force.
summary:
- Emphasis on employment-related rights, including equal pay for equal work; non-compliance may result in fines or legal action.
- Recognition that deficiencies in employee data and information management can harm privacy.
- Policies and governance (S1-1): Group-wide policies addressing impacts, risks, and opportunities related to the workforce; internal and public governance documents available (with further details in section MDR-P).
- Human rights commitments: Based on UDHR, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO Fundamental Principles, and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child; alignment with UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
- Explicit prohibition of discrimination, child labor, and forced labor; support for freedom of association and collective bargaining; human trafficking not expressly in the policy but prohibited in operating markets; expectation that consultants follow the same standards; further information referenced in Policies, S4-1.
- Whistleblower process available to employees and external stakeholders to report violations of obligations and policies.
- Healthy and sustainable working environment: Internal Work Environment Directive covering physical, digital, organizational, and social factors; systematic risk assessment, action, and follow-up via a Group-wide agenda.
- Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI): Policy ensures equal opportunities and zero tolerance for discrimination, harassment, sexual harassment, and bullying across a broad set of protected characteristics.
- Leadership and governance for DEI: Board and senior management expected to reflect diverse backgrounds; DEI owned by a Group Executive Committee member with DEI Leads in each home market; key activity plan in place.
- Prevention and monitoring: Regular employee surveys on inclusion and experiences of discrimination/harassment; training, workshops, clear procedures for investigations; managers and Group HR required to investigate alleged inappropriate behavior; transparency about policies and procedures.
- Ongoing measurement: Tracking equal treatment metrics (e.g., gender distribution in management, senior roles, sick leave, parental leave, age distribution, and equal pay) at unit and market levels; support networks for marginalized groups (e.g., LGBTQ+).
- Engagement with workforce (S1-2): Code of Conduct signed annually; communication via managers, intranet, meetings, newsletters; biannual “Town Hall” with CEO and management; European Works Council; dialogue with trade unions and safety reps; board includes employee representatives; “People Pulse” surveys for feedback and well-being.
- Manager responsibilities: Continuous dialogue on well-being and work situation; actions taken under the Work Environment Directive if risks are identified.
- Remediation processes (S1-3): Procedures to investigate reported irregularities and take appropriate measures; support (e.g., counseling, psychological aid) for affected individuals.
- Identified potential negative impact areas: Employment terms, equal treatment and opportunities, and other work-related rights.
- Reporting channels: Employees can report concerns via their manager, Group HR, Group-wide whistleblower process, or an internal digital incident system.
text:
Swedbank has established processes for engaging with the employees and employee representatives about actual and potential impacts on its own work -
force. The Code of Conduct, which is adopted by Swedbank’s Board of Directors and signed by employees annually, sets out the expectations of each employee’s 
conduct. It provides guidance for the day-to-day work and serves as an ethical 
compass. Dialogue with employees takes place primarily via the immediate man-
ager and as internal communication via various channels such as the intranet, 
physical and digital meetings, and newsletters and emails. Twice a year, the Group Executive Committee (GEC) meets employees physically and digitally at 
a 'Town Hall' meeting where employees can pose questions directly or digitally 
to Swedbank’s CEO and management.
Swedbank is also in continuous dialogue with employee representatives in 
 various forums. A Group-wide European Works Council (EWC) was established 
in Swedbank in 2007. This is a cross-border forum for information and collabora-tion with employee representatives from different countries in Europe where 
Swedbank operates. In Sweden, there is an ongoing dialogue with representa -
tives from the trade unions and health and safety representatives, in accordance with the collective agreements. In addition, Swedbank’s Board of Directors also 
includes two employee representatives with two deputies. Employee surveys are 
another channel for engaging with employees. The People Pulse survey gives 
employees the opportunity to give their views on the business and their own well-being via their responses to a number of questions. 
Swedbank’s Work Environment Directive states that it is the manager’s respon -
sibility to ensure continuous dialogue with employees about their well-being and 
work situation through individual discussions. If the individual discussions reveal 
an issue that may have a negative impact on the employee’s working environment 
or health, the manager takes measures in accordance with the manager’s respon -
sibility and the Work Environment Directive.

title: Employment terms, equal treatment and equal opportunities
heading: 6.1.6.1 Employment terms, equal treatment and equal opportunities
start_phrase: All employees can report suspected potential or actual misconduct by contacting their immediate manager or, if necessary, the Group HR unit.
summary:
- Overview of employment-related rights and risks, highlighting compliance obligations on equal pay and employee data privacy, with potential legal consequences for breaches.
- Group-wide governance: policies and directives accessible internally and publicly; Code of Conduct signed annually; references to broader governance sections.
- Human rights framework: commitments based on UDHR, EU Charter, ECHR, ILO Core Principles, UNCRC, and UN Guiding Principles; zero tolerance for discrimination; respect for freedom of association, collective bargaining, and bans on child and forced labor; safe, healthy working conditions with statutory hours and remuneration; expectations extended to consultants; whistleblowing encouraged. Human trafficking not explicitly in policy but prohibited in operating markets; measures required if direct violations occur.
- Healthy and sustainable working environment: Work Environment Directive covering physical, digital, organizational, and social factors; systematic risk assessment, action, and follow-up via a Group-wide agenda.
- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI): equal opportunities, zero tolerance of discrimination/harassment; broad set of protected characteristics; commitment to diverse leadership; DEI governance via GEC member and market DEI Leads; recurring employee surveys on inclusion and misconduct; mandatory investigations by HR/managers even on rumors; ongoing training, workshops, and communications; monitoring of gender distribution, sick leave, parental leave, age, and equal pay; employee information on procedures; support networks (e.g., LGBTQ+); trained investigators and whistleblower channels.
- Workforce engagement (S1-2): multiple channels including managers, intranet, meetings, newsletters, CEO/GEC Town Halls; structured dialogue with employee representatives via European Works Council and Swedish union/health & safety forums; employee board representation; People Pulse surveys; managers responsible for ongoing well-being discussions and actions.
- Remediation processes (S1-3): procedures to investigate irregularities and take corrective measures; support such as counseling; identified potential negative impact areas include employment terms, equal treatment/opportunities, and other work-related rights. Multiple reporting avenues: managers, Group HR, whistleblower system, digital incident reporting, unions, EWC, and H&S reps; social dialogue and potential union negotiations on breaches. No specific process to assess remedy effectiveness.
- Employee data handling: GDPR compliance, data protection officers, incident reporting, and employee data access rights.
- Work injuries: compensation and support mechanisms in Sweden (Försäkringskassan, TFA, occupational health) and the Baltic countries (general and private health insurance including psychological support); employer responsibility for continuous risk reduction.
- Whistleblowing: Group-wide process for reporting suspected misconduct; regular follow-up to ensure channel effectiveness and dialogue with whistleblowers.
- Actions on material impacts, risks, and opportunities (S1-4):
  - Strategy: comprehensive policies, systematic work environment management, continuous training, and open dialogue; sustainability-focused culture; definition of “sustainable employees” (manageable workload, work/life balance, respectful and inclusive climate); procurement risk controls (digital compliance checks, duality); sustainability upskilling for the green transition.
  - Workforce dependency: emphasis on attracting, retaining, and developing specialist talent; safe environment and personal development drive performance and long-term results.
  - Key actions: rollout of systematic health and safety work in the Baltics; fair and competitive pay via job architecture review; new skills development programs.
  - Implementation: regular one-on-ones to surface risks; anonymous whistleblowing option; quarterly management reviews under the Sustainable Employee Agenda using indicators (survey results, incident reports, sickness, turnover, business changes) to produce risk assessments and action plans; annual physical H&S inspections per site with central follow-up.

title: Handling of employee information
heading: 6.1.6.2 Handling of employee information
start_phrase: Swedbank is committed to protecting personal data and the rights of individuals, and has processes in place to ensure compliance with the General Data Protec- tion Regulation (GDPR).
summary:
- Employee incident reporting and social dialogue: Multiple channels to raise concerns (internal reporting system, trade unions, European Works Council, health and safety reps). Ongoing dialogue with employee representatives, co-determination in Sweden, and unions’ right to negotiate compensation for breaches of collective agreements. Cross-reference to collective bargaining and social dialogue (S1-8).
- Handling of employee information: Strong GDPR compliance with DPO oversight. Personal data used for service delivery, payments, credit/risk assessment, product improvement, AML/CFT and crime prevention. Personal data incidents treated as operational incidents; employees can request access to their data. More in S4-1.
- Human rights: Guided by Human Rights and Diversity, Equity and Inclusion policies; commitment to diversity, equal treatment and inclusion. Remediation required for direct human rights violations affecting employees or customers, though no set process to assess remedy effectiveness.
- Work injuries: Compensation via Försäkringskassan and TFA in Sweden; general health insurance in the Baltics plus employer-provided private health insurance with psychological support. Employer continuously improves the working environment and mitigates health risks.
- Whistleblowing: Group-wide process for reporting suspected misconduct (Code breaches, legal/policy violations). Cases followed up and channels’ effectiveness monitored. More in G1-1.
- Strategies for material impacts, risks and opportunities (S1-4): Comprehensive policies and systematic work environment management, continuous training and dialogue. “Sustainable employees” defined as those with manageable workload, work/life balance, and a respectful, inclusive climate. Procurement controls (digital compliance checks, dual decision-making) to prevent conflicts of interest and corruption. Sustainability training to support the green transition. More on anti-corruption in G1-3.
- Dependency on workforce: Business success relies on retaining, motivating and attracting skilled employees, especially specialists. Safe environment and development opportunities drive performance, long-term relationships, and sustainable results.
- Actions on significant impacts/risks/opportunities: Embed human rights, diversity and inclusion in culture and decisions; strengthen engagement, inclusion and fair pay. Many actions are ongoing, annual, or planned for 2025.
- Working conditions priorities and key actions: Aim for an engaging, inclusive, and developmental workplace that boosts profitability, efficiency, innovation and customer loyalty. Key actions include (1) implementing systematic work environment management in the Baltics, (2) ensuring fair, competitive pay via pay-based job architecture review, and (3) launching new skills development programs.
- Systematic health and safety management: 2024 rollout in the Baltics for group-common procedures. Regular manager–employee one-on-ones to discuss workload, health and risks, with follow-up measures. Option to report anonymously or escalate to higher management. Quarterly “Sustainable Employee Agenda” reviews by management using survey results, incident reports, sickness and turnover data, and business changes to assess risks and set action plans. Annual physical H&S inspections of each workplace (lighting, acoustics, ventilation, furniture), with risk assessments, corrective measures, and central follow-up.
text:
Handling of employee information 
Swedbank is committed to protecting personal data and the rights of individuals, 
and has processes in place to ensure compliance with the General Data Protec-
tion Regulation (GDPR). It is important that both Swedbank's employees and cus-
tomers feel confident about how their personal data is used and protected. Swed -
bank uses personal information to provide services, issue payments, and assess credit applications and risks, but also to improve products and quality though 
customer surveys and market analyses. The processing of personal information 
is also part of the work to prevent money laundering and financing of terrorism, and to prevent and investigate criminal activity. Swedbank’s data protection offi-
cers monitor the bank’s compliance. Personal data incidents must be reported 
as an operational incident, i.e. a deviation from ongoing operations. Swedbank 
employees may request information about which personal data is processed by 
Swedbank. There is additional information about Protection of personal data in 
accordance with GDPR in S4-1.

title: Respect for human rights
heading: 6.1.6.3 Respect for human rights
start_phrase: Respect for human rights is fundamental to Swedbank’s work, for which the Human Rights Policy and the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Policy set the frame- work.
summary:
- Employee incident and concern reporting:
  - Systems for day-to-day incident reporting with potential negative impact.
  - Additional channels via trade unions, European Works Council representatives, and health and safety reps per local laws.
  - Ongoing dialogue with employee representatives, including Sweden’s co-determination process.
  - Trade unions may initiate negotiations if collective agreement obligations are breached; further details in S1-8.

- Handling of employee information and GDPR:
  - Commitment to GDPR compliance and protecting personal data.
  - Personal data used for service delivery, payments, credit assessment and risk, product improvement (surveys/market analysis), AML/CFT, and crime prevention/investigation.
  - Data protection officers oversee compliance.
  - Personal data incidents treated as operational incidents.
  - Employees can request access to their processed personal data; more in S4-1.

- Respect for human rights and DEI:
  - Framework set by the Human Rights Policy and the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Policy.
  - Support for diversity, equal treatment, and inclusion.
  - Commitment to remedy direct human rights violations affecting employees or customers.
  - No specific process established to assess remedy effectiveness.

- Work injuries and health support:
  - Sweden: compensation via Försäkringskassan and TFA; access to occupational healthcare.
  - Baltics: compensation via general health insurance plus private health insurance from Swedbank, including psychological support.
  - Employer responsibility to reduce health risks and strengthen effective practices.

- Whistleblowing:
  - Overarching process encouraging reporting of suspected misconduct (e.g., Code of Conduct breaches, legal or policy violations).
  - Follow-up on reports and regular checks to ensure channels function; more in G1-1.

- Strategies for material impacts, risks, and opportunities (S1-4):
  - Comprehensive policies and systematic work environment management.
  - Continuous training, dialogue, and feedback to promote a safe workplace.
  - “Sustainable employees” defined as those able to manage workload, maintain work/life balance, and work in a respectful, supportive, inclusive climate.
  - Procurement risk controls through digital compliance checks and dual decision-making to prevent conflicts of interest and corruption.
  - Sustainability training to build capabilities for a greener, climate-friendly economy; more on anti-corruption in G1-3.

- Dependency on workforce:
  - Employees are foundational to long-term development and growth.
  - Focus on retaining, motivating, and attracting talent, especially specialists.
  - Aim for safe environments, personal development, and long-term relationships; sustainable employees drive sustainable customer relationships and results.

- Actions on significant impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - Integrate human rights into decisions and embed diversity and inclusion in culture.
  - Promote sustainable employees and good working environments to enhance employer attractiveness and profitability.
  - Actions target engagement, DEI, and fair wages; some continue in 2025 and recur annually.

- Working conditions and key actions:
  - Goal: engaging, attractive workplace with influence and development opportunities to drive profitability, efficiency, innovation, and customer loyalty.
  - Key actions:
    - Implement systematic work environment management in the Baltic countries.
    - Ensure fair and competitive pay via a job architecture review.
    - Launch new skills development programs.

- Systematic work environment practices:
  - 2024 rollout of group-common health and safety procedures in the Baltics.
  - Regular one-on-one manager-employee meetings to discuss work situation, health, and well-being; managers act on identified risks.
  - Anonymous whistleblowing option or escalation to manager’s manager.
  - Quarterly Sustainable Employee Agenda reviews by management teams using indicators (survey results, incident reports, sickness, turnover, business/external changes) to assess risks and set action plans.
  - Annual physical health and safety inspections at each workplace (e.g., lighting, acoustics, ventilation, furniture); deficiencies risk-assessed, remediated, and followed up centrally.
text:
Respect for human rights is fundamental to Swedbank’s work, for which the 
Human Rights Policy and the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Policy set the frame-
work. Swedbank supports the principles of diversity, equal treatment and inclusion. 
Swedbank is aware that incidents can occur despite efforts to counteract 
them. If the Group’s operations lead to a direct violation of human rights, Swed-
bank must take measures to remedy the situation, for both employees and 
 customers. 
Swedbank has not established a specific process for assessing whether 
a remedy to a situation would be effective.

text:
Work injuries
Employees who have suffered an work injury can receive compensation from Försäkringskassan (the Swedish social insurance system) and Trygghets -
försäkring vid arbetsskada (TFA) (work injury insurance) in Sweden. If necessary, employees can also receive support from the occupational healthcare scheme. 
In the Baltic countries, employees can receive compensation from the general 
health insurance system in the event of an work injury. In addition to general 
health insurance, Swedbank provides private health insurance for employees in 
the Baltic countries, which also includes psychological support.
As an employer, Swedbank is responsible for the working environment, where 
measures are taken on a continuous basis to reduce risks of ill health in the 
 working environment, while continuously strengthening what works well.

text:
Reporting suspected potential or actual misconduct 
The Group’s overarching whistleblower process encourages all employees and other stakeholders to report suspicions of potential or actual business miscon-
duct, such as breaches of the Code of Conduct, statutory violations or failure to 
comply with the Group’s policies. 
Swedbank follows up on reports and cases received via the Group’s whistle -
blower process and channels, and ensures that the channels function well by

title: Actions on material impacts, risks and opportunities, S1-4 - Introduction
heading: 6.1.7 Actions on material impacts, risks and opportunities, S1-4
start_phrase: Swedbank has implemented comprehensive policies and systematic work envi- ronment management to ensure that its own practices do not negatively affect employees.
summary: Swedbank’s S1-4 strategies outline actions to manage material impacts, risks and opportunities related to employees and procurement, including comprehensive policies and systematic work environment management to prevent negative effects on employees, continuous training with dialogue and feedback to ensure a safe workplace, and a definition of “sustainable employees” emphasizing manageable workloads, work/life balance, and a respectful, supportive, inclusive climate. text:
Actions on material impacts, risks and 
 opportunities, S1-4 
Strategies
Swedbank has implemented comprehensive policies and systematic work envi-
ronment management to ensure that its own practices do not negatively affect 
employees. Through continuous training and opportunities for dialogue and feed -
back, a safe working environment is promoted. Swedbank’s operations have a strong focus on sustainability. According to Swedbank’s definition of sustainable 
employees, every employee must feel that they can manage their work situation, 
that they have a good work/life balance, and that there is a respectful, supportive and inclusive working climate. In terms of procurement, risks relating to conflicts 
of interest and corruption are prevented by built-in digitalised compliance checks 
and duality in the decision-making process. As part of the transition to a greener 
and more climate-friendly economy, employees undergo sustainability training to 
build new skills in line with the area and new requirements, and to be able to meet 
customers to provide advisory services and to offer new products. 
There is additional information about anti-corruption and bribery in Prevention 
and detection of corruption and bribery, G1-3.

text:
Dependencies on own workforce 
Swedbank’s employees are the foundation for our business and a prerequisite for ensuring long-term development and growth. It is important that Swedbank can 
retain, motivate and attract competent employees. Employees with specialist 
expertise are a success factor and important for the Group. Swedbank seeks to 
offer a safe work environment where personal development is encourage and to 
create the conditions for good performance and long-term relationships. Sustain -
able employees can build sustainable customer relationships, which in turn can create sustainable results for the Group.

title: Swedbank works systematically for a sustainable working environment
heading: 6.1.7.2.1.1 Swedbank works systematically for a sustainable working environment
start_phrase: To ensure a sustainable working environment and a sustainable working climate, Swedbank works consistently and systematically with the working environ ment.
summary:
- Incident and concern reporting: Multiple channels for employees to report work-related incidents and concerns, including internal reporting systems, trade unions, European Works Council representatives, and health and safety reps; ongoing social dialogue via European Works Council meetings and Sweden’s co-determination process; unions can negotiate compensation for collective agreement breaches; references to collective bargaining coverage.
- Personal data handling: Strong GDPR compliance with clear purposes for processing (service delivery, payments, credit/risk assessment, surveys/market analysis, AML/CFT, crime prevention); Data Protection Officers oversee compliance; personal data incidents classified as operational incidents; employees can request access to their data; additional GDPR details referenced.
- Human rights: Commitment anchored in Human Rights and Diversity, Equity and Inclusion policies; intent to remedy direct violations affecting employees or customers, though no defined process to assess remedy effectiveness.
- Work injuries and health: Compensation frameworks in Sweden (Försäkringskassan, TFA) and the Baltics (general health insurance plus private health insurance with psychological support); employer duty to continuously improve the working environment.
- Whistleblowing: Group-wide process and channels for reporting suspected misconduct (Code of Conduct breaches, legal/policy violations); systematic follow-up and channel effectiveness checks; further policy references provided.
- Strategy and governance (S1-4): Systematic work environment management, continuous training, and feedback to ensure safe, inclusive, and sustainable workplaces; “sustainable employees” defined by manageable workload, work/life balance, and respectful climate; procurement controls include digital compliance checks and dual decision-making to mitigate conflicts of interest and corruption; sustainability training to build new skills for advisory and product development; anti-corruption information referenced.
- Workforce dependency: Business success relies on attracting, retaining, and motivating competent specialists; focus on safe environments, personal development, and long-term relationships to drive sustainable customer relationships and results.
- Actions on impacts, risks, and opportunities: Integrate human rights, DEI, and good working conditions into operations; actions target engagement, inclusion, and fair wages; several initiatives continue into 2025 and recur annually.
- Working conditions initiatives:
  - Key actions: Implement systematic health and safety management in the Baltics; ensure fair and competitive pay via job architecture review; expand skills development programs.
  - Systematic practices: Regular manager–employee one-on-ones addressing workload, health, and risks; anonymous whistleblowing options; quarterly Sustainable Employee Agenda reviews using surveys, incident data, sickness, turnover, and business changes to generate risk assessments and action plans; annual physical workplace inspections with follow-up; occupational health provider in Sweden and health insurance in the Baltics; wellness initiatives; Group-wide workplace concept “Swedbank at Work.”
- Compensation and pay equity: Transparent Salary Policy with structured criteria; market-aligned salaries using job architecture; Sweden’s minimum wage via collective agreements; Baltic reference wages via external providers; commitment to equal pay for equal work; annual checks against country standards; 2024 review of job architecture to support fairness and competitiveness.
- Learning and development: Multi-format learning (formal training, LinkedIn Learning, mentorships, workshops, on-the-job); 2024 programs include Inspire forward leadership, Project Management Programme, Java upskilling, and ESG strengthening for corporate client executives; effectiveness tracked via KPIs (training hours, turnover, sick leave, salary review outcomes, pay gaps, equal treatment, engagement).
- DEI focus: Group-wide DEI Policy, including Board application; rotating Chief Diversity Officer on the executive committee to embed DEI; management skills programs (reverse mentoring, expert sessions) to address unconscious bias; salary equity mapping and corrective actions to ensure equal pay; DEI positioned as a lever for attraction, retention, loyalty, and business continuity.
- Employee networks and inclusion practices: Swedbank Women in Tech, LGBTQ+ network GLaS, and Young Professionals to foster networking, innovation, and retention; flexible hours and prayer rooms to accommodate religious practices; participation in external DEI benchmarks; outcomes monitored via turnover, sick leave, pay gap, equity, and engagement metrics.
- Employee data rights and privacy safeguards: Annual GDPR reviews, personal data deletion projects, updated processing principles; policies for data collection, storage, access, and deletion; internal and external audits; regular staff training; data minimization; Retention Rule and Data Processing registries to manage deletions; strict access controls; robust security and incident response with reporting channels; compliance overseen by Group Privacy and Privacy Managers; mechanisms for employees to question and provide feedback on data handling.
text:
Swedbank works systematically for a sustainable working environment
To ensure a sustainable working environment and a sustainable working climate, 
Swedbank works consistently and systematically with the working environ  ment. 
In 2024, implementation of the systematic health and safety work began in the Baltic countries in order to achieve Group common procedures for work-related 
health. A key aspect of this work is the manager’s close dialogue with each 
employee, based on one-on-one meetings. These meetings entail regular discus-
sion between manager and employee of the employee's work situation, health 
and well-being, and give employees the opportunity to raise any problems or risks 
they may experience in the course of their work. If there is any kind of work envi -
ronment risk, the manager will take action and follow up on the results.
Employees also have the opportunity to whistleblow anonymously or to 
 contact the manager’s manager if they experience problems.
To identify any working environment risks and take appropriate actions from 
an organisational perspective, the businesses’ management teams work on a quarterly basis according to a joint bank work environment agenda called the 
Sustain  able Employee Agenda. Based on the agenda, the management teams 
systematically review indications of potential work environment risks, based on, 
for example, the results of employee surveys, incident reporting, sickness rates, 
staff turnover, and changes in the business or external circumstances. The man-
agement teams then draw up risk assessments and action plans to deal with 
 situations that arise and to work preventively. 
An annual physical health and safety inspection is carried out for each branch/
workplace, whereby a systematic review is conducted to see how lighting, acous-
tics, ventilation, furni  tur e, furnishings, etc. function and are experienced by the 
employees. After this inspection, deficiencies are risk assessed and measures are taken. Health and safety inspections are followed up annually at central level.

 matters, Swedbank in Sweden has a nationwide occupational health provider 
that offers extensive prevention, remediation and follow-up/rehabilitation services. 
In the Baltic countries, equivalent needs for health-related services are covered 
by health insurance policies provided by Swedbank for employees. Swedbank 
also offers wellness initiatives to improve health throughout the Group. 
To support the organisational, social and digital working environment at the 
workplace, Swedbank has developed the Group-wide workplace concept Swed-
bank at Work, which is gradually being implemented in all home markets.

text:
Competitive and fair pay
Swedbank works systematically with salary analyses to ensure that they are 
competitive and fair. Salaries and benefits are an element of the working condi-
tions offered that can help retain and attract new talent in a highly competitive 
industry. At Swedbank, the Salary Policy is reported openly and transparently, and 
salary criteria are used in a structured way to provide an objective assessment of 
employees’ competence and performance, and the degree of difficulty of the 
work. Swedbank seeks to offer competitive salaries that are matched to relevant 
market pay levels, based on the set job architecture. In Sweden, the minimum wage is laid down in collective agreements and in the Baltic countries, reference 
wages are calculated using independent external payroll data providers. Swed-
bank works in a structured manner with the principle of equal pay for equal work, 
or work of equal value. 
Swedbank conducts an annual review to ensure that all employees have a 
salary at the level of the standard reference salary in each country of operation, 
linked to legal regulations and collective agreements. To ensure that Swedbank can offer competitive and fair salaries, Swedbank’s job architecture, which forms 
the basis for the salaries set, was reviewed in 2024.

text:
Development and learning 
In a fast-changing and complex environment, learning and development are 
 crucial to staying up to date and relevant. In the Swedbank Group, learning and 
development take place in many ways and in different formats, both through 
formal training and together with colleagues while performing regular work 
tasks. Swedbank promotes a learning culture that encourages and supports 
employees to take responsibility for their own development and employability. 
Employees are offered various opportunities to develop the competencies they 
need, both in existing and future roles. There are opportunities to participate in 
LinkedIn Learning courses, mentorship programmes, workshops, team discus -
sions and other formal training in different formats. In 2024, a variety of skills 
development initiatives were launched to enable both managers and employees 
to develop in their current role or prepare for future roles. Examples of these are 
the Inspire forward leadership development programme, which aims to prepare 
selected leaders for strategic leadership roles, and the Project Management Pro-
gramme, which aims to develop the employee’s project management skills in 
their current role. Additional examples include the opportunity to broaden your 
tech role and apply for upskilling in JAVA programming, as well as an upskilling initiative aimed to strengthen client executives on the corporate side within ESG.
Effectiveness is followed up by means of key indicators for training hours, 
staff turnover,  sick leave, annual salary review and salary setting, pay gaps, equal 
treatment and engagement.

text:
Equal pay for equal work
Gender balance throughout the organisation can enable Swedbank to reduce the 
structural effects that can have a negative impact. Equal pay for equal work 
denotes that pay is set on a fair basis for all employees and reduces potential 
 discrimination. 
Swedbank's remuneration strategy aims to attract and retain a workforce with 
the diversity, ability, experience and skills to deliver in accordance with Swed-bank’s strategy in an inclusive and equitable working environment. Swedbank’s 
annual salary equity mapping and work on unfair pay differences indicate that 
equity is important. This is expected to contribute to making Swedbank a more 
attractive employer for potential talent seeking a fair and inclusive working envi-
ronment. It also means taking responsibility for the well-being of employees and 
creating a trusting relationship with both current and future employees. Employ -
ees who feel fairly treated are less likely to seek other employers and their loyalty 
will be stronger. Lower staff turnover means lower costs of recruiting and training 
new employees, while contributing to business continuity.

text:
Other work-related rights
To prevent, mitigate and remedy significant negative impacts on the company’s 
own workforce when it comes to inadequate handling of employee information 
and data, Swedbank has taken the following actions.
Key actions: 
• Annual GDPR review
• Project for deletion of personal data
• Updating of principles for the processing of employees’ personal data
Swedbank has clear guidelines and policies for how employee information 
should be handled, including collection, storage, access and deletion. Compli-
ance with these policies is monitored through internal and external audits con -
ducted by Internal Audit, Group Compliance, Group Risk or external companies. 
All employees receive regular training on data protection, privacy issues and the 
Group’s information management policies.
Swedbank ensures that only the information absolutely necessary for the 
 business is collected, in order to minimise the amount of personal data that is 
handled, while any unnecessary data is deleted. Swedbank uses the Retention 
Rule Registry and Data Processing Registry to easily follow up on deletion proce-
dures for each system/process in Swedbank. There is also strict access control, 
to ensure that only authorised persons have access to sensitive information.
Swedbank has robust security solutions to prevent data breaches and incor-
rect handling of personal data. There are clear processes to follow in the event of 
a data incident or data breach, and a dedicated channel via which employees can 
report suspected security incidents. Swedbank ensures compliance with relevant data protection regulations such as the GDPR (General Data Protection Regula -
