heading: 6.1.7.4 Follow-up on actions
start_phrase: A number of metrics and indicators have been implemented to follow up and ensure that the actions and initiatives implemented by Swedbank lead to good results.
summary:
- GDPR and data governance: In 2024 Swedbank ran a Group-wide GDPR review covering employees, consultants, candidates, and customers, with annual cadence. It launched a multi‑year personal data deletion project (2024–2025) to harmonize and register deletion periods across systems, and updated principles for processing employees’ and consultants’ personal data, to be consulted in 2025 and revised continuously. Additional GDPR information is referenced in S4-1.

- Monitoring and follow-up: Swedbank uses defined metrics and indicators to track outcomes of actions and initiatives. The People Pulse survey ran three times in 2024, covering nine themes (engagement, NPS/commitment, sustainable employees, strategic direction, compensation, performance development, leadership, work culture, equal treatment). Managers analyze and act on team results.

- Health, safety, and absence: Sick leave (short and long term) is monitored in each home market and at Group level, including oversight by Group Risk. Management teams’ work environment risks and action plans are reviewed quarterly by the central health and safety committee. The Sustainable Employee Index is a key KPI for business area managers and is followed quarterly alongside equal opportunity issues, sickness rates, and incidents.

- Performance management: “Performance Development” supports goal setting aligned to strategy, with annual manager-employee reviews that assess performance, conduct, and development.

- Equal opportunities and data: Equal opportunity and anti-discrimination efforts are measured via the annual survey. Swedbank tracks gender and age (via personal identity numbers) but does not collect other protected characteristics (e.g., LGBTQ+, ethnicity, disability). Additional sick leave detail is referenced in note G13.9.

- Workforce metrics and targets (S1-5): Strategic workforce focus on employee engagement and a sustainable workforce. Targets from 1 Jan 2024:
  - Sustainable Employee Index ≥80
  - Engagement Index ≥80
  - Equity and diversity: achieve 40/60 gender balance (women/men) at top management and among successors to top management; maintain equal pay for equal work and reduce the gender pay gap.
  Scope covers Group employees across Swedbank’s home markets and selected international locations; some data involves assumptions and is not externally validated.

- Target-setting and governance: Process owners in Group HR propose targets based on prioritized areas and survey insights; Group HR management reviews, Head of Group HR elevates to GEC/CEO, and the CEO adopts. Targets are intended to be consistent over time; no methodological changes in the year. Employee representatives on the Board support follow-up. Results are reviewed quarterly by GEC and reported annually; targets apply to the 2024 financial year.

- 2024 results highlights: Engagement remained high and stable; strongest scores in team collaboration, learning and development, and meaningful work. Sustainable employee measures stayed high, reflecting the value of combining workplace flexibility with in-person collaboration.
text:
Follow-up on actions
A number of metrics and indicators have been implemented to follow up and 
ensure that the actions and initiatives implemented by Swedbank lead to good 
results. 
The People Pulse employee survey was conducted three times in 2024. The 
purpose is to understand how employees are doing and how they perceive, under -
stand and act in relation to Swedbank's strategically important areas. The aim of the survey is to track and promote changes in how the day-to-day work is per -
formed and to encourage continuous dialogue and an open feedback culture in 
every unit. The questions were related to nine areas: engagement, commitment 
(NPS), sustainable employees, strategic  dir ection, compensation, performance 
development, leadership, work culture and equal treatment. All managers are 
responsible for analysing the results and  following up on them with their team.
Follow-up of preventive actions concerning sick leave and intentional absence 
takes place in the respective home market and for the overall Group. Sick leave, 
as both long and short-term absence, is also monitored by the Group Risk unit. 
Performance Development is a tool that supports each employee in setting 
targets and development activities that contribute to Swedbank’s strategic 
 direction. The purpose of the annual performance review is for the manager 
and employee to summarise and evaluate targets for performance and conduct, 
and make a final performance assessment.
On a quarterly basis, the management teams’ work related to the work environ -
ment is followed up by Swedbank’s central health and safety committee, where 
each business unit reports its greatest work environment risks and an action plan 
to address them. Furthermore, the Sustainable Employee Index is followed up as 
a key indicator for business area managers at Swedbank. 
On a quarterly basis, Swedbank’s central health and safety committee follows up 
on the Sustainable Employee Index and equal opportunities issues, both of which are measured in People Pulse. Sickness rates and incidents are also followed up 
by each business area reporting its results and action plans with activities.
Swedbank measures and evaluates equal opportunities and anti-discrimina -
tion initiatives via the annual employee survey. The Sustainable Employee Index 
is also monitored as a key indicator at management level in GEC. Swedbank also 
follows up data regarding gender and age, based on personal identity numbers. Swedbank does not gather other grounds for discrimination such as identity (e.g. 
LGBTQ+), ethnicity or functional impairment. There is additional information 
about sick leave in note G13.9.

summary:
- Scope: Summarizes Swedbank’s 2024 approach and performance on employee training/skills development (ESRS S1-13) and health and safety metrics (ESRS S1-14), including methodologies, data sources, assumptions, and key results.

- Training and skills development (S1-13):

  - Competence standards: High competence expectations across roles; mandatory Group-wide courses on ethics, security, anti-corruption/bribery, and AML/CFT, with a 100% participation target for mandatory training.

    - High participation in regular performance and career development reviews (around 91–93% in 2024, broadly in line with 2023).

    - Review participation ratio covers employees with main assignments, broken down by gender.
    - Average training hours calculated as total completed hours per gender divided by total employees per gender; headcount figures align with ESRS S1-6.

    - Quality checks ensure completeness (all employment types/countries) and consistency (vs prior reports).

- Health and safety metrics (S1-14):
  - Scope and exclusions: Reports occupational accidents and work-related ill health occurring at or due to work; commuting incidents are excluded.
  - Reporting system: Incidents are reported per local legislation to authorities and internally through a Group incident system following a common routine.
  - Coverage and governance: 100% of employees are covered by the Group’s health and safety system in all operating countries; subject to external reviews (e.g., Sweden’s Work Environment Authority) and annual internal audits.
  - Assumptions: For Finland, Norway, USA, China, and PayEx (not fully covered by the incident system), accident frequency is assumed equal to other parts of the Group.

Calculation methodology 
In the Group, work-related injuries are reported as work-related accidents and work-related ill health according to the legislation in force in each country to 
respective authorities. Work-related accidents, work-related illnesses and 
work-related ill health are also reported internally as incidents in Swedbank’s

to a common bank routine.
The Work Environment Indicators table presents internally reported occupa -
tional injuries in the form of work-related accidents and illnesses that have also 
been reported to authorities. These occupational injuries have occurred at the 
workplace or due to of the work. Accidents that occur in connection with travel 
to or from work, so-called road accidents are not included.At Swedbank, all employees are covered by the Group’s health and safety system, 
regardless of the form of employment. Swedbank’s work environment system 
means that the Group applies local health and safety legislation in all countries 
where it operates and internal systematic work environment management is operated in each country.
Swedbank’s health and safety system is subject to external review. For exam -
ple, type: it can be mentioned that in Sweden, the Swedish authorities carry out 
via the Swedish Work Environment Authority, annual reviews of how Swedbank 
structures and manages the systematic the work environment work, and the 
results of the work environment work, against the background of the EU’s and 
Sweden’s health and safety legislation. Swedbank also conducts internal audits of work environment management annually.
Assumptions
The incident reporting system extends across the Group, with the exception of Finland, Norway, the USA and China, as well as PayEx. For these parts of the 
organisation, the same frequency of occupational accidents is assumed as for 
the other parts.

title: Work-life balance, S1-15
heading: 6.1.15 Work-life balance, S1-15
start_phrase: All Swedbank employees are entitled to parental leave through collective agree- ments or local legislation.
summary:
- Work-life balance and parental leave: All employees are entitled to parental leave via collective agreements or local law. Swedbank emphasizes flexibility as part of its equity and diversity work, offering part-time options for returnees, flexible hours, and offsite work when roles allow.
- Parental leave metric and scope: Measures the proportion of employees entitled to parental leave who actually took it, reported by legal gender (Male/Female) as of 31 December 2024. Additional country and gender detail is referenced in note G13.9.
- Parental leave assumptions: Employees outside home markets (5% of workforce) who are on leave on 31 December 2024 are assumed to be on parental leave; within this group, 5% of women and 2% of men are assumed to have taken leave.
- Parental leave results: 2024 vs 2023 share taking leave—Female: 16% (16%); Male: 15% (13%); Total: 16% (15%).
- Remuneration indicators purpose: Disclose gender pay gaps, CEO-to-median employee pay ratio, and equal pay for equal work gaps to assess remuneration inequality within the Group.
- Methodologies:
  - Gender pay gap: Difference between men’s and women’s gross hourly wages relative to men’s wage; scope is all Group employees; positive means men earn more.
  - CEO pay ratio: CEO’s annual total remuneration relative to the median of all employees (excluding the highest paid); scope is all Group employees.
  - Equal Pay Gap: Comparison of average salary index for men and women by job level and market in home markets; positive means men earn more.
- Data sources and quality: Data drawn from HR and finance systems; missing legal-entity data gathered from entity representatives; checks for completeness and consistency against prior reports.
- Remuneration assumptions: Where entity data is missing, assume results align with other entities. Since home markets are ~95% of the workforce, the Group median total remuneration is assumed equal to the home markets’ median.
- Reported outcomes:
  - Gender pay gap (all employees), 2024 (2023): Sweden 19% (19%); Estonia 29% (29%); Latvia 29% (30%); Lithuania 32% (33%); Swedbank Group 28% (29%).
  - CEO total remuneration ratio vs employees’ median, 2024 (2023): Group 31 (32).
  - Equal Pay Gap (equal work), 2024 (2023): Sweden 1.6% (1.9%); Estonia 0.1% (1.1%); Latvia 0.2% (0.9%); Lithuania –0.2% (0%); Total (home markets) 1.1% (1.5%).
- Clarifications: Gender is measured as legal gender (Male/Female).
text:
All Swedbank employees are entitled to parental leave through collective agree-
ments or local legislation. Flexibility is an important factor in equity and diversity 
work and has long been a natural part of the Group’s ways of working. Employees 
returning from parental leave can work part-time and are offered flexible arrange -
ments to the extent possible. To make everyday life easier, Swedbank also offers employees flexible working hours and the opportunity to work offsite, when the 
role allows. 
Calculation methodology
Proportion of employees entitled to parental leave who have taken parental leave, 
divided by gender, Male/Female. In the reporting of family leave, parental leave is 
reported at the end of the year on 31 December 2024.
Assumptions
All employees outside Swedbank’s home markets that are on leave on 31 December 
2024 are assumed to be on parental leave. Based on this assumption, 5 per cent 
of female and 2 per cent of male employees took parental leave in this group. 
Employees outside Swedbank’s home markets consist of 5 per cent of all

- Remuneration indicators (S1-16)
  - Purpose: show gender pay gaps, CEO-to-median pay ratio, and equal pay for equal work, to assess remuneration inequality.
  - Methodologies:
    - Gender pay gap = (men’s gross hourly wage − women’s) relative to men’s; scope: all Group employees; positive % means men earn more.
    - CEO total remuneration ratio = CEO’s annual total remuneration / median annual total remuneration of all other employees; scope: all employees.
    - Equal Pay Gap = comparison of average salary index for men vs women per job level and market; scope: home markets; positive % means men earn more.
  - Data sources and quality: HR and finance systems; missing data obtained from legal entities; checks for completeness and consistency with prior reports.
  - Assumptions: where entity data is missing, align with observed totals; Group median remuneration assumed equal to home markets’ median (home markets ≈95% of workforce).

    - Gender pay gap 2024 (2023): Sweden 19% (19), Estonia 29% (29), Latvia 29% (30), Lithuania 32% (33), Group 28% (29).

    - Equal Pay Gap 2024 (2023): Sweden 1.6% (1.9), Estonia 0.1% (1.1), Latvia 0.2% (0.9), Lithuania −0.2% (0), Total 1.1% (1.5).

- Consumers and end-users (S4): information-related impacts
  - Materiality: handling sensitive customer information assessed as a material topic across the value chain.
  - Strategy: robust personal data protection embedded in strategy; products and services designed to meet GDPR requirements.
  - Risk management: processes to identify, manage, and mitigate data-protection risks for new/changed products, processes, and organizational changes.
  - Potential impacts: inadequate data handling can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, customer anxiety, and financial risk.
  - Affected stakeholders: existing/prospective customers, employees and consultants (and related parties), and branch visitors.
  - Vulnerable groups: minors, elderly, individuals with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance data.

- Governance and policies for data protection (S4-1)
  - Key documents: Code of Conduct; Policy for Human Rights (aligned with UN Guiding Principles); Policy for Conduct Risk; Customer Complaint Policy.
  - Commitments: compliance with laws on fundamental rights including personal data protection; due diligence to prevent and address negative impacts in own operations and business relationships.
  - Conduct Risk Policy principles cover product design/distribution, data processing, and market conduct risks; Complaint Policy ensures effective handling and prevention of recurring issues.
  - GDPR application: processing requires a legal basis and balancing of interests vs individuals’ rights; applies to all data subjects whose data Swedbank processes; customer communications provide detailed information on processing practices.
text:
The tables presenting pay gaps provide information on the percentage difference between women’s and men’s salaries and the ratio between the remuneration of 
the highest paid employee and the median remuneration of all employees. Differ-
ences in equal pay for equal work are also reported. The purpose is to provide an 
understanding of the pay gaps between female and male Swedbank employees 
and to give insights into the extent of remuneration inequality, and whether there 
are large pay gaps within Swedbank between women’s and men’s salaries and 
the ratio between the remuneration of the highest paid employee and the median remuneration of all employees. Differences in equal pay for equal work are also 
reported. The purpose is to provide an understanding of the pay gaps between 
female and male Swedbank employees and to give insights into the extent of 
remuneration inequality, and whether there are large pay gaps within Swedbank.
Calculation methodology
Gender pay gaps are calculated as the difference between the gross hourly wage 
for all men and the gross hourly wage for all women, in relation to the men’s gross 
hourly wage. The scope of application is all employees within the Group. A posi-
tive percentage means that men have higher remuneration than women and 
vice versa.
Total remuneration ratio of the CEO compared to employees is calculated  
as the annual total remuneration of the highest paid individual (CEO) in relation 
to the median for the annual total remuneration of all employees (excluding the highest paid individual). The scope of application is all employees within 
the Group.
Equal Pay Gap is calculated as a comparison between average salary index 
for men and women per job level and market. The scope is Swedbank’s home 
markets. A positive percentage means that men have higher remuneration than 
women and vice versa.
Data used for calculations is retrieved from HR and finance systems. If data on 
a specific legal entity is missing from the systems, a representative of the legal entity is asked to provide this information. To ensure the quality of the data, 
Swedbank checks that the data is complete (if all employment forms and coun -
tries are included in the data) and that it is  consistent (if the data matches previ -
ous annual and monthly reports).Assumptions
If certain legal entities do not have this information, their results are assumed to be consistent with the total percentage observed for the other legal entities. 
Since Swedbank’s employees in the home market account for around 95 per cent 
of the entire Swedbank Group’s workforce, it is assumed that the median of the 
total remuneration per year for the Swedbank Group is equal to the median of the 
total remuneration for Swedbank’s home markets.

title: Strategy and business model, SBM-3
heading: 6.2.2 Strategy and business model, SBM-3
start_phrase: For Swedbank, the protection of sensitive customer information is imperative and customers must feel confident about how the Group handles personal data.
summary:
- Focus and scope: Section S4 covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers and end-users across the value chain, identified as material in the Group’s assessment.
- Strategic importance: Protecting sensitive customer information is core to the business model and strategy. The bank designs products and services to meet GDPR requirements and operates structured policies, guidelines and processes to ensure correct, secure data handling.
- Risk management: Swedbank has processes to identify, manage and mitigate risks in personal data processing, including for new or changed products, processes and organizational changes, ensuring alignment with strategy.

  - Policy for Human Rights (UN Guiding Principles; due diligence to prevent and address adverse impacts in own operations and business relationships)
  - Policy for Conduct Risk (principles for product design, distribution, data processing, and market conduct)
  - Customer Complaint Policy (standards for handling complaints and preventing recurrence)

text:
For Swedbank, the protection of sensitive customer information is imperative 
and customers must feel confident about how the Group handles personal data. 
In the materiality assessment performed during the year, information-related 
impacts for consumers and end-users were assessed as material, particularly 
in relation to the handling of sensitive customer information.
Swedbank offers a wide range of financial services that entail significant 
responsibility for handling sensitive customer data. This responsibility is funda-
mental to the Group’s strategy and activities, as it requires that all data handling takes place in a correct and secure manner that prevents harm to customers and 
other stakeholders. Swedbank has processes to identify, manage and mitigate 
risks that may arise in connection with the processing of personal data. Swed-
bank’s handling of personal data is based on structured working methods based 
on policies, guidelines and processes according to the requirements of the Gen-
eral Data Protection Regulation (GDPR
1). This means that the Group’s products 
and services are designed according to the Regulation's requirements. This pro -
tects both customers and employees when personal data is processed. Swed -
bank has processes to ensure that risks associated with new or changed prod-ucts, processes and organisation are managed and are compatible with the 
Group’s strategy. The provision of financial products and services involves the 
processing of a large amount of data, the inadequate handling of which may lead 
to a breach of personal privacy, lost of trust, distrust and anxiety among custom-ers, which may constitute a financial risk for Swedbank. The stakeholders that 
can be affected include existing and prospective customers, employees, includ -
ing consultants, and their related parties, and visitors to Swedbank’s branches. 
Through the interpretation and application of GDPR and guidance from author-
ities, Swedbank has identified customer groups at higher risk in the event of data protection breaches. Minors, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities are con-
sidered vulnerable groups in data protection as they may have difficulty under -
standing the significance of personal data and finding and processing informa -
tion on its management and protection. Customers with health-related insurance are at greater risk of sensitive personal data, which has special protection under 
GDPR, falling into the wrong hands during a data breach. 
Swedbank is committed to robust personal data protection for all individuals, 
aware that correct handling is crucial to maintain trust.Managing impacts, risks and opportunities

Emphasizes compliance with laws on fundamental rights and GDPR, with personal data rights integrated into human rights commitments.
text:
Policies, S4-1
Swedbank has policies and governance documents addressing impacts, risks 
and opportunities related to consumers and end-users, including handling sensi -
tive customer information. The main governance documents at policy level are:
• Code of Conduct
• Policy for Human Rights 
• Policy for  Conduct Risk
• Customer Complaint Policy 
It is important for Swedbank to act in accordance with laws and regulations on the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals, including the fundamental 
right to the protection of their personal data. The Code of Conduct states the 
Group’s values and includes commitments regarding data protection, including the fundamental right to the protection of personal data. The Policy for Human 
Rights is based on the UN Guiding Principles for Business and Human Rights. 
This forms the basis for the work and highlights that Swedbank must act with 
due diligence in both its own operations and in business relations. The work 
focuses on taking precautionary measures and preventing negative impacts, as 
well as preventing human rights violations and actively addressing them if they 
occur, even if the Group itself has not directly contributed to these impacts. 
The Policy for Conduct Risks forms the basis for managing conduct risks and 
outlines the principles to be observed when the group designs, distributes, and evaluates financial products and services, during data processing, and in han-
dling market conduct-related risks. Swedbank’s Policy regarding customer com -
plaints forms the foundation for receiving and handling customer complaints against Swedbank and describes how employees should manage incoming com -
plaints and how the group should work to minimise future complaints. Personal 
data rights are included as part of Swedbank’s commitment to respect human 
rights by following EU guidelines related to GDPR.

title: Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
heading: 6.2.3.1 Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
start_phrase: GDPR is based on established and internationally recognised conventions and principles for the protection of human rights.
summary:
- Scope and materiality: The S4 Consumers and end-users section covers Swedbank’s information-related impacts on consumers/end-users, identified as a material topic in the downstream value chain. Protecting sensitive customer data is central to the Group’s strategy. Mishandling data can cause privacy breaches, loss of trust, anxiety, and financial risk. Affected stakeholders include customers, prospects, employees/consultants, and visitors. Vulnerable groups include minors, the elderly, people with disabilities, and customers with health-related insurance.

- Governance and policies: Swedbank manages these impacts via the Code of Conduct, Human Rights Policy (aligned with UNGPs), Conduct Risk Policy, and Customer Complaint Policy. The right to personal data protection is treated as a human right. GDPR compliance underpins product/service design and data processing. Risk management follows the three lines of defence with independent controls, supported by a Data Protection Officer function. The Group does not currently track cases of failures to respect international principles in the downstream value chain.

- GDPR compliance and stakeholder information: Personal data processing requires a legal basis, with transparent information provided through websites, apps, branches, and customer meetings. Redress/compensation for data breaches follows GDPR and applicable law. The approach is aligned with SDGs, ILO, OECD, and UN guidance to promote ethical practices and human rights.

- Procedures for contact and rights (S4-2): Swedbank explains what data is collected, why, legal grounds, and processing practices, enabling customers to exercise their rights. Data handling adheres to GDPR principles: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.

- Complaints and incident handling: Customer complaints are logged, reviewed quarterly, and used to drive improvements; cases close when repeat complaints cease. Employees receive regular information security training. In the event of non-compliance or incidents, affected individuals are notified without undue delay via direct channels or public notices if necessary. The CEO has ultimate responsibility; operational incident management lies with designated coordinators; effectiveness is tested via first- and second-line controls and benchmarking against authority guidance and case law. Customer satisfaction is monitored via regular surveys (NKI).

- Remediation (S4-3): Data Breach Guidelines govern incident response and evaluation of remedial sufficiency. Customers can escalate issues through the customer centre, branches, Data Protection Officer, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and then to external authorities (e.g., ARN, IMY) or consumer advisory bodies.

- Data processors: A three-step due diligence process covers pre-contract assessments (technical/organizational/contractual measures), ongoing monitoring of security posture, and off-boarding to ensure return/erasure of personal data per contract.

- Actions and strategies (S4-4): Ongoing work spans regulatory compliance, risk identification, customer communication, and tool/system support. “Data protection by design and by default” is embedded in product and service development. Expected outcomes are not specified due to uncertainty; no progress metrics are provided as this is the first year of CSRD-aligned reporting.

- Training and awareness: Annual and role-based information security training is mandatory across all countries. Swedbank runs a yearly security month, regular briefings, and continuous phishing simulations. Mandatory and voluntary GDPR/data protection training aims to strengthen employee awareness and, indirectly, customer and societal understanding of personal data protection.
text:
Protection of personal data in accordance with GDPR
GDPR is based on established and internationally recognised conventions and 
principles for the protection of human rights. The Regulation holds Swedbank 
responsible for considering the individual’s perspective and right to protection 
of their personal data. No processing of personal data may take place without a 
legal basis and careful consideration of Swedbank’s interests and the individual’s 
right to protection of personal data. These rules and considerations apply not 
only to Swedbank’s customers, but to everyone whose personal data is pro-
cessed by Swedbank. Contact with end-users and consumers regarding the pro-cessing of personal data takes place by providing detailed information on the 
1) Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free 
movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation).
128 Swedbank Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 – Board of Directors’ reportFinancial reports Sustainability report Corporate governance report Financial analysis Business Areas Value creationprocessing of personal data and a data protection officer. They can also reach 
out to Swedbank via  v arious contact channels such as chat, letters or visits to 
Swedbank’s physical branches, which are described in detail on the Group’s web-
sites. Redress, in the form of compensation, in the event of a personal data 
breach takes place in accordance with GDPR and other applicable legislation. 
The Policy for Human Rights concerns the handling of personal data. The 
Policy follows international principles and guidelines such as the UN Sustainable 
Development Goals, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, 
and guidelines from the ILO, International Labour Organisation and the OECD, 
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. This underlines the Group’s work for ethical business practices and human rights, which includes the 
right to protection of their personal data, privacy and family life. Swedbank does 
not currently measure the number of reported cases of failure to respect these 
international principles and guidelines involving consumers and/or end-users in 
the downstream value chain.
Data protection permeates all handling of personal data. The group’s risk man-
agement is based on the principle of three lines of defence, whereby a structured chain of responsibility with independent controls ensures that non-compliance is 
followed up, managed and reported. This not only reduces risks and improves 
operational efficiency in Swedbank, but also builds trust among customers, 
employees and stakeholders. The Group’s commitment to continuous compli-
ance promotes a culture of transparency and accountability that upholds individ -
uals’ right to privacy and contributes positively to society. Additional information on Swedbank's governance documents can be found in Swedbank’s governance documents, MDR-P .

title: Procedures for contacts, S4-2
heading: 6.2.4 Procedures for contacts, S4-2
start_phrase: Swedbank publishes information on external websites, at customer meetings and in applications about how and why the Group collects and processes cus - tomers’ personal information and data, and how customers can assert their rights.
summary:
- Bank-wide commitment to GDPR-compliant processing, customer redress for personal data breaches, and multiple contact channels (chat, mail, branches, web).
- Human Rights Policy aligned with UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles, ILO and OECD guidelines, emphasizing privacy and data protection; no current tracking of downstream human-rights noncompliance cases.
- Governance and risk management via three lines of defence with independent controls; CEO holds ultimate accountability for personal data handling; designated incident coordinators manage operations.
- Transparent customer information on data collection, purposes, legal bases, processing and retention, with access to DPO, customer service, and authorities; tools such as register extract forms provided.
- Seven GDPR-aligned data protection principles guide all processing: lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability.
- Complaint handling integrates customer feedback into improvements: complaints logged, reviewed quarterly, followed by evaluation, testing, and closure; actions routed through data breach or complaint processes as needed.
- Incident response and notification: affected individuals contacted promptly (phone/email/website); processes assessed through first- and second-line controls and by referencing regulatory guidance and case law; customer satisfaction tracked via surveys (NKI).
- Remediation (S4-3): Data Breach Guidelines define actions for incidents with significant negative impacts and require evaluation of action sufficiency; overall GDPR compliance embedded in policies and directives.
- Communication and escalation options: customers can elevate matters to the DPO, complaints officer, or customer ombudsman; if unresolved, external bodies (ARN, IMY, municipal advisers, Consumer Banking and Finance Agency) are available.

text:
Swedbank publishes information on external websites, at customer meetings and in applications about how and why the Group collects and processes cus -
tomers’ personal information and data, and how customers can assert their rights. The Group thereby makes it possible for customers to maintain their right 
to protection of their own personal data. Swedbank’s handling of personal data 
must always be conducted in line with the Group’s established processes that are 
based on seven data protection principles.  
These seven principles are:
a.  Lawfulness, transparency and accuracy
b. Limitation of purpose
c. Data minimisation
d. Accuracy
e. St orage minimisation
f. Integrity and confidentiality (security)
g. Liability
Complaint handling and continuous evaluation
Customers can submit complaints directly to Swedbank, where they are regis -
tered in the bank’s internal system for handling customer complaints. These complaints are an important source for Swedbank to identify and prioritise nec-
essary improvements based on customer requests. Through its complaint han-
dling process, the customer’s perspective can be integrated into Swedbank’s 
decisions on measures. The customer complaint process includes follow-up, 
evaluation and implementation of improvement measures. Swedbank reviews 
and addresses complaints on a quarterly basis, to identify and implement solu-tions. The improvements are tested and evaluated, whereby the case is closed 
when no further complaints are received. If actions are needed, they are handled 
according to the bank’s processes for personal data breaches or customer com-
plaints. Swedbank employees receive regular training to enhance their compe -
tence in information security. Read more in Actions and Strategies, S4-4.
If Swedbank fails to comply with personal data processing regulations, the 
affected persons must, if possible, be contacted by telephone or e-mail. If this is 
not feasible, information can be provided via the website or other public channels. 
Contact with the individuals affected must take place as soon as possible and 
without delay. The ultimate responsibility for the correct and lawful handling of 
personal data within Swedbank lies with the CEO. The operational responsibility 
for handling personal data incidents is delegated to personal data incident coordi -
nators and decision-makers. Swedbank evaluates that the processes are appro -
priate through operational controls, analysis and follow-up in the first and second lines of defence. In addition to Swedbank’s assessment of personal data risk 
levels, guidelines, reports and investigations by authorities, and established 
national and international court practice, are applied in matters relating to the right 
to respect for family life, privacy and correspondence, as well as the right to pro -
tection of personal data. This is then used for comparison with Swedbank’s estab -
lished data protection processes, so that any gaps can be identified and remedied. 
Swedbank conducts regular customer surveys (NKI) to monitor customer satis -
faction with the aim of improving the group’s processes.

title: Communication channels and data processors
heading: 6.2.5.1 Communication channels and data processors
start_phrase: It is vitally important to Swedbank that consumers and end-users have the oppor - tunity to submit suggestions for improvement, any problems, and positive or neg - ative feedback.
summary:
- Emphasis on data protection as part of Swedbank’s human rights commitment, aligned with UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles, ILO and OECD guidelines; recognition of the rights to privacy, family life and personal data protection.
- Transparency for customers on how and why personal data is collected and processed, legal bases, purposes, retention, and rights; information provided via websites, apps, customer meetings, and accessible forms and contacts (including DPO).
- Governance and risk management through the “three lines of defence,” with independent controls, continuous compliance, and CEO accountability; operational handling by incident coordinators; use of regulatory guidance and case law to benchmark and close process gaps.
- Redress and breach handling in line with GDPR and applicable law; prompt notification to affected individuals via phone/email or public channels when needed.
- Seven data protection principles underpin all processing: lawfulness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality (security), and accountability.
- Complaint management: customers’ complaints are recorded, reviewed quarterly, and used to prioritize improvements; follow-up, testing, and closure when complaints cease; issues routed via personal data breach or complaint processes as appropriate; customer satisfaction monitored through NKI surveys.
- Contact and escalation channels (S4-2): customers can use chat, letters, branches, customer center; escalate to the Data Protection Officer, complaints officer, or customer ombudsman; external recourse includes ARN, IMY, municipal consumer advisers, and the Swedish Consumer Banking and Finance Agency.
- Remediation (S4-3): GDPR-compliant processes guided by internal policies and Data Breach Guidelines to manage incidents with significant negative impact and assess sufficiency of actions.
- Data processors: a three-step due diligence lifecycle—pre-contract assessment of technical/organizational/contractual safeguards, ongoing security monitoring, and off-boarding to ensure return/erasure of data; established DPO function.

text:
Communication channels and data processors
It is vitally important to Swedbank that consumers and end-users have the oppor -
tunity to submit suggestions for improvement, any problems, and positive or neg -
ative feedback. The easiest way for consumers and end-users to reach Swed-bank for this purpose is by calling the customer centre or visiting local branches. 
If, after the first decision, the customer is still not satisfied with the answer from 
Swedbank, and would like to further investigate the matter, Swedbank’s data 
 protection officer, complaints officer or customer ombudsman can be contacted, 
by post or email. If, after review by Swedbank’s customer ombudsman, the cus-tomer is not satisfied with the final decision, the customer can contact the 
 Swedish National Board for Customer Disputes (ARN), the Swedish Authority for 
Privacy Protection (IMY), the home municipality’s consumer adviser or the 
 Swedish Consumer Banking and Finance Agency. Information about this can be 
found on Swedbank’s website. Swedbank also has data processors, as compa -
nies that handle Swedbank’s registered personal data on behalf of Swedbank, 
and has established a three-step due diligence process. This entails:
1.  Assessment of potential data processors before a contract is established, to 
ensure that appropriate technical, organisational and contractual complemen -
tary measures are in place, to ensure compliance with the GDPR requirements and to fulfil contractual obligations.
2.  Monit oring that established data processors maintain and continue to develop 
the security aspects of handling personal data.
3.  An off-boarding phase to ensure that the data processor returns and erases all 
personal data in accordance with the established data processor contract. 
Swedbank has well-developed processes and procedures for handling custom -
ers’ personal data in accordance with GDPR, and the Group has also established a Data Protection Officer function. However, there is no follow-up or reporting on 
how aware customers are of this work. Swedbank informs about how personal data is processed in an easy-to-understand and structured manner, so that cus-
tomers can easily access information about what data is collected, for what pur-
pose, what the legal grounds are and how the data is processed during and after 
the customer relationship, e.g. forms for requesting register extracts and contact 
details for the Group’s data protection officer, customer service and the relevant 
data protection authority.

title: Training
heading: 6.2.6.1 Training
start_phrase: For Swedbank, it is crucial that employees have extensive knowledge of informa-tion security, which helps to build a stronger and more resilient organisation.
summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s data protection and privacy governance, grounded in GDPR and aligned with international human rights frameworks (UN SDGs, UNGPs, ILO, OECD). Redress for personal data breaches follows applicable law.
- Governance and risk management use the three lines of defence, with independent controls, ongoing compliance monitoring, and Board reporting. The CEO holds ultimate responsibility; operational incident handling is delegated to coordinators/decision-makers.
- Transparent customer communication on how and why personal data is processed, rights and legal bases, and easy access to forms, contact details, and guidance via web, branches, chat, mail, and phone.
- Data protection is guided by seven core principles (lawfulness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability).
- Complaints and remediation: structured complaint intake and tracking, quarterly reviews, follow-up and improvement loops, and defined escalation to the data protection officer, complaints officer, customer ombudsman, and external authorities (ARN, IMY, municipal advisers, and sector bodies). Incident notification to affected individuals occurs promptly through available channels.
- Procedures for remediation and incidents are set out in policies, instructions, directives, and Data Breach Guidelines, including assessment of actions’ sufficiency.
- Data processors: a three-step due diligence lifecycle—pre-contract assessment, ongoing monitoring, and off‑boarding with return/erasure—ensures GDPR-compliant processing on Swedbank’s behalf.
- Actions and strategies (S4-4): regulatory compliance, risk identification, customer communication, and “data protection by design and by default” in products/services. First year aligned to CSRD; expected outcomes not quantified due to uncertainties.
- Training: annual and role-based information security and GDPR training across all countries, a yearly security month, regular briefings, and simulated phishing; completion is monitored to ensure coverage.
- Continuous follow-up: global monitoring of EU rules and case law, annual updates to public information, integration of improvements via complaint and incident processes, and compensation for individuals harmed by data protection failures.
- Data Protection Officer: accessible to all data subjects; oversees GDPR compliance, runs impact assessments and balancing tests, and reports quarterly/annually to the Board. Personal data retention aligns with purpose and legal obligations (e.g., AML, accounting); incidents are reported to authorities when required. No serious human rights incidents related to customers were reported during the year.
- Customer ombudsman: dedicated team managing the complaint and improvement processes; adheres to Swedish FSA timelines (initial handling within 14 days, with updates if extended).
- Metrics and targets (S4-5): overarching aim to minimise the number and impact of incidents; no outcome-based targets reported. Group-wide metrics published on:
  - Enquiries and complaints to the Data Protection Officer (from individuals and supervisory authorities), showing a notable increase in 2024.
  - Employee completion rates for information security training, with high coverage across countries.
  - Metrics are based on internal systems and not externally validated.
- Not measured: the number of reported downstream failures to respect international human rights principles involving consumers/end-users.
text:
Training
For Swedbank, it is crucial that employees have extensive knowledge of informa-tion security, which helps to build a stronger and more resilient organisation. By 
understanding that security is a shared responsibility, Swedbank can effectively 
strengthen its combined ability to resist different types of threats. Within its own 
operations, the Group’s employees undergo annual training and in-depth role-
based training in information security in all countries in which the Group oper-
ates. As part of this initiative, a security month is organised each year, with lec -
tures aimed at training and informing employees about current security issues. 
In addition, information sessions on current security topics are held on a regular 
basis. To further maintain and reinforce security awareness among employees, 
simulated phishing tests are performed continuously. Swedbank provides man-
datory training and voluntary in-depth training in  personal data processing in 
accordance with GDPR. The purpose is to increase awareness of data protection among employees, but also indirectly for customers and society at large, 
enabling conscious and well-informed choices regarding personal data.

title: Follow-up
heading: 6.2.6.2 Follow-up
start_phrase: Swedbank has a global monitoring system to adapt data protection processes to new regulations, practices and guidelines from the EU, and also an improvement process linked to customer complaints, which entails follow-up, evaluation and improvement measures.
summary:
- Focus on Swedbank’s data protection governance, monitoring, and continuous improvement, including annual follow-up of public information, a global system to track EU regulatory changes, and integration of customer-complaint learnings into corrective actions managed via incident and complaint processes.
- Emphasis on training: ongoing follow-up to ensure employees complete information security and personal data handling training; high completion rates reported by country for 2022–2024, measured via internal systems.
- Clear accountability structure: a Data Protection Officer (DPO) within Group Compliance monitors GDPR compliance, is accessible to customers, employees and other data subjects, and reports quarterly and annually to the Board on alignment with external regulations and the bank’s risk appetite.
- Risk management processes: data protection impact assessments, balancing of interests, and product processes used to assess necessity, fairness, proportionality, and to mitigate risks to individuals’ data rights; monitoring of safeguards when new systems and processes are developed.
- Data handling principles: processing based on balancing individual rights with business needs, retention limited to necessity and extended where required by law (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal purposes), and reporting of personal data incidents to authorities when required by GDPR.
- Redress and accountability: individuals may receive compensation if harmed due to inadequate data protection procedures; no reported serious human rights issues or incidents related to customers during the year.
- Customer ombudsman function: dedicated unit with seven ombudsmen and two complaint analysts overseeing complaint and improvement processes; adherence to the Swedish FSA standard to process or update customers within 14 days.
- Metrics and targets: objective to minimize the number and impact of personal data incidents; no outcome-based targets or time-series effectiveness comparisons reported. Metrics include counts of enquiries and complaints to the DPO (by country) and employee training completion rates, covering 2022–2024, sourced from internal systems and not externally validated.
text:
Follow-up
Swedbank has a global monitoring system to adapt data protection processes to 
new regulations, practices and guidelines from the EU, and also an improvement 
process linked to customer complaints, which entails follow-up, evaluation and 
improvement measures. If improvement measures become relevant, they are 
handled in accordance with Swedbank’s personal data incident process or cus-
tomer complaint process. Swedbank’s information on personal data handling 
is followed up annually and any changes are provided via the Group’s website. 
Swedbank also monitors that measures are implemented when new systems  
and processes are developed, to maintain data protection principles. If Swed -
bank inflicts harm on an individual due to a lack of data protection procedures, 
the  individu al is entitled to compensation from Swedbank in accordance with 
 legislation and internal procedures.

title: Data protection officer
heading: 6.2.6.3 Data protection officer
start_phrase: In order for Swedbank to determine whether the processing of personal data is appropriate, necessary and fair, and to identify any risks related to personal data handling, privacy and data, the Group has processes in place, such as impact assessments, balancing of interests and the product process.
summary:
- Ongoing follow-up ensures employees complete training on handling personal data.
- Swedbank operates a global monitoring system to align data protection processes with evolving EU regulations, practices, and guidelines, and runs an improvement process tied to customer complaints.
- Improvement actions are managed through the personal data incident or customer complaint processes; public information on personal data handling is reviewed annually and updated on the Group website.
- Data protection is embedded in new systems and processes; individuals may receive compensation if harmed due to inadequate procedures, per law and internal rules.
- Risk-based processes include impact assessments (DPIAs), balancing of interests, and product process reviews to ensure processing is appropriate, necessary, fair, and proportionate, with measures to minimize risks.
- A Data Protection Officer (within Group Compliance) monitors GDPR compliance, is accessible to customers, employees, and other data subjects, and provides quarterly and annual reports to the Board on alignment with external requirements and Swedbank’s risk appetite.
- Personal data is retained only as long as necessary for purposes and legal obligations (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal needs), sometimes beyond contract duration.
- GDPR-reportable personal data incidents are reported to authorities; no serious human rights issues related to customers were reported during the year.
- The Customer Ombudsman unit (seven ombudsmen, two complaint analysts) manages complaints and improvements, adhering to Swedish FSA timelines: process within 14 days, with customer notification if more time is needed.
- Targets: aim to minimize the number and impact of personal data incidents; no outcome-based effectiveness targets or time comparisons are reported.
- Governance: Group Compliance sets minimum standards (including data protection) and monitors compliance across the Group; reporting to the Board is covered under the DPO section.
- Metrics collected via internal systems (not externally validated) and covering the entire Group:
  - Enquiries to the DPO from individuals: 128 (2024), 31 (2023), 19 (2022); by country in 2024: Sweden 12, Estonia 11, Latvia 1, Lithuania 4.
  - Enquiries from data protection authorities: 3 (2024), 9 (2023), 11 (2022); 2024 breakdown: Sweden 0, Estonia 2, Latvia 0, Lithuania 1.
  - Complaints to the DPO from individuals: 112 (2024), 6 (2023), 15 (2022); 2024 breakdown: Sweden 11, Estonia 0, Latvia 0, Lithuania 1.
  - Employee completion of information security training (%): Sweden 93.9 (2024), 98.6 (2023), 98.5 (2022); Estonia 99, 99.7, 99.7; Latvia 97.3, 99.7, 99.2; Lithuania 99.1, 99.7, 99.6.
- Purpose of metrics: transparency on enquiries/complaints to the DPO and on staff training coverage to protect sensitive information and maintain security.
text:
Data protection officer
In order for Swedbank to determine whether the processing of personal data is appropriate, necessary and fair, and to identify any risks related to personal data 
handling, privacy and data, the Group has processes in place, such as impact 
assessments, balancing of interests and the product process. Swedbank has 
implemented an impact assessment process. This is part of the Group’s risk 
assessment when handling personal data and means that risks to individuals’ 
right to protection of personal data must be identified, and assessed in accor -
dance with the principle of proportionality, and measures taken to minimise these 
risks must be described. Customers, employees and other types of data subjects 
can contact Swedbank’s data protection officer. The data protection officer of 
the compliance unit is responsible for monitoring Swedbank’s compliance with 
GDPR. Within Group Compliance, the role of Data Protection Officer, as outlined 
by GDPR, involves quarterly and annual reporting to the Board on how Swed-
bank’s data protection efforts align with external regulations, requirements, 
and Swedbank’s risk appetite.
Swedbank ensures that the processing of personal data takes place by balanc-
ing the individual’s right to protection of their personal data with the Group’s right to process data. Swedbank processes personal data for as long as necessary for 
the collection purpose and in accordance with statutory or other provisions. After 
the agreement expires, the data is retained for such purposes as accounting, anti-
money laundering measures, capital adequacy requirements and legal purposes. 
This means that Swedbank sometimes has to retain data for longer than the duration of the agreement. Swedbank reports personal data incidents when there 
is a GDPR requirement for such incidents to be reported to the authorities. There 
were no reports of serious human rights issues and incidents related to Swed-
bank customers during the year.

title: Customer ombudsman
heading: 6.2.6.4 Customer ombudsman
start_phrase: The Group has a unit for data protection work and a customer ombudsman unit.

- Ongoing follow-up ensures employees complete training in handling personal data.
- Governance and monitoring:
  - Global monitoring system adapts data protection processes to new EU regulations, practices, and guidelines.
  - Continuous improvement tied to customer complaints, with measures handled via personal data incident or complaint processes.
  - Annual follow-up of public information on personal data handling; updates provided on the Group’s website.
  - Controls to ensure data protection measures are implemented when new systems and processes are developed.
  - Individuals harmed due to inadequate data protection may receive compensation per legislation and internal procedures.
- Data protection risk management and oversight:
  - Processes include impact assessments (DPIAs), balancing of interests, and the product process to ensure processing is appropriate, necessary, fair, and proportionate, with documented risk mitigation.
  - Data subjects (customers, employees, others) can contact the Data Protection Officer (DPO).
  - The DPO within Group Compliance monitors GDPR compliance and reports quarterly and annually to the Board on alignment with external regulations, requirements, and Swedbank’s risk appetite.
- Processing principles, retention, and incidents:
  - Processing balances individuals’ rights with Swedbank’s legitimate processing needs.
  - Data retained as long as necessary for the collection purpose and per statutory requirements (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal), potentially beyond contract duration.
  - Personal data incidents are reported to authorities when required by GDPR.
  - No reports of serious human rights issues or incidents related to customers during the year.
- Customer ombudsman and complaints handling:
  - Dedicated unit with seven customer ombudsmen and two complaint analysts manages the complaint and improvement processes.
  - Complies with Swedish FSA timelines: complaints processed within 14 days; if more time is needed, customers are informed within 14 days.
- Metrics and targets (S4-5):
  - Target: minimize the number and consequences of personal data incidents; continuous adaptation and improvement of methods.

title: Metrics and targets, S4-5
heading: 6.2.7 Metrics and targets, S4-5
start_phrase: Swedbank seeks to minimise the number and consequences of personal data incidents.
summary:
- Follow-up and monitoring of data protection: Ongoing checks to ensure employees complete personal data handling training; a global system tracks EU regulatory changes and feeds an improvement process tied to customer complaints; incidents and improvements are handled via established personal data incident or complaint processes. Information on personal data handling is reviewed annually, and data protection controls are embedded when new systems/processes are developed. Individuals harmed by deficient procedures may receive compensation per law and internal rules.

- Data Protection Officer (DPO) and risk processes: Swedbank uses impact assessments, balancing of interests, and product processes to ensure processing is appropriate, necessary, fair, and proportionate, with mitigations documented. The DPO within Group Compliance monitors GDPR compliance and reports quarterly and annually to the Board against external requirements and the bank’s risk appetite. Customers, employees, and other data subjects can contact the DPO.

- Data processing principles and incident reporting: Personal data processing balances individual rights with the bank’s need to process data; retention follows purpose necessity and legal requirements (e.g., accounting, AML, capital adequacy, legal) and can exceed contract duration. Personal data incidents are reported to authorities when GDPR requires. No serious human rights issues/incidents related to customers were reported during the year.

- Customer ombudsman and complaints handling: A dedicated unit (seven ombudsmen, two complaint analysts) manages complaints and improvements, adhering to Swedish FSA timelines—aim to resolve within 14 days or inform the customer within 14 days if more time is needed.

- Metrics and targets for data protection: Objective is to minimize the number and impact of personal data incidents; methods are continually improved, but no outcome-based targets or time comparisons are reported. Group Compliance defines minimum standards and oversees compliance. Metrics cover:
  - Enquiries and complaints to the DPO: Significant increase in 2024 in enquiries (128) and complaints (112) from individuals; enquiries from data protection authorities decreased in 2024 (3). Data comes from data subjects and authorities; metrics are group-wide and not externally validated.
  - Information security training: High completion rates, though lower in Sweden and Latvia in 2024 (Sweden 93.9%, Estonia 99.0%, Latvia 97.3%, Lithuania 99.1%). Measured via internal training platforms; not externally validated.

- Business conduct (G1) scope: Covers whistleblower protection, supplier relationship and payment practices, corporate culture, and anti-corruption/bribery, with impacts/risks mapped across the value chain.

- Policies and governance for business conduct: Trust and a sustainable vision guide operations. Key governance documents include the Code of Conduct and policies on Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk. Documents are available internally (public ones on the website). The Board and Group Executive Committee actively oversee culture; values permeate governance.

- Code of Conduct and culture controls: Applies to all employees/subsidiaries; included in onboarding. Annual ethics training and attestation are mandatory and tracked as KPIs. Regular employee surveys (three times yearly) support open culture and managerial follow-up. Mandatory role-based trainings are specified; ethics training addresses anti-corruption, bribery, and benefits, with guidance for real situations. Certain roles require licenses (e.g., SwedSec), with annual ethics components.

- Handling deviations, fraud, and violations: Employees are encouraged to report cultural or rule deviations. A risk-based anti-fraud framework includes preventive/detective controls and standardized processes for investigating regulatory breaches and internal fraud. High-risk processes have enhanced controls. Reports can be made to managers or the Internal Fraud unit; specialized units (Internal Fraud and HR/FM) investigate. Serious breaches can lead to employment actions (warnings, termination) based on investigation outcomes.

title: Policies, G1-1 - Introduction
heading: 7.1.1 Policies, G1-1
start_phrase: Trust from customers, shareholders, employees, business partners and society at large is crucial for Swedbank’s operations.
summary: Overview of Swedbank’s business conduct governance and culture framework. Emphasizes trust from customers, shareholders, employees, partners, and society, and aligns with the Group’s vision of a financially sound and environmentally, socially, financially, and ethically sustainable society. Lists key governance documents addressing impacts, risks, and opportunities in business ethics and conduct: Code of Conduct; Policy for Conduct Risk; Policy on Conflicts of Interest; Policy on Financial Crime Risk; Policy on Personal Account Dealing; Policy on Enterprise Risk Management; and Policy for Operational Risk. Notes availability on the intranet and public website, with details in “Swedbank governance documents, MDR-P.” Highlights ongoing oversight of corporate-culture issues by the Board of Directors and the Group Executive Committee (including the CEO), and references related sections on strategy (SBM-1) and governance roles (GOV-1).
text:
Policies, G1-1
Trust from customers, shareholders, employees, business partners and society 
at large is crucial for Swedbank’s operations. Swedbank’s strategic direction 
describes the Group’s purpose, vision, customer promise, values and foundation. 
The Group’s vision is a society that is financially sound and sustainable, which 
means a society that is sustainable from an environmental, social, financial and 
ethical perspective. 
Swedbank has policies and governance documents that address impacts, 
risks and opportunities related to business conduct. Governance documents that concern business conduct set out the standards for the Group’s corporate culture 
and describe processes for managing business ethics issues. The main gover-
nance documents are Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Policy on Con-
flicts of Interest, Policy on Financial Crime Risk, Policy on Personal Account Deal-
ing, Policy on Enterprise Risk Management and Policy for Operational Risk. The 
governance documents are available on Swedbank’s intranet. The public gover-
nance documents are available on Swedbank’s external website. The governance documents are presented in section Swedbank governance documents, MDR-P .
Corporate-culture related issues are discussed on an ongoing basis by both 
the Board of Directors and the Group Executive Committee, which includes the 
CEO. Swedbank’s values permeate all  governance documents adopted by the 
Group Executive Committee and CEO. Further information on the strategic direc-
tion, vision and values can be found in sections Strategy, business model and 
value chain, SBM-1 and corporate culture in sections Role of the Board of 
 Directors and the CEO, GOV-1.

title: Code of Conduct
heading: 7.1.1.1 Code of Conduct
start_phrase: The basic document to ensure that Swedbank has a good corporate culture is the Code of Conduct, which constitutes the Group’s ethics policy.
summary:
- Scope: Governance information – G1 Business conduct in Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability Report 2024, covering whistleblower protection, supplier relationship management (including payment practices), corporate culture, and anti-corruption/bribery across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream), with identified impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Strategic context: Emphasis on trust from stakeholders and the Group’s vision of a financially sound and sustainable society; business conduct embedded in strategic direction, values, and culture.
- Governance framework: Key policies include the Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk; documents accessible internally and selected ones publicly; oversight by the Board and Group Executive Committee.
- Code of Conduct: Serves as the ethics policy for all employees and subsidiaries; defines expected behavior in transactions and relationships; integrated into onboarding.
- Training and KPIs: Mandatory annual ethics training for all staff and executives, with focus on anti-corruption/bribery and benefits; role-specific training requirements; Swedsec-licensed staff complete annual knowledge updates with ethics content; annual confirmation of Code understanding tracked as a KPI.
- Culture measurement: Employee surveys held three times a year on strategy, leadership, and culture; managers required to act on results to foster open dialogue and continuous improvement.
- Whistleblowing and incident vigilance: Employees encouraged to report deviations from rules and values; protection for whistleblowers highlighted as a material topic.
- Anti-fraud and compliance controls: Risk-based anti-fraud framework with technical and manual controls in high-risk processes; standardized processes for detecting, preventing, reporting, and investigating suspected fraud and regulatory breaches.
- Reporting and investigation process: Incidents can be reported to managers or the Internal Fraud unit; system support exists for risk/irregularity handling; investigations conducted by Internal Fraud and Group HR & Facility Management.
- Consequences and accountability: Serious violations may lead to employment actions (warnings or termination), decided by management based on investigative recommendations.
text:
Code of Conduct
The basic document to ensure that Swedbank has a good corporate culture is the Code of Conduct, which constitutes the Group’s ethics policy. The Code of 
Conduct describes how employees should handle business transactions and 
relationships. Every employee is expected to act in accordance with Swedbank’s 
values and must observe the Code of Conduct, other internal rules, laws and 
 regulations, and good practice, within their area of responsibility. 
The Code of Conduct applies to all employees of Swedbank and its  subsidiaries  
and is part of the introduction programme for new employees. All employees 
undergo ethics training and confirm annually that they have accessed, read and 
understood the Code of Conduct. This is followed up as one of the KPIs for the 
business conduct area. Three times a year, Swedbank conducts employee sur -
veys on issues relating to strategic direction, leadership and corporate culture. The surveys aim to encourage continuous dialogue and an open corporate  culture, where employees’ opinions are taken into account. All managers must 
follow up on the results within their unit. 
The Code of Conduct states that employees must undergo all mandatory train -
ing required for their position and role at Swedbank. Training requirements are set out in the respective internal regulations, which specify the type of training 
required for the respective roles. Swedbank’s annual ethics training consists of 
a basic mandatory training for all employees and the Group Executive Commit-
tee, including the CEO. The ethics training highlights, among other things, Swed-
bank’s position on corruption and bribery, and how benefits should be assessed, and also provides examples and guidance on what constitutes appropriate 
action in particular situations. Certain positions and roles demand specialized 
knowledge and skills, necessitating regular updates to  specific licenses and cer -
tifications. Employees holding a Swedsec license are required to complete an annual knowledge update, which includes a section on ethics each year.

title: Mechanisms for handling deviations and violations
heading: 7.1.1.2 Mechanisms for handling deviations and violations
start_phrase: All Swedbank employees are encouraged to remain vigilant for any incidents in their daily work that may constitute a breach of the rules Swedbank is required to follow.
summary:
- Scope and focus: G1 Business conduct covers Swedbank’s approach to corporate culture, protection for whistleblowers, management of supplier relationships (including payment practices), and anti-corruption/bribery, mapped across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream) with identified impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Governance and policies: Business conduct is guided by a suite of Group policies and governance documents—Code of Conduct, Policy for Conduct Risk, Conflicts of Interest, Financial Crime Risk, Personal Account Dealing, Enterprise Risk Management, and Operational Risk—aligned to Swedbank’s purpose, vision, and values. Documents are maintained on the intranet and, where public, on the external website; oversight involves the Board and Group Executive Committee.
- Code of Conduct and culture: The Code applies to all employees and subsidiaries, integrated into onboarding, with annual ethics confirmation and mandatory training. Culture and leadership are monitored via employee surveys three times a year; managers are required to follow up. Role-based and license (e.g., Swedsec) training include ethics components.
- Managing deviations, fraud, and market abuse: The bank maintains a risk-based anti-fraud framework with technical and manual controls in high-risk processes, standardized investigation procedures, and potential employment actions for violations. Market surveillance is conducted under the EU Market Abuse Regulation to detect suspicious orders/transactions.
- Bribery and corruption risk assessment: Conducted at least biennially or as needed, assessing geography and business changes. Higher risks are identified among customer-facing staff and procurement roles handling large contracts, recruitment, and consulting. Group Compliance monitors risk trends and control effectiveness.
- Supplier governance: High ethical standards are enforced through the Purchasing Instruction and Supplier Code of Conduct. Suppliers must sign the Code (or show equivalent commitments); deviations escalate to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee. Ongoing monitoring showed ~200 additional suppliers met the Code requirement in 2024. Supplier selection must be objective, transparent, fact-based, with sustainability criteria; procurement is extensively digitized to identify and manage risks.
- Whistleblower framework: Internal and external stakeholders can report irregularities, corruption, bribery, and policy breaches via channels compliant with the EU Whistleblower Directive and Swedish law, including an anonymous, encrypted web portal managed by an external provider. Authorized, independent handlers manage cases, with conflict-of-interest safeguards. The Board receives quarterly updates on case volumes and themes; separate internal fraud processes also exist.
- Key actions and metrics (2024): 
  - 95% of employees completed mandatory ethics training (94% in 2023); training refreshed with real-life dilemmas, with bank confidentiality training planned. Completion rates reported to the Board from Q4 2024.
  - 158 whistleblower reports received (126 in 2023); continued awareness-raising planned for 2025.
  - Annual updates to governance documents; strengthened mandates for independent whistleblower channel managers.
  - No significant standalone sustainability capex/opex identified; activities integrated into operating costs.
text:
Mechanisms for handling deviations and violations 
All Swedbank employees are encouraged to remain vigilant for any incidents in 
their daily work that may constitute a breach of the rules Swedbank is required to 
follow. Employees are encouraged to report incidents that deviate from the 
Group’s corporate culture and values. 
Swedbank’s fraud prevention and investigation efforts address issues related 
to ethical violations, bribery, and corruption. The internal  governance documents 
require Swedbank, in accordance with legal and regulatory obligations, to ensure 
a robust and risk-based anti-fraud framework. There is also a requirement to establish and maintain controls to detect, prevent and report any suspected fraud 
against Swedbank. The internal regulations also include a requirement to ensure 
a uniform process for investigating regulatory breaches by employees, as well as 
suspected internal fraud within Swedbank.
Technical and manual control systems have been implemented to detect inter -
nal fraud in particularly high-risk processes. Employees who discover deviations 
can report this to their immediate manager, who will document and deal with the incident, or contact the Internal Fraud unit. Swedbank has system support for a 
number of processes and work tasks for the purpose of identifying, reporting on 
and following up internal risks and irregularities. The Internal Fraud and Group 
Human Resources & Facility Management units investigate reported cases. If an 
investigation reveals serious regulatory violations, this may result in actions under 
employment law such as a warning or termination of employment. The employ -
ee’s manager and their manager will decide on actions in line with employment 
law based on a recommendation from the units involved in the investigation.

ment at least every other year or when necessary. The risk assessment should 
include an assessment of risks associated with for example the countries in

be higher in units with customer-facing staff and procurement staff managing

and of expected quality to ensure the Group’s risk exposure remains low.
Swedbank’s Purchasing Instruction describes general purchasing principles, 
which include transparency, honesty, competitiveness and compliance with the Code of Conduct. Swedbank’s Supplier Code of Conduct describes the Group’s 
business ethics requirements for suppliers. According to the Purchasing Instruc-
