title: The whistleblower process
heading: 7.1.1.3 The whistleblower process
start_phrase: It is also possible for internal and external stakeholders to report irregularities and misconduct within the operations through Swedbank’s whistleblower pro - cess.
summary:
- Anti-bribery and corruption risk management: Swedbank performs a descriptive-to-quantitative risk assessment at least biennially (or as needed), covering country exposure and operational changes. 2023 insights indicate higher risks in customer-facing and procurement units handling large contracts, recruitment, and consulting. Group Compliance continuously monitors risk trends and tests control effectiveness to keep exposure low.

- Supplier governance and procurement standards: The Purchasing Instruction and Supplier Code of Conduct set principles of transparency, honesty, competitiveness, and compliance with the Code of Conduct. Suppliers must sign the Code or show equivalent policies; deviations escalate to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee. Compliance is tracked continuously; about 200 additional suppliers met the Code requirement in 2024. Procurement is guided by objective, transparent, fact-based evaluations with multiple alternatives and embedded sustainability criteria, supported by a digitized process for risk identification and management.

- Market surveillance: In line with the EU Market Abuse Regulation, Swedbank identifies and reports suspicious transactions and orders to deter market abuse and strengthen market integrity and trust.

- Whistleblower framework: Aligned with the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive and the Swedish Whistleblower Act, the process protects against retaliation and enables internal and external parties to report irregularities, including corruption, bribery, and Code of Conduct breaches. Reports can be made openly or anonymously via an encrypted, third-party-hosted channel. Independent, authorized units manage investigations, handle conflicts of interest, and report case volumes and themes to the Board quarterly. Relevant staff receive ongoing training. In 2024, 158 whistleblower reports were received (up from 126), with plans to further raise awareness in 2025. Separate internal fraud processes exist.

- Culture, ethics, and training: All employees are expected to acknowledge the Code of Conduct and complete annual mandatory ethics training (95% completion in 2024 vs. 94% in the prior year). Training content was refreshed with real-world dilemmas; new modules (e.g., banking confidentiality) are planned. Topics include responsible business conduct, diversity and inclusion, conflicts of interest, secrecy/confidentiality, whistleblowing, and anti-corruption/bribery. Completion is followed up annually and reported to the Board from Q4 2024. Business ethics governance documents are updated annually.

- Resourcing: No significant standalone operating or capital expenditures are identified for sustainability action plans; costs are integrated into ongoing operations.

- Overall emphasis: Strengthening controls, transparency, and accountability across risk assessment, supplier relations, market surveillance, whistleblowing, and ethics training to uphold regulatory compliance and a strong ethical culture.
text:
The whistleblower process
It is also possible for internal and external stakeholders to report irregularities 
and misconduct within the operations through Swedbank’s whistleblower pro -
cess. The procedures established by Swedbank to protect whistleblowers are in accordance with the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive and the Swedish 
Whistleblower Act
2. Protection includes a ban on taking preventive actions and 
on retaliation against whistleblowers. Swedbank’s Group-wide whistleblower 
 process enables employees and both internal and external stakeholders to report 
irregularities, corruption and bribery, and other misconduct within the operation. 
This may concern violations of the Code of Conduct, non-compliance with legis -
lation or deviations from policies. Incidents deemed to constitute whistleblowing are handled in accordance with the whistleblower process. Employees with 
authority to assume responsibility for managing internal reporting channels 
and procedures undergo continuous internal and external training.
Information about the Group’s whistleblower process can be found in the  
Code of Conduct, and is also available on the Group’s internal and external web -
sites. Employees also attend mandatory annual ethics training, which includes 
information about the Group’s whistleblower process. 
If there is any suspicion of irregularities within the operation, this must be 
reported to the head of Group Compliance or the head of Group Internal Audit, or 
in full anonymity via a web-based reporting and communication channel hosted 
by an external provider. An investigation will then be initiated. The whistleblower 
can submit reports openly or anonymously, and remain anonymous in the dia -
logue. Reports and messages are encrypted and treated as strictly confidential. 
The whistleblower unit concerned at Swedbank will investigate the incident. 
The investigation observes the integrity of the whistleblower and the person(s) 
appointed under the regulatory handling process within the respective investigating 
whistleblower unit. Authorised employees within each unit are independent and 
autonomous, with a specially regulated mandate to manage reporting channels 
and procedures. On any conflict of interest, the incident is transferred to another investigating whistleblower unit. The Board of Directors is informed of the 
number of whistleblower cases and the overall matters in connection with the 
quarterly reporting. In addition to the statutory whistleblower process, processes 
are in place at the internal fraud unit for investigating suspected incidents 
 classified as internal fraud. For further information on fraud, see section 
 Financial Crime.

on the protection of persons reporting misconduct.

title: Key actions
heading: 7.1.1.4 Key actions
start_phrase: To maintain and strengthen the corporate culture within our own operations, Swedbank took a number of key actions during the year.
summary:
- Swedbank performs a Group-wide bribery and corruption risk assessment at least every two years (or as needed), covering country risk and changes in operations. Recent assessments and 2023 investigations indicate higher risk in customer-facing units and procurement handling large contracts, recruitment, and consulting.
- Group Compliance continuously monitors risk developments and tests the effectiveness and quality of controls and processes to keep exposure low.
- Purchasing Instruction sets principles of transparency, honesty, competitiveness, and adherence to the Code of Conduct; the Supplier Code of Conduct must be signed or matched by equivalent supplier policies. Deviations are escalated to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee. In 2024, roughly 200 more suppliers committed to the Code.
- Market surveillance operates under the EU Market Abuse Regulation to detect and report suspicious transactions and orders, supporting market integrity and trust.
- A Group-wide whistleblower process, aligned with the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive and Swedish law, enables internal and external reporting of irregularities, including corruption, bribery, policy breaches, and legal non-compliance, with protections against retaliation.
- Multiple reporting channels exist, including anonymous, encrypted web-based submissions via an external provider. Investigations are handled by independent, authorised whistleblower units with conflict-of-interest safeguards; the Board receives quarterly summaries.
- Employees managing whistleblower channels receive ongoing training; separate processes exist within the internal fraud unit for suspected internal fraud.
- Ethics and security training is mandatory annually for employees and consultants; 95% completed ethics training in 2024 (94% in the prior year). Training includes realistic dilemmas and topics such as conflicts of interest, banking secrecy, whistleblowing, and anti-corruption; updates and new modules (e.g., bank confidentiality) are planned.
- Governance documents related to business ethics and the whistleblower process are updated annually; completion rates are followed up and reported to the Board from Q4 2024.
- In 2024, 158 whistleblower reports were received (126 in the prior year). Swedbank will continue awareness-raising on the whistleblower process in 2025.
- No significant standalone operating or capital expenditures were identified for sustainability action plans; these are embedded in ongoing operations.
- Supplier relations emphasize ethical selection, risk-based segmentation, tailored controls, and follow-up, guided by the Code of Conduct, Purchasing Instruction, and Supplier Code of Conduct (available internally and publicly).
- The digitised procurement process enforces fair, objective, transparent, fact-based evaluations, considers multiple alternatives, includes sustainability criteria, and mandates compliance with rules on gifts, benefits, bribes, and personal relationships.

Key actions
To maintain and strengthen the corporate culture within our own operations, 
Swedbank took a number of key actions during the year. Swedbank has con -
ducted internal training in ethics and security. All employees in the Group are expected to confirm that they have read and understood Swedbank’s Code of 
Conduct. Swedbank’s ethics training is an annual mandatory training course for 
all employees and consultants. The share of employees who took this training in 
2024 was 95 percent. Previous year it was 94 percent. During the year, the ethics 
training was revised with new and reality-inspired business ethics dilemmas, and for the coming year, new dilemmas are planned along with a training on bank con-
fidentiality. The ethics training relates to expectations of employees on topics 
related to responsible business conduct, such as diversity and inclusion, con -
flicts of interest, banking secrecy and confidentiality, whistleblowing and anti-cor-
ruption and  briber y. The proportion of employees who have completed the train -
ing courses is followed up annually and reported to the Board of Directors as 
from Q4 2024. Governance documents relating to business ethics are updated 
annually. The key actions to create awareness, contribute to fulfilling the objec -
tive of the policy for how the Group is expected to manage business and relation -
ships in accordance with the Code of Conduct. 
A key measure to strengthen control of compliance with the Group’s internal 
and external regulations, and to strengthen the protection of whistleblowers, is that Swedbank has established a special mandate for authorised employees who 
manage internal reporting channels and procedures. Employees who manage 
reporting channels and the procedure must be independent and autonomous. 
The whistleblower process means that violations can be detected, investigated 
and remedied effectively, leading to greater transparency and accountability 
within the Group. Governance documents relating to the whistleblower process 
are updated annually. In 2024, the Group received 158 reports via the Group’s whistleblower process. Previous year it was 126 reports. In 2025, Swedbank will 
continue to work on activities aimed at raising awareness of the whistleblower 
process. The key actions include the Group’s employees, and internal and 
 external stakeholders. 
Swedbank has not identified significant operating or capital expenditure 
 specifically for action plans in the area of sustainability; these expenses are 
an integral element of Swedbank’s running costs.

title: The procurement process facilitates sustainability work
heading: 7.1.2.1 The procurement process facilitates sustainability work
start_phrase: The Purchasing Instruction sets the framework for how supplier relationships are to be conducted.
summary:
- Group-wide anti-bribery and corruption risk assessment: descriptive-to-quantitative review at least biennially; higher risk in customer-facing units and procurement handling large contracts, recruitment, and consulting; Group Compliance monitors risk trends and tests control effectiveness.
- Purchasing and supplier governance: Purchasing Instruction mandates transparency, honesty, competitiveness, and Code of Conduct compliance; Supplier Code of Conduct required (or equivalent policies), with deviations escalated to a sustainability committee; ~200 additional suppliers committed in 2024; continuous monitoring.
- Market surveillance: detection and reporting of suspicious transactions/orders under the EU Market Abuse Regulation to enhance market integrity.
- Whistleblower framework: EU Directive and Swedish law–aligned protections; multiple internal/external channels including anonymous, encrypted web portal run by an external provider; independent, authorized units manage cases, with conflict-of-interest safeguards; Board receives quarterly updates; 158 reports in 2024 (vs 126 in 2023); ongoing awareness and annual governance document updates; specialized mandate strengthens retaliation protection and process integrity.
- Culture and training: mandatory annual ethics training for employees and consultants (95% completion in 2024; revised with real-world dilemmas; bank confidentiality training planned); employees attest to the Code of Conduct; results reported to the Board from Q4 2024.
- Supplier relations (G1-2): digitized, risk-based procurement including conflict-of-interest checks, dual approvals, consultant background checks, and outsourcing risk assessments; staff training and guidance; sustainability questionnaires with >100 follow-up dialogues in 2024; action plans for underperforming suppliers; potential sustainability audits; material breaches can terminate contracts.
- Supplier program enhancements: Supplier Code update planned for Q1 2025 (ESG data, gift rules, whistleblower link); digitized identification of high-impact suppliers; building a central unit to assess first-line and strategic suppliers; no special procedures for vulnerable suppliers; compliance metrics track process adherence.
- Anti-corruption program (G1-3): policies (Code of Conduct, Financial Crime Risk Policy, Anti-Bribery & Corruption Instruction); guidance on gifts/events; in-depth mandatory training for high-risk contract owners; secondary occupation registration; supplier anti-bribery clauses and due diligence; independent investigations (Internal Fraud, HR&FM) with quarterly reporting to CEO/Board.
- Financial note: no significant standalone sustainability capex/opex; costs integrated into ongoing operations.
text:
The procurement process facilitates sustainability work
The Purchasing Instruction sets the framework for how supplier relationships are to be conducted. The Purchasing Instruction names a number of guiding criteria 
for how relationships should be conducted. This includes that all procurement 
activities must be conducted in line with Swedbank’s Supplier Code of Conduct, 
that employees and suppliers must ensure compliance with the principles regard-
ing restrictions related to gifts and other benefits, and bribes and personal rela -
tions, and that the procurement process is conducted on a fair and honest basis. The Purchasing Instruction's guidelines also state that suppliers should be selected on the basis of an objective, transparent and fact-based evaluation, with 
comparison of several alternatives, and that sustainability aspects should be 
included in the evaluation of both new and existing suppliers. Based on the Pur-
chasing Instruction, the Group has developed a procurement process that has 
been extensively digitised to facilitate processes that include identification and 
management of risks.

Swedbank Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 – Board of Directors’ reportAs part of the procurement process, a check is made for potential conflicts of 
interest between clients and potential suppliers, as well as an investigation into 
the supplier’s work regarding corruption and bribery. Duality is also applied in the 
contract approval process, which supports greater objectivity in decision-making 
and reduces the risk of corruption. To reduce the risk of unethical conduct, 
a background check is made when consulting services are procured, which 
includes criminal record extracts, external commitments and financial status.
To reduce the risks associated with outsourcing and critical suppliers, a com -
prehensive assessment and risk management process is undertaken in the areas of data and information security, business continuity and other relevant areas.
To support compliance with the procurement process, there are also:
• Training courses for employees in the procurement organisation that are 
 conducted as part of the introduction process and are also available to other 
 parties such as purchasers and contract owners.
• Guides and manuals for procurement and risk management.
• Sustainability as an indirect incentive since employees’ goals include adhering 
to the procurement process.
A sustainability assessment is undertaken that covers environmental, social and 
business ethics issues, and is conducted via a questionnaire in which the supp -
lier’s responses are evaluated and, if necessary, followed up. In cases where a supplier fails to fulfil sustainability expectations, Swedbank seeks to create an 
activity plan together with the supplier to improve the supplier’s sustainability 
management in the long term. The number of dialogues to follow up on suppliers’ 
responses and challenge their sustainability work exceeded 100 in 2024. Swed-
bank does not currently follow up on local or certified suppliers, as the need is 
considered to be limited.

title: Supplier Code of Conduct
heading: 7.1.2.2 Supplier Code of Conduct
start_phrase: Swedbank’s Supplier Code of Conduct includes requirements in the areas of human rights, working conditions, business ethics and the environment, and the content is expected to be distributed onwards in the supplier’s value chain.
summary:
- Procurement governance and due diligence:
  - Checks for conflicts of interest, and supplier due diligence on corruption and bribery.
  - Duality in contract approvals to enhance objectivity and reduce corruption risk.
  - Background checks for consultants (criminal record, external commitments, financial status).
  - Outsourcing and critical supplier risk assessments covering information security, business continuity, and other areas.
  - Support tools: procurement training for employees and relevant stakeholders, guides/manuals, and sustainability-linked performance incentives.

- Supplier sustainability management:
  - Sustainability assessments via questionnaire covering environmental, social, and business ethics; follow-ups and activity plans where expectations are not met.
  - Over 100 supplier dialogues in 2024 to challenge and follow up on sustainability work.
  - Limited follow-up on local/certified suppliers due to perceived low need.

- Supplier Code of Conduct (SCoC):
  - Requirements on human rights, working conditions, business ethics, and environment; expected to cascade in the supplier value chain.
  - Recommends supplier whistleblower programs.
  - Non-signing triggers dialogue, escalation to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee, and potential process deviation; violations constitute material breach and may end the relationship.

- Key actions and organizational enhancements:
  - Planned SCoC update in Q1 2025 to strengthen ESG requirements, gifts policy, and whistleblowing links across key geographies.
  - Digitalized identification of suppliers with significant sustainability impacts.
  - Expanded and centralized first-line supplier assessment capacity, including a central unit for strategic supplier management; intended to cover the full supplier base and support governance targets through 2026.
  - First year of CSRD-aligned reporting; no prior action progress metrics presented.
  - No special procedures for vulnerable suppliers.

- Monitoring and evaluation:
  - Procurement process compliance metric includes mandatory risk minimization pre-contract.
  - SCoC compliance verified via supplier follow-up questions.
  - Sustainability audits performed for major sustainability risks.
  - No distinct OPEX/CAPEX earmarked for sustainability action plans; costs embedded in ongoing operations.

- Anti-corruption and anti-bribery (G1-3):
  - Employee awareness through Code of Conduct training, new training on third-party risks, and guidelines on gifts/events.
  - Key governance documents: Code of Conduct, Policy on Financial Crime Risk, Instruction on Anti-Bribery and Corruption; accessible internally and publicly where applicable; Code translated in home markets.
  - Annual 30-minute ethics training (covers corruption/bribery basics, regulations, risk assessments), plus online training for employees/consultants on regulatory topics, benefits, and reporting; in-depth mandatory course for high-risk contract owners.
  - Employees register secondary occupations; suppliers must sign sustainability requirements or include equivalent anti-bribery clauses; targeted bribery/corruption questionnaires during procurement.
  - Allegations investigated by Internal Fraud and Group HR & Facility Management, independent from implicated units; Group Compliance assesses and reports outcomes to the CEO and Board quarterly.
  - Whistleblower channels for internal and external stakeholders to report suspected corruption and bribery.
text:
Supplier Code of Conduct
Swedbank’s Supplier Code of Conduct includes requirements in the areas of 
human rights, working conditions, business ethics and the environment, and the 
content is expected to be distributed onwards in the supplier’s value chain. It also 
recommends that suppliers set up their own whistleblower programmes. If a 
 supplier does not sign the Code of Conduct, a dialogue is initiated with the sup -
plier to reach agreement on signing and/or possible exemptions. The matter is 
escalated to the purchasing unit’s sustainability committee, where a decision is 
made. If the deviation is not approved it leads to a process deviation, which is 
 followed up as part of the procurement process. If the supplier is in violation of 
the agreed requirements in the Supplier Code of Conduct, this is considered a material breach of contract, which may mean that the collaboration with the 
 supplier is terminated.

text:
Prevention and detection of corruption  
and bribery, G1-3
Swedbank’s work to prevent corruption and bribery focuses on creating aware-
ness among employees by such means as training on the Group’s Code of Con-
duct and a new training programme on what employees should be aware of in 
relation to third parties, such as suppliers and consultants. There are also guide-
lines on gifts and events. The purpose of the training programmes and guidelines 
is to help employees act in accordance with the Code of Conduct and  ethical 
rules, and to reduce the risk of bribery and corruption not being  disco vered. 
The main governance documents are Code of Conduct, Policy on Financial 
Crime Risk and Instruction on Anti-Bribery and Corruption. The governance docu -
ments are available on Swedbank’s intranet. The public governance documents 
are available on Swedbank’s external website. The  governance documents are 
presented in section MDR-P .
At the supplier level, there are requirements linked to bribery and corruption in 
the Supplier Code of Conduct, which is signed in the purchasing process. In addi -
tion, suppliers are asked to answer questions relating to bribery and corruption in 
order to identify any elevated risk, which is then managed as part of the procure-
ment process.
Swedbank informs employees about governance documents relating to busi-
ness ethics and business conduct under the annual ethics training programme. 
In addition, all policies are available on Swedbank’s intranet and updates are 
communicated through newsletters. All employees have access to the intranet 
and all governance documents. The Code of Conduct has also been translated into local languages in the Group’s home markets. 
Swedbank’s annual ethics training, which lasts 30 minutes, includes a section 
on corruption and bribery at a basic level that covers external and internal regula-
tions, risk assessments and preventive information. There is online training at 
Group level for both employees and consultants, with general information about 
regulatory requirements, the risk of insider trading, prohibited, permitted and 
inappropriate benefits and activities, and the reporting process. All units in the Group, including those exposed to risk, are required to undergo the basic manda -
tory ethics training programme on an annual basis. The new training programme mentioned above is an in-depth, mandatory course for contract owners with high-
risk contracts.
Employees also register any secondary occupations, which are followed up by 
both employee and manager. Suppliers sign the Group’s sustainability requirements 
or have equivalent separate clauses on the prevention of corruption and bribery. 
At Swedbank, allegations or incidents relating to bribery and corruption are 
investigated by Internal Fraud and Group Human Resources & Facility Manage -
ment. The parties conducting the investigations are independent of the employees 
and departments being investigated. Group Human Resources & Facility Man -
agement reports allegations and incidents of corruption and bribery to Group Compliance, which assesses the incident. Group Compliance reports the out-
come to the CEO and the Board of Directors on a quarterly basis. Further infor -
mation about Swedbank’s mechanisms and procedures is described above.
As described above, Swedbank also has a whistleblower process whereby 
suspected corruption and bribery can be reported by internal and external stake-
holders, and where the allegations are investigated by the respective whistle -
blower unit.

title: Key actions
heading: 7.1.3.1 Key actions
start_phrase: Swedbank took a number of key actions in its own operations during the year to address the risk of Swedbank being exposed to corruption and bribery.
summary:
- Focus area: Anti-corruption, bribery prevention, and business ethics, with governance, training, monitoring, incident handling, and payment practices.

  - Standard supplier payment terms: 30 days; average actual payment term ~31 days.

text:
Key actions
Swedbank took a number of key actions in its own operations during the year 
to address the risk of Swedbank being exposed to corruption and bribery. In 
 addition to ethics training for all the Group’s employees targeted training for the 
Group’s contract owners with high-risk contracts was provided. The purpose of the training is to increase awareness of the risk of bribery and corruption and 
of the Group’s guidelines for accepting gifts and events. The ratio of employees 
who have undergone the training programmes is followed up regularly. Gover-
nance documents relating to bribery and corruption are updated annually. 
 Registers for events and sponsorships have been introduced. A Group-wide risk 
assessment will be completed during Q1 2025 and the final report will be sent 
to the Group Executive Committee. In the coming years, Group-wide training 
courses regarding gifts and events will be launched for managers and customer  -
facing staff. The key actions contribute to meeting the governance documents' goal to increase awareness of bribery and corruption. Development in this area 
is reported quarterly to the Board of Directors. For further information on ethics 
training, see section Policies, G1-1. 
Swedbank has not identified significant operating or capital expenditure 
 specifically for action plans in the area of sustainability; these expenses are 
an integral element of Swedbank’s running costs.

title: Metrics and targets
heading: 7.1.3.2 Metrics and targets
start_phrase: Swedbank seeks to achieve a high level of business ethics and good conduct in the financial market.
summary:
- Focus on anti-corruption and bribery controls: group-wide ethics training for all employees, targeted training for contract owners on high-risk contracts, annual updates to governance documents, and new registers for events and sponsorships. A Group-wide bribery/corruption risk assessment will be completed in Q1 2025, with expanded training for managers and customer-facing staff to follow. Progress is reported quarterly to the Board. Sustainability-related action plan costs are embedded in operating expenses, not separately identified.

- Governance, metrics, and oversight: Swedbank aims for high business ethics with zero tolerance for bribery and corruption and a Board-set low risk appetite. Group Compliance monitors compliance risks, evaluates rule effectiveness, proposes minimum standards, and advises operations; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board. Internal processes track culture, whistleblower protection, anti-corruption, and supplier relationship management, but no public, outcome-oriented targets or time-series comparisons are published. Exceedances of supplier risk appetite are escalated to the CEO and Board.

- Incident handling and data gaps: Internal investigations address suspected rule breaches; employment actions may follow, and suspected crimes are reported to police. Operational risks identified are escalated per risk procedures. Quarterly follow-up of suspected corruption cases is conducted by HR & Facility Management and Group Compliance. Swedbank lacks 2024 data on employee convictions/fines for bribery/corruption due to no systematic follow-up; the Internal Fraud unit will build follow-up processes. Metrics are not externally validated.

- Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) surveillance: Group-wide systems support STOR (Suspicious Transaction and Order Report) monitoring and reporting by geography; data use is internal and not externally validated. 2024 saw 121 STORs (Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5), compared to 2023: 202 and 2022: 57; the 2023 increase is linked to certain Baltic agencies’ focus on specific trading patterns.

- Supplier payment practices (G1-6): Standard supplier payment terms are 30 days; average actual payment terms are 31 days. Overall, Swedbank pays invoices in 27 days on average (21 days for SMEs). Payments within the 30-day standard: 57% overall, 71% for SMEs. Payments within agreed actual terms: 71% overall, 58% for SMEs. In the Baltics, invoices are paid immediately after approval; in Sweden, on the due date. SME status is determined via Moody’s (<250 employees). Metrics are based on internal invoice data covering ~90% of supplier invoices (including Baltic subsidiaries) and are not externally validated. Ten legal proceedings for late payments are outstanding for SMEs; none for all enterprises.
text:
Metrics and targets
Swedbank seeks to achieve a high level of business ethics and good conduct in the financial market. To evaluate the work, Swedbank has established internal 
processes to follow-up on corporate culture, protection for whistleblowers and 
anti-corruption and bribery. Swedbank does not publish any measurable out -
come-oriented goals to monitor the effectiveness of policies and actions in these areas, nor comparisons over time.
The Group’s independent compliance function, Group Compliance, works to 
monitor and identify the Group’s compliance risks, evaluate the effectiveness of Swedbank’s internal rules and actions to maintain good business ethics, prevent 
bribery and corruption and maintain whistleblower protection. Group Compliance 
is also tasked with proposing and defining minimum standards in these areas. To 
ensure that Swedbank’s work is aligned with the Board of Directors’ risk appetite 
regarding compliance risks, the unit also provides advice and support to operations.
Swedbank has zero tolerance of bribery and corruption. The Board of Directors 
determines Swedbank’s low risk appetite in this area. The Board of Directors has by delegation established internal processes and metrics to evaluate the work 
and ensure that risk tolerance is complied with and continuously followed up by 
Group Compliance. Swedbank conducts a general risk assessment to identify 
and understand the risks regarding bribery and corruption to which the Group is 
exposed. The Group’s Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and 
the Board of Directors on the effectiveness of Swedbank’s work on business 
ethics issues, to prevent bribery and corruption, based on external and internal regulations, requirements, and risk appetite.
To evaluate the work, Swedbank has established internal processes to follow  -
-up management of relationships with suppliers. Swedbank does not publish any 
measurable outcome-oriented goals to monitor the effectiveness of policies and 
actions in this area, nor comparisons over time. If the risk exposure in terms of 
supplier risk exceeds the adopted risk appetite, this is reported to the CEO and 
Board of Directors.

title: Incidents of corruption and bribery, G1-4
heading: 7.1.4 Incidents of corruption and bribery, G1-4
start_phrase: Swedbank has processes for conducting internal investigations of employees in the event of suspected violations of rules, including suspected bribery or corrup - tion.
summary:
- Anti-corruption actions and governance: Swedbank rolled out ethics training for all employees and targeted training for contract owners handling high-risk contracts, with ongoing tracking of completion. Governance documents on bribery and corruption are updated annually; registers for events and sponsorships have been introduced. A Group-wide corruption/bribery risk assessment will be completed in Q1 2025 and reported to the Group Executive Committee. New Group-wide training on gifts and events for managers and customer-facing staff will be launched. Progress is reported quarterly to the Board. No specific operating or capital expenditure is earmarked for sustainability actions; costs are embedded in normal operations.
- Metrics, targets, and oversight: The bank aims for high business ethics and good market conduct but does not publish outcome-oriented, time-series goals in anti-corruption, whistleblowing, or supplier management. Group Compliance independently monitors compliance risks, evaluates the effectiveness of internal rules, proposes minimum standards, and advises operations. The Board sets zero tolerance and a low risk appetite for bribery and corruption; the Chief Compliance Officer reports quarterly to the CEO and Board. Supplier risk management is monitored internally, with escalation to the CEO/Board if risk exceeds appetite.
- Incidents and investigations (G1-4): Internal processes exist to investigate suspected violations (including bribery/corruption), apply employment actions, report crimes to police, and escalate operational risks to HR & Facility Management and relevant risk units. Quarterly follow-up of suspected corruption cases is conducted by HR & Facility Management and Group Compliance. Swedbank lacks 2024 data on employee convictions/fines due to no systematic follow-up; the Internal Fraud unit will develop tracking processes. Metrics are not externally validated.
- Market abuse surveillance (MAR): The bank tracks and reports STORs (suspected insider trading, market manipulation, unlawful disclosure) Group-wide using internal systems; metrics are reported by geography and are not externally validated. STORs: 121 (2024) vs 202 (2023) vs 57 (2022); 2024 breakdown—Sweden 44, Estonia 17, Latvia 55, Lithuania 5. Variations reflect, among other things, local agency focus in the Baltics in 2023.
- Payment practices (G1-6): Standard supplier payment terms are 30 days (negotiable). Average actual payment terms are 31 days; 57% of payments are within the 30-day standard, and 71% are on time per contract terms. Invoices in the Baltics are paid immediately after approval; in Sweden, on the due date. Average actual payment time is 27 days overall and 21 days for SMEs (<250 employees, identified using Moody’s data). Metrics derive from the internal invoice system covering ~90% of supplier invoices (Sweden and Baltic subsidiaries) and are not externally validated. The report discloses the number of legal proceedings regarding late payments.
text:
Swedbank has processes for conducting internal investigations of employees in the event of suspected violations of rules, including suspected bribery or corrup -
tion. If an internal investigation reveals that rules have been violated, this may 
result in actions under employment law. If a crime is suspected, it is reported to 
the police. If the investigation identifies an operational risk, the risk is reported to 
Group Human Resources & Facility Management and the relevant risk unit in 
accordance with Swedbank’s risk management procedures. The Group Human Resources & Facility Management and Group Compliance units undertake 
 quarterly follow-up of suspected cases of corruption in the Group.
Swedbank lacks data regarding employees’ convictions or fines for bribery 
and corruption in 2024, as no systematic follow-up was conducted. The Internal 
Fraud unit will develop processes to follow up if police reports lead to convictions 
regarding cases of corruption and bribery. The metrics are not validated by 
another external body.
The table entitled Market surveillance according to the Market Abuse 
 Regulation (MAR) presents information about suspected market abuse. Financial 
actors are obliged to report suspicions of market abuse in the form of insider 
trading, market manipulation and unlawful disclosure of insider information. Swedbank uses several different systems to support measurement of the 
number of STOR (Suspicious Transaction and Order Report), as the official term 
for a notification of suspected market abuse to competent authorities under 
MAR. These STOR metrics cover the entire Group and are reported separately by 
geographical area within Swedbank’s home market countries. No external infor-
mation is used to calculate the number of STOR. The metrics are not validated by 
another external body.

heading: 7.1.5 Payment practices, G1-6

  - Metrics are not externally validated.

Swedbank's standard 30-day payment terms apply to contracted suppliers, 
 irrespective of size. The terms may be subject to negotiation and thereby differ 
between contracts. The average actual payment terms on invoices are 31 days. 
This is regulated in the Purchasing Instruction, internal training programmes and 
information on the intranet. Swedbank also uses standardised payment terms to 
manage invoices internally before they are due for payment. 
The ratio of payments made within the 30-day standard is 57 percent. The 
number of payments made on time, based on the invoice’s current terms, is 71 
percent. In the Baltic countries, invoices are paid immediately after approval, and 
in Sweden, after approval they are paid on the due date. Payment practices are calculated based on the Group’s invoice management system. Swedbank on 
average pays its suppliers within 27 days. For small and medium-sized enter -
prises, the figure is 21 days. To determine which suppliers are small or medi-um-sized, information is obtained from Moody’s. 
In the table entitled Payment practices, Swedbank presents information about 
payment terms, in particular with regard to late payments to small and medium  -
sized enterprises. The purpose is to provide transparency on the agreed payment 
terms and the average actual payment time, in particular with regard to late pay-
ments to small and medium-sized enterprises. Swedbank uses internal data 
about supplier invoices to measure payment times. External data on the number 
of employees at suppliers is used to produce the metric for small and medium  -
sized enterprises. Companies by less than 250 employees have been categorized as small or medium sized. Only those companies for which Swedbank can obtain 
information and thus determine whether they are small or medium-sized are 
included when the respective KPIs broken down into small and medium-sized 
enterprises are presented. The metrics presented are collected from the Group’s 
managemnet invoice system based on circa 90 per cent of supplier’s invoices to 
Swedbank. The data includes supplier invoices addressed to Swedbank and the 
Baltic subsidiaries. The metrics are not validated by another external body.

heading: 7.2.2.1 Entity-specific information
start_phrase: Swedbank plays a central role in the financial system through its provision of ser- vices related to payments, financing, investments and financial advice.
summary:

Bribery/corruption disclosures are in G1-3 and G1-4; cybersecurity is covered in note G3, section 3.4.

text:
Entity-specific information
Swedbank plays a central role in the financial system through its provision of ser-
vices related to payments, financing, investments and financial advice. Financial 
crime is a widespread societal problem, to which the banking sector is exposed 
through its commercial operations. To investigate and determine whether finan-
cial crime constitutes a material sustainability topic for Swedbank, work was 
undertaken as part of the double materiality assessment in which internal 
experts gave their opinions and assessments, taking into account input from 
stakeholders and the results from analyses and surveys. Experience from the Group’s current work and historical shortcomings regarding money laundering 
were also included in this work.
Financial crime was assessed as material for Swedbank and the area is 
reported as entity-specific. Any deficiencies in Swedbank’s processes and con-
trols to prevent money laundering, financing of terrorism and fraud may have a 
negative impact on customers, society and other stakeholder groups. This can 
also pose a financial risk through reduced trust, fines and sanctions. More infor-mation about work to prevent financial crime can be found in the risk note, 
 section 3.7.

Policies

Fraud

title: Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
heading: 7.2.3.1 Money laundering, financial sanctions, corruption and facilitation of tax evasion
start_phrase: Swedbank works actively to identify and prevent all forms of financial crime where Swedbank is used for illegal transactions using the proceeds from criminal activity or for transfers intended to finance terrorism.
summary:
The excerpt outlines Swedbank’s comprehensive approach to preventing financial crime and fraud.

- Scope and commitment: Addresses money laundering, terrorist financing, financial sanctions violations or circumventions, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion. Emphasizes regulatory, systemic, and moral obligations, including actions within Swedbank and downstream in the value chain.
- Risk-based framework: Enterprise-wide identification and assessment of financial crime risks driving controls. Core components include customer due diligence and risk assessment, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting, and sanctions screening of customers and transactions.
- Training and culture: Strong focus on compliance culture supported by mandatory training for all employees and tailored, risk-based programs for higher-risk roles and areas.
- Technology enablement: Ongoing investment in tools and systems to enhance sanctions screening and monitoring, strengthened in response to geopolitical developments, particularly Russia’s war against Ukraine.
- Collaboration: Active participation with Swedish law enforcement and other banks, including SAMLIT Financial Crime Prevention and multiple information-sharing initiatives to improve understanding and operational effectiveness.
- Fraud strategy: Three-tier approach—prevent, detect, investigate—backed by enhanced product and channel security, reinforced transaction monitoring, and streamlined processes. A dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme coordinates efforts, targets reduced customer losses, and ensures implementation of the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s industry-wide measures (aimed for full implementation by end-2025). Support for affected customers includes stopping ongoing fraud, recovering funds, and established complaint handling for unauthorized transactions.
- Industry coordination on fraud: Joint initiatives among major Swedish banks, the Swedish Bankers’ Association, and SAMLIT to share fraud trends, modus operandi, and assess the impact of implemented measures.
- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite: Low risk appetite for financial crime formalized through internal regulations. While Swedbank does not publish measurable outcome metrics, effectiveness is followed up internally. Group Compliance independently monitors regulatory compliance risks; the AML Officer for Controlling and Reporting (OCR) within Group Compliance reports to the Board quarterly and annually. Internal rules define prohibited activities, higher-risk circumstances requiring enhanced measures, and explicit control responsibilities for risk owners.
- Data-driven risk assessment: Annual, comprehensive assessments across customers, products, geographies, and channels, with applications that allow risk owners to continuously monitor alignment with risk appetite.
- 2024 fraud trends: Overall fraud remained high but declined in H1 2024 versus the prior year; customer losses also decreased, attributed to stronger controls, processes, and greater public awareness. Notable decline in vishing/smishing; increase in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.
text:
Swedbank works actively to identify and prevent all forms of financial crime 
where Swedbank is used for illegal transactions using the proceeds from criminal 
activity or for transfers intended to finance terrorism. Swedbank and its senior 
management take their work against financial crime seriously. The Group has 
regulatory, systemic and moral obligations towards its customers, shareholders 
and society at large to maintain effective and robust measures to prevent and 
protect its systems, products and services from being misused for criminal pur-
poses. As one of the biggest actors in the Nordic and Baltic countries, Swedbank has developed proactive measures that are applied to prevent financial crime, 
both in its own operations and downstream in the value chain. This enables the 
Group to meet its commitments and ensure an approach that is adapted to and 
aligned with the risks of financial crime to which Swedbank is exposed through 
its operations. This is Swedbank’s response to the challenges posed by financial 
crime and aims to support the continuous improvement and development of the 
measures taken for the effective management of risks relating to money launder -
ing, financing of terrorism, violation or circumvention of financial sanctions, 
 bribery and corruption, and the facilitation of tax evasion. These actions are 
 continuously adapted and updated on the basis of new risks or needs arising 
from changes in the world around us.
Swedbank works continuously with developing internal processes, routines 
and controls linked to the prevention of financial crime. Key elements are actions for customer due diligence and customer risk assessment, transaction monitor -
ing and regulatory reporting of suspected money laundering and financing of 
 terrorism, as well as sanction screening of customers and transactions. 
A key starting point for this in Swedbank’s own operations is the identification 
and understanding of the risks to which the Group is exposed to, and Swedbank 
has therefore established a robust and sophisticated risk assessment that forms 
the basis for and informs the action taken. This ensures an appropriate and risk-
based approach. Another important element is the combination of training and 
a compliance culture, both of which are crucial factors in the effective manage-
ment of risks linked to financial crime. Swedbank places great emphasis on 
ensuring that all employees receive the training and information they need, nec-essary for their specific roles and responsibilities. Beyond basic training, which is 
intended for all employees, a customised training program is developed based on 
identified risks. This program aims to strengthen areas with the greatest need for 
knowledge and those facing significant risks. Training is essential for developing 
and maintaining a strong compliance culture in Swedbank. The ability of employ -
ees to manage risks is essential for effectively combating financial crime. 
Swedbank also invests in technical development in its own operations that 
enables, streamlines and facilitates appropriate working methods. Technical 
developments are crucial in relation to combating financial sanctions and the 
work to ensure that Swedbank does not violate financial sanctions or help cir-
cumvent financial sanction regimes. Given the prevailing geopolitical situation, 
not least through Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the conditions have 
changed and the challenges in this area have increased. Swedbank works contin -
uously to develop the Group’s ability to combat violations of financial sanctions in 
the value chain, not only by boosting awareness and overall risk management 
competence in Swedbank, but also through new technical solutions for screening 
transactions and customer relationships.
The effectiveness of Swedbank’s internal programmes also depend on ade -
quate and relevant collaboration with Swedish law enforcement agencies and 
other banks. Swedbank participates actively in SAMLIT Financial Crime Preven-
tion, a collaborative body between the police and the five largest banks in Sweden. Swedbank has also participated in and works actively on multiple infor-
mation-sharing initiatives with law enforcement agencies. Together, these exter -
nal activities and sharing initiatives provide increased understanding, knowledge and efficiency in internal activities to prevent financial crime.

title: Fraud
heading: 7.2.3.2 Fraud
start_phrase: Swedbank’s work to prevent and investigate fraud is based on three strategic levels of action: prevent, detect and investigate.
summary:
- Focus: Swedbank’s actions and preventive measures against money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions violations, bribery/corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion, plus its fraud prevention approach, governance, and observed trends.
- Risk-based framework: Robust group-wide risk assessment drives controls; continuous process, routine, and control development for CDD, customer risk assessment, transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and regulatory reporting.
- People and culture: Strong compliance culture supported by mandatory and role-specific, risk-tailored training to strengthen high-risk areas.
- Technology: Ongoing investments in systems that enhance screening and monitoring; heightened focus on sanctions compliance due to geopolitical developments, notably Russia’s war against Ukraine.
- External collaboration: Active participation in SAMLIT and other information-sharing initiatives with law enforcement and major banks to improve understanding, detection, and prevention of financial crime.
- Fraud strategy: Three-pronged approach—prevent, detect, investigate—supported by stronger product/channel security and enhanced monitoring; alignment with the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s industry-wide measures targeted for full implementation by end-2025.
- Anti-Fraud Programme: Bank-wide coordination to reduce customer losses, implement industry measures, and improve incident handling; direct customer support to stop ongoing fraud, recover funds, and manage claims.
- Governance, metrics, and oversight: Low risk appetite for financial crime; internal follow-up without publishing outcome-based targets; Group Compliance independently monitors regulatory compliance; OCR function within Group Compliance reports quarterly/annually to the Board on AML/CFT performance.
- Internal regulations: Define prohibited activities, higher-risk circumstances, required enhanced measures, and explicit controls for risk owners to maintain comprehensive oversight.
- Annual, data-driven risk assessment: Evaluates exposure by customer, product, geography, and channels; tools enable risk owners to monitor alignment with risk appetite in detail.
- 2024 trends: Overall fraud volumes and customer losses decreased in H1 2024; notable decline in vishing/smishing; rise in investment fraud; other fraud types largely stable.
text:
Fraud
Swedbank’s work to prevent and investigate fraud is based on three strategic 
levels of action: prevent, detect and investigate. These actions contribute to 
combat fraud and are continuously strengthened through enhanced product and 
channel security, reinforcement of transaction monitoring and streamlined 
related processes. In spring 2024, the Swedish Bankers’ Association, together 
with the largest Nordic banks, developed a package of measures for all banks to 
further strengthen customer protection against fraud, both in own operations and 
downstream in the value chain. The measures are to be introduced as soon as 
 possible, with the ambition of full implementation are by the end of 2025. The banking industry’s proposal outlines what banks believe other societal actors need to do to enhance their efforts against fraud.
Swedbank has long been committed to continuously enhancing customer pro-
tection against fraud through various measures. These include, for example, 
product development, monitoring of transactions and daily operations to manage 
and investigate fraud attempts and incidents, etc. A special Anti-Fraud Pro-
gramme has been initiated to help prevent fraud and increase customer protec-
tion by enabling effective collaboration between Swedbank’s various units. The programme is also responsible for following up and ensuring development 
towards Swedbank’s target of reducing customer losses as a consequence of 
fraud and ensuring that Swedbank implements the Swedish Bankers' Associa-
tion’s package of measures. 
Swedbank is continuously working to help affected customers by stopping 
 ongoing fraud, and by recovering funds and restoring affected customers’ 
accounts. If a customer has been the victim of fraud, the customer is encouraged 
to report the incident to the police and file a complaint to Swedbank about unau-
thorised transactions, which are subsequently handled according to established 
 procedures.
A joint fraud collaboration has been established between the biggest Swedish 
banks with the aim of sharing information about fraud trends and new modus operandi. The collaboration with the Swedish Bankers’ Association and SAMLIT 
Financial Crime Prevention takes place within various fraud areas and working 
groups, partly to share practical examples, experiences, and lessons from daily 
ongoing operations, and partly to follow up and evaluate the effects of the mea-
sures banks have introduced as a result of the Swedish Bankers’ Association’s 
package of measures.

title: Metrics and targets
heading: 7.2.4 Metrics and targets
start_phrase: Swedbank has a low risk appetite for financial crime.
summary:
- Focus and scope: Swedbank’s actions to prevent financial crime, including money laundering, terrorism financing, violations/circumventions of financial sanctions, bribery and corruption, and facilitation of tax evasion.
- Risk-based framework: A robust, data-driven enterprise-wide risk assessment informs customer due diligence, customer risk scoring, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting, and sanctions screening.
- Continuous improvement: Ongoing development of internal processes, routines, and controls; emphasis on combining strong compliance culture with mandatory baseline and role-specific training.
- Technology enablement: Investments in advanced screening and monitoring solutions, especially for sanctions compliance, heightened by geopolitical developments (e.g., Russia’s war against Ukraine).
- Collaboration and information sharing: Active participation in SAMLIT (with police and Sweden’s largest banks) and other initiatives; interbank fraud collaboration via the Swedish Bankers’ Association to share trends and modus operandi.
- Fraud strategy: Three-tier approach—prevent, detect, investigate—supported by stronger product/channel security, enhanced transaction monitoring, and streamlined processes. A dedicated Anti-Fraud Programme coordinates efforts, targets reduced customer losses, and implements the industry-wide package of measures slated for full rollout by end-2025.
- Customer support: Ongoing assistance to stop active fraud, recover funds, restore accounts, and guide victims to report to police and submit unauthorized transaction claims.
- Governance, metrics, and risk appetite: Low risk appetite formalized through internal regulations; Group Compliance (including the AML Officer for Controlling and Reporting, OCR) independently monitors and reports quarterly/annually to the CEO and Board. Internal rules define prohibited activities, higher-risk scenarios, and required controls. Annual, data-driven general risk assessment covers customers, products, geographies, and channels; thresholds tied to risk appetite trigger escalations; progress in fraud prevention reported to top management.
- Outcomes and trends: Overall fraud volumes and customer losses decreased in H1 2024 versus 2023, notably for vishing/smishing; investment fraud increased; other fraud types remained stable.
- Training outcomes: High completion rates for AML/CFT training (97–98% across countries in 2023–2024). Methodological notes clarify scope (e.g., PayEx, Swedbank Fastighetsbyrå) and state metrics are not externally validated.
text:
Metrics and targets
Swedbank has a low risk appetite for financial crime. Swedbank has imple -
mented internal processes for follow-up to effectively evaluate the work. Swed -
bank does not publish any measurable outcome-oriented goals to monitor the effectiveness of policies and actions in these areas, nor comparisons over time. 
Active efforts are being made to prevent Swedbank and its customers from 
being exploited or exposed to financial crime. The low risk appetite is established 
through internal regulations and is continuously monitored by Swedbank’s inde -
pendent compliance function, Group Compliance, which works with the group’s 
regulatory compliance risks. The role of officer for controlling and reporting obli -
gations (OCR), in accordance with the anti-money laundering regulations, is situ -
ated in Group Compliance. The OCR reports to the Board of Directors quarterly and 
annually on how Swedbank’s effort to prevent financial crime function in rela- tion 
to external regulations, requirements and Swedbank’s risk appetite. 
Regulations include for example, prohibited activities, customer relationships 
and  pr oducts. They also address circumstances with increased risk, necessitat -
ing special measures both before initiating a customer relationship and on an 
ongoing basis thereafter. Additionally, the regulations require explicit controls 
that the risk owner must implement to have a comprehensive risk overview of 
their area of responsibility.
The general risk assessment is conducted annually within relevant risk areas. 
The assessment is data-driven and indicates Swedbank’s risk exposure based on 
customer, product, geographical area and distribution channels. Through a data application, risk owners can continuously monitor in detail how for example a 
specific product, customer segment, and/or geography aligns with Swedbank’s 
risk appetite 
As one of Sweden’s largest banks, fraud via Swedbank’s products and services 
reflects the general development of fraud in society. Despite the fraud volume 
remaining high, a decrease was noted in the first half of 2024 compared to the 
previous year. This trend is confirmed in the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority’s statistics on payment service fraud and the Police Authority’s statis -
tics on proceeds of crime from fraud. Customer losses due to fraud in Swedbank also decreased during the year. The decrease can be assumed to be an effect of 
the bank’s work on enhanced security in products, controls and processes, as 
well as increased awareness of fraud in society. For fraud through social manipu-
lation via phone and text messages, called vishing/smishing, the decrease is par-
ticularly noticeable. On the other hand, there has been an increase in investment fraud, where fraudsters trick customers into investing in false or misleading 
investment opportunities. The levels of other types of fraud remained largely 
unchanged during the year.

summary:
- Purpose and scope: A comprehensive index (IRO‑2) showing which ESRS disclosure requirements Swedbank covers in its 2024 Sustainability Report, where each appears (page references), and how they link to the bank’s materiality process (IRO‑1). It also maps required datapoints from related EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3, EU Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law) and flags where items are included, not material, not applicable, or subject to phase‑in.
- General information and governance: Disclosures on the basis of preparation, specific circumstances, strategy/business model/value chain (SBM‑1/2/3), stakeholder interests (including S1 and S4 perspectives), processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO‑1), governance roles (GOV‑1/2), integration of sustainability in incentives (GOV‑3), due diligence statement (GOV‑4), and internal controls over sustainability reporting (GOV‑5).
- Environmental (E1 focus): Transition plan for climate change mitigation, climate‑related policies, actions/resources, targets, and metrics; reporting of Scope 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions and intensity; alignment with MDR policy/action/target/metric minimums; several energy and physical risk datapoints noted as not material, not applicable, or phased in.
- Social:
  - S1 (own workforce): Policies, engagement, remediation channels, actions and effectiveness, targets, and a wide set of metrics (diversity, adequate wages, training/skills, health and safety, work‑life balance, remuneration/pay gap), with MDR linkages.
  - S4 (consumers and end‑users): Policies, engagement, remediation, actions and effectiveness, targets, and metrics.
  - Selected S1/S2/S3 datapoints on human rights, child/forced labour risks, accidents, and grievance mechanisms included; many value chain and incident‑type datapoints marked not material or phase‑in.
- Governance (G1): Business conduct and culture, supplier relationship management, anti‑corruption and anti‑bribery prevention/detection, incidents, payment practices; related policies, actions, targets and metrics; references to whistleblower protection and fines.
- Company‑specific: Financial crime prevention presented under MDR policy/action/target/metric structure.
- Cross‑regulatory mapping: A detailed table links ESRS datapoints to SFDR Annexes, Pillar 3/Article 449a templates, Benchmark Regulation (Paris‑aligned/Climate Transition Benchmarks), and EU Climate Law, indicating where Swedbank reports each item, and explicitly noting:
  - Not applicable areas (e.g., involvement in controversial weapons, certain fossil fuel/chemical/tobacco activities; several E1 physical risk portfolio metrics under phase‑in).
  - Not material topics (e.g., several pollution, water/marine, biodiversity/ecosystem, and waste datapoints; some human rights incident indicators; GHG removals/carbon credits).
  - Phase‑in items for physical risk exposures and some safety metrics.
- Navigation aid: Page references throughout the tables enable direct location of each disclosure within the Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 (Board of Directors’ report section).

title: Tables according to the EU Taxonomy regulation - Introduction
heading: 9 Tables according to the EU Taxonomy regulation
start_phrase: The EU Taxonomy-specific tables for credit institutions are tables 0 to 5 below.
summary: This section introduces Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy reporting tables for credit institutions (Tables 0–5) and points to further disclosures on pages 78 and 98–99. It summarizes 2024 KPIs: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock with environmentally sustainable assets of SEK 64,290m, Turnover-based GAR 3.37% (CapEx-based 3.59%), asset coverage 73.39%, and exclusions of 34.79% (numerator) and 26.61% (denominator); GAR flow SEK 10,264m with ratios 3.08%/3.15%, 99.63% coverage, and exclusions of 53.97%/0.37%; AUM KPI SEK 32,571m; trading book SEK 96m; and a note that fees/commission income and trading book KPIs will first be reported for 2025. Detailed turnover-based GAR tables provide 2024 breakdowns by asset class and counterparty (financial and non-financial undertakings, households, etc.) and by alignment type (use of proceeds, transitional, enabling) across the six environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO): total assets SEK 2,599,066m; GAR-covered assets SEK 1,907,412m; not covered SEK 691,654m; excluded from numerator SEK 663,530m; taxonomy-eligible SEK 1,055,790m; with notable aligned exposure in households’ residential mortgages (SEK 58,221m). Off-balance sheet exposures for undertakings subject to NFRD include financial guarantees and assets under management with eligible/aligned amounts by objective. Comparative 2023 tables show total assets SEK 2,521,956m, GAR assets SEK 1,876,715m, and taxonomy-eligible SEK 1,030,626m, with aligned amounts likewise detailed (e.g., residential mortgages SEK 23,257m).

title: Assets for calculation of GAR
heading: 1. Assets for calculation of GAR
start_phrase: Capex based
summary:
- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures, capex‑based, from Swedbank’s 2024 Annual and Sustainability Report (Board of Directors’ report), with 2024 figures and 2023 comparatives.
- Scope and structure:
  - Breakdowns by EU Taxonomy environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water & Marine Resources (WTR), and (for 2024) Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention & Control (PPC), and Biodiversity & Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Segmentation of assets:
    - GAR numerator and denominator: loans and advances, debt securities and equity instruments not held for trading (HfT).
    - Assets excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator: exposures to SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD/CSRD, non‑EU counterparties not subject to NFRD/CSRD, derivatives, on‑demand interbank loans, cash and cash‑like items, and other assets (e.g., goodwill, commodities).
    - Assets not covered for GAR: central governments and supranationals, central bank exposures, and trading book.
  - Counterparty categories: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (with detail on residential mortgages, building renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral obtained.
- Metrics reported:
  - Total assets, total GAR assets, and detailed “of which” disclosures for taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned exposures by objective.
  - Taxonomy‑aligned exposures further split into use‑of‑proceeds (e.g., green bonds), transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Prominent disclosure of household mortgage exposures (loans collateralised by residential property), including taxonomy eligibility and alignment; separate identification of building renovation loans.
  - Corporate (non‑financial undertaking) exposures shown with taxonomy eligibility and alignment by objective.
- Off‑balance sheet:
  - For undertakings subject to NFRD/CSRD disclosure obligations, reporting of financial guarantees and assets under management (AUM), including “of which” debt securities and equity instruments, with taxonomy eligibility and alignment (and the same use‑of‑proceeds/enabling splits). A footnote clarifies totals cover overall volumes, not only holdings in NFRD/CSRD companies.
- Year‑over‑year view:
  - 2024 tables provide comprehensive figures across objectives, with small volumes in CE/PPC/BIO; 2023 comparatives are presented for CCM/CCA/WTR and total, enabling users to observe changes in taxonomy‑eligible and aligned exposures between years.

title: GAR sector information
heading: 2. GAR sector information
start_phrase: Turnover based
summary:
- Source and scope: Extract from Swedbank’s Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 (Board of Directors’ report), section “2. GAR sector information,” presenting EU Taxonomy-aligned Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures for 2024.
- Framework and structure:
  - Breakdown by NACE sector codes.
  - Split by client type: Non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD vs. SMEs/other non‑financial corporates not subject to NFRD.
  - Two performance metrics: turnover-based and capex-based.
  - Coverage of all six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each sector and objective: Gross carrying amount (SEKm) and “of which environmentally sustainable.”
- Turnover-based highlights:
  - Comprehensive sector-by-sector tables for CCM/CCA/WTR and for CE/PPC/BIO, with totals.
  - Aggregate total shows SEKm 38,981 gross carrying amount and SEKm 5,774 environmentally sustainable.
  - Significant taxonomy-aligned turnover appears in:
    - Production of electricity (NACE 35.11) with a large CCM-aligned share.
    - Renting and operating of own or leased real estate (68.20), notably CCM and CCA-aligned amounts.
    - Manufacture of railway locomotives and rolling stock (30.20), and selected machinery/equipment categories (e.g., lifting/handling equipment, non‑domestic cooling and ventilation).
    - Pipeline transport (49.50) showing full alignment in the disclosed amount.
    - Waste collection (38.11) contributing under CE/PPC.
  - Many sectors show zero or minimal alignment for CCA and WTR; electricity transmission (35.12) shows zero alignment.
- Capex-based highlights:
  - Parallel sector-by-sector disclosure for CCM/CCA/WTR and CE/PPC/BIO, with totals.
  - Aggregate total shows SEKm 38,981 gross carrying amount and SEKm 9,985 environmentally sustainable, indicating higher capex alignment than turnover alignment.
  - Largest capex alignment in:
    - Production of electricity (35.11) with substantial CCM-aligned capex.
    - Real estate activities (68.20) across CCM and CCA.
    - Selected manufacturing of equipment and transport (e.g., instruments and appliances, cooling/ventilation equipment, railway rolling stock, medical and dental instruments).
    - Waste collection (38.11) under CCM and contributions under CE/PPC.
  - Several activities (e.g., electricity transmission 35.12) remain at zero aligned capex.
- Overall observations:
  - Climate Change Mitigation dominates the environmentally sustainable amounts; Adaptation, Water, and the four non‑climate objectives (CE, PPC, BIO) are smaller and concentrated in a few sectors.
  - Alignment is largely concentrated in NFRD‑subject non‑financial corporates; SMEs/other corporates often show limited or zero aligned amounts.
  - Detailed, auditable mapping of exposures to EU Taxonomy via NACE codes supports transparency of Swedbank’s green financing footprint by sector and objective.

title: GAR KPI stock
heading: 3. GAR KPI stock
start_phrase: Turnover based
summary:
- Section overview: Presents Swedbank’s Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI stock for both turnover-based and capex-based indicators, covering 2024 and 2023, as part of the Annual and Sustainability Report 2024 (Board of Directors’ report).
- Scope and methodology: Shows the proportion of total covered assets that are EU Taxonomy-eligible and Taxonomy-aligned across all six environmental objectives (Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and marine resources, Circular economy, Pollution prevention and control, Biodiversity and ecosystems). Breakdowns include “of which” categories for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities. Figures are reported for assets included in both the numerator and denominator.
- Portfolio breakdown: Disaggregates by asset type and counterparty category—loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds bonds), equity instruments; financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), and certain local government exposures.
- 2024 turnover-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.71% of covered assets; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 3.37%.
  - Alignment is largely driven by the household mortgage portfolio (households: eligible 54.47%, aligned 3.05%).
  - Non-financial undertakings: eligible ≈ 0.96%, aligned ≈ 0.30; financial undertakings: eligible ≈ 0.28%, aligned ≈ 0.02.
  - Minimal exposure to CE/PPC/BIO objectives (eligible roughly 0.12/0.02/0.01; aligned near 0.00–0.01).
  - “Of which” amounts for use-of-proceeds and transitional/enabling activities are very small; coverage of total assets in denominator ≈ 73.39%.
- 2024 capex-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.98%; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 3.59%.
  - Households still dominate aligned share (3.05%); non-financial undertakings aligned ≈ 0.52%.
  - Very small use-of-proceeds (~0.02) and transitional (~0.13) shares; total assets coverage ≈ 73.39%.
- 2023 turnover-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.73%; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 1.36%.
  - Households aligned ≈ 1.24%; non-financial undertakings eligible ≈ 0.61%, aligned ≈ 0.12.
  - Use-of-proceeds and transitional/enabling negligible; total assets coverage ≈ 74.42%.
  - Tables for CE/PPC/BIO are largely blank/immaterial for 2023.
- 2023 capex-based highlights:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible ≈ 55.89%; taxonomy-aligned ≈ 1.41%.
  - Small “of which” amounts (use-of-proceeds and transitional each ~0.06); households aligned ≈ 1.24%; non-financial undertakings eligible ≈ 0.73%, aligned ≈ 0.16.
  - Total assets coverage ≈ 74.42%.
- Overall message: The GAR is predominantly driven by the mortgage book; taxonomy alignment increases from 2023 to 2024 in both turnover- and capex-based views, while exposures to other environmental objectives beyond climate remain very limited, and use-of-proceeds/transitional/enabling shares are minor.

title: GAR KPI flow
heading: 4. GAR KPI flow
start_phrase: Turnover based
summary:
- The section presents Swedbank’s EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI flow for 2024, showing how much of the bank’s covered assets are taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned.
- Two calculation perspectives are disclosed:
  - Turnover-based
  - CapEx-based
- Results are reported across all six environmental objectives:
  - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM)
  - Climate Change Adaptation (CCA)
  - Water and Marine Resources (WTR)
  - Circular Economy (CE)
  - Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC)
  - Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO)
- For each perspective and objective, the tables show:
  - Proportion of total covered assets that are taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned
  - “Of which” breakdowns: use-of-proceeds, transitional, enabling
  - Coverage of total assets
  - Scope: assets included in both numerator and denominator of the GAR (loans and advances, debt securities including use-of-proceeds bonds, equity instruments not held for trading)
- The exposure breakdown covers:
  - Financial undertakings (credit institutions and other financial corporations, including investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings)
  - Non-financial undertakings
  - Households (including residential mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
  - Local government financing and collateral obtained
- Key 2024 highlights (Turnover-based):
  - Total taxonomy-eligible share: 35.61% of covered assets
  - Total taxonomy-aligned share: 3.08%, of which 0.02 pp use-of-proceeds and 0.10 pp transitional
  - Households dominate eligibility and alignment: 34.54 pp eligible and 2.73 pp aligned, driven by residential mortgages (34.34 pp eligible; 2.73 pp aligned)
  - Non-financial undertakings: 1.04 pp eligible; 0.35 pp aligned
  - Financial undertakings: 0.03 pp eligible; 0.01 pp aligned
  - Asset coverage: 99.63% of total assets
  - By objective: climate-related categories drive almost all eligibility; CE, PPC, and BIO exposures are minimal (low basis points)
- Key 2024 highlights (CapEx-based):
  - Total taxonomy-eligible share: 35.91% of covered assets
  - Total taxonomy-aligned share: 3.15%, of which 0.03 pp use-of-proceeds, 0.13 pp transitional, and 0.01 pp enabling
  - Households: 34.54 pp eligible; 2.73 pp aligned (largely residential mortgages)
  - Non-financial undertakings: 1.30 pp eligible; 0.42 pp aligned
  - Financial undertakings: 0.07 pp eligible; ~0.00 pp aligned
  - Asset coverage: 99.63% of total assets
  - CE, PPC, and BIO remain negligible under this view as well
- Overall takeaway:
  - Swedbank’s GAR is predominantly driven by residential mortgage exposures.
  - Taxonomy alignment remains in the low single digits, with slightly higher figures under the CapEx-based approach.
  - Non-climate objectives (CE, PPC, BIO) currently contribute marginally to eligibility and alignment.
